Quantum Prime--Zeta: A Critical-Line Dark-State Quantum Error Sensor on Live IBM Heron Processors
authors: Waleed SalahEldin Elsayed Elgamal
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Fault-tolerant discrete quantum error correction (QEC) codes impose severe physical-to-logical qubit overheads that remain prohibitive for near-term superconducting processors suffering from coherent calibration drift, idle dephasing, and correlated hardware noise bursts. Building directly upon our machine-verified Lean 4 uniqueness theorem for theantisymmetric Dirichlet $\eta$-functional (`DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24549046`), we construct and experimentally validate a hardware-native 4-qubit Ising $R_{ZZ}$ spectator interferometer clocked at the first non-trivial Riemann zero ($t_1 \approx 14.134725$). By Walsh--Hadamard phase decomposition onto linear heavy-hex topology, the interferometer compiles to depth 27 with only 8 two-qubit $\mathrm{CZ}$ gates on IBM Heron processors---a $14.8\times$ depth reduction over generic multi-controlled synthesis---achieving $1.000000$ unitary fidelity and $0/20{,}000$ ideal critical-line false alarms. Executed live on three 156-qubit IBM Heron superconducting processors (`ibm_fez`, `ibm_kingston`, and `ibm_marrakesh`) using dynamical decoupling, Pauli twirling, and unitary-only mid-circuit FPGA dynamic feed-forward (`if_test((c_syn,0b0100))`), the spectator sensor achieves a $0.04\%$ ($3/8{,}192$ shots) critical-line dark-state error floor and consistently separates coherent algorithmic trajectories from hardware error tails across five canonical algorithms: Shor's factoring algorithm ($97.41\%$ period-4 Fourier peak fidelity on `ibm_fez`; $48.96\%$ factoring yield on `ibm_kingston`), QAOA Max-Cut ($55.25\% \rightarrow 75.05\%$ optimal cut probability on `ibm_marrakesh`), Grover's search ($39.64\% \rightarrow 57.91\%$ target state recovery on `ibm_fez`), Bernstein--Vazirani ($88.17\% \rightarrow 91.84\%$ single-shot recovery on `ibm_fez`), and VQE Transverse-Field Ising ground-state estimation. Finally, statevector scaling benchmarks demonstrate $93.6\%$ VQE energy error reduction, $+102.9\%$ deep QAOA optimal-cut gain, and blind 39-qubit Shor period discovery for semiprimes $5353 = 53 \times 101$, $2491 = 47 \times 53$, and $4747 = 47 \times 101$.

title: Harnessing quantum-enhanced Hybrid Transformer Model for predicting long-term wind energy losses: a multimodal fusion approach to climate-driven variability
authors: M. Kowsigan, Krishnesh Mathur, Yashvi Diya Singh, Armaan Rashid Pathan
abstract: Wind energy has become increasingly important in addressing the world’s energy issues. However, estimating long-term energy losses from climate change has been a challenge. This study presents a Quantum-Enhanced Hybrid Transformer Model for predicting long-term wind energy losses resulting from climate variability. In contrast to conventional methods that primarily focus on short-term forecasting, the proposed approach combines Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA), weather and climate data via quantum feature encoding and transformer attention procedures. The proposed model relies on quantum computing principles to process multimodal data simultaneously, thus considering complex interdependencies of climate changes and wind energy output. The observed experimental results show better performance than conventional machine learning and deep learning techniques in several evaluation metrics. The model, presented with the wind farm data, provides steady projections for the short-term (2030–2040) and long-term (2050–2079) periods, alongside well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. Therefore, the proposed approach provides meaningful information for renewable energy planning in different climate scenarios.

title: Boosting quantum teleportation fidelity via multistate loss functions and optimized measurements
authors: Josiah Mccarty, Allison Brattley, Kunal K. Das
journal: Journal of Physics B Atomic Molecular and Optical Physics
abstract: In a recent paper, we developed a machine learning algorithm for quantum teleporation that can be applied to a broad set of states, measurements and unitary operators across platforms. Here, we present an improved algorithm that shows significant increases in teleporation fidelity for diverse spin coherent systems. This is achieved by replacing the single state loss function with a multistate one, and the inclusion of optimization of the measurement variables.

title: Trace-distance binary tree AdaBoost for trainable quantum multi-class classification
authors: Xin Wang, Yabo Wang, Rebing Wu
abstract: We propose a Trace-distance binary Tree AdaBoost (TTA) multi-class quantum classifier, a practical pipeline for quantum multi-class classification that combines quantum-aware reductions with ensemble learning to improve trainability and resource efficiency. TTA builds a hierarchical binary tree by choosing, at each internal node, the bipartition that heuristically maximizes the trace distance between average quantum states; each node trains a binary AdaBoost ensemble of shallow variational quantum base learners. By confining intrinsically hard, small trace distance distinctions to small node-specific datasets and combining weak shallow learners via AdaBoost, TTA distributes capacity across many small submodels rather than one deep circuit, mitigating barren-plateau and optimization failures without sacrificing generalization. Empirically TTA achieves top test accuracy (≈ 100%) among quantum and classical baselines, is robust to common quantum errors, and realizes aggregate systems with almost 10 000 cumulative layers and 0.2 M parameters, implemented as many shallow circuits. Our results are empirical and implementable on near-term platforms, providing a resource-efficient route to scalable multi-class quantum machine learning.

title: Obtaining the Negative of an Image Using Quantum Programming with Python/Qiskit
authors: Hasan suay Tanın, Davut KESEN, Mehmet Şahin
abstract: This study investigates the implementation of grayscale color inversion (negation), a fundamental image processing operation in digital images, using quantum computing principles. While the conversion of 8-bit grayscale (0–255) pixels to their opposite values is performed using a logical NOT operation in classical computing, this operation is modeled in quantum computing using a Pauli-X gate defined on qubits. An implementation is developed using the Qiskit 2.x library to preserve the original resolution of the images and manage simulation complexity with a grayscale value set (2⁸ = 256 tones). The study demonstrates the mathematical equivalence of basic quantum gate operations with classical image processing operators, while also highlighting the limitations of quantum simulations on classical hardware and the necessity of superposition-based image representation models (NEQR/FRQI) required for true quantum advantage. In conclusion, this hybrid approach provides a practical basis for the development and validation of more complex quantum computer vision algorithms before the widespread availability of fault-tolerant physical quantum hardware. In this study, each pixel value of the image was sequentially sent to a quantum circuit. In this quantum circuit, the incoming grayscale level was processed using the 256 - incoming_value operation, and a negative of the image was created by forming a matrix again. A QLUT table can be created to perform this task in a shorter time.

title: A Comprehensive Survey on Emerging Trends in Quantum Computing: From Nisq to Fault-Tolerant Systems
authors: K. Malathi, R. Mariappan, M. Vikram, S. Vinothayani, M. Vinoth, N. Vimalraj
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Quantum computing is rapidly evolving from noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices toward fully fault-tolerant architectures capable of reliable large-scale computation. This survey presents a comprehensive analysis of emerging trends shaping this transition, focusing on hardware advancements, algorithmic innovations, and error correction strategies. NISQ systems, while limited by decoherence and gate imperfections, have enabled significant progress in hybrid quantum–classical models, variational algorithms, and quantum simulation tasks. Recent developments in quantum error mitigation and fault-tolerant coding schemes, including surface codes and logical qubit optimization, are paving the way for scalable quantum processors. Additionally, progress in quantum hardware technologies such as superconducting circuits, trapped ions, and photonic systems is accelerating practical deployment. This study further highlights key challenges including noise resilience, qubit scalability, and resource overhead. Finally, we outline future directions toward achieving robust fault-tolerant quantum computing and its potential impact on cryptography, optimization, and machine learning applications across scientific and industrial domains.

title: Sparse QPD Estimates Amino Acid Pair Energies on a Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor
authors: inquantio
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Researchers proposed sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), a method that measures only selected time points of a quantum autocorrelation signal and reconstructs the remaining information using classical computation. Numerical simulations involving 23 configurations of an arginine–tryptophan pair showed that sparse QPD could reduce the total quantum evolution cost by approximately tenfold compared with conventional QPD under the tested conditions. Using the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor, the researchers implemented a reduced molecular electronic-structure model with three qubits and circuits containing up to 448 two-qubit gates. Some energy estimates met the chemical-accuracy threshold, but the experiments did not establish consistent accuracy across all runs or a reduction in actual hardware execution time. [Quantum Biology Society] The amino acids that make up proteins interact through electrostatic forces, hydrogen bonds, and the electronic structures of their molecular groups. These interactions influence how proteins fold, assemble, and perform biological functions. In particular, interactions between charged amino acid residues and aromatic side chains depend on both their spatial arrangement and the distribution of electrons around them. Accurately describing these interactions requires quantum mechanical calculations of electronic energies. However, performing high-accuracy calculations repeatedly for many different molecular configurations can be computationally expensive. Quantum computers offer a possible alternative because they can represent quantum states of electrons using quantum circuits. Yet current quantum processors face an important limitation. To estimate molecular energies, they must repeatedly execute circuits and collect statistical information from measurements that are affected by noise. A collaborative research team from ETH Zurich in Switzerland and the University of Copenhagen in Denmark developed an approach intended to reduce this measurement burden. The researchers, Davide Castaldo, Marvin Kronenberger, Marek Miller, Sélène Forget, Gemma C. Solomon, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen, Matthias Christandl, and Markus Reiher, proposed sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD). Davide Castaldo, Matthias Christandl, and Markus Reiher were listed as corresponding authors. The researchers applied their method to electronic-structure calculations involving an interacting arginine–tryptophan amino acid pair. They combined numerical simulations with experiments on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. Their results suggested that quantum measurement costs could be reduced by exploiting the limited number of important frequencies present in molecular quantum signals. The study, titled "Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor," was posted to arXiv on November 17, 2026, as a preprint that has not yet undergone peer review. ■ Recovering Molecular Energies Without Measuring Every Quantum Signal Calculating the electronic energy of a molecule is fundamentally a quantum mechanical problem. Electrons do not occupy arbitrary energies. Instead, the electronic Hamiltonian, a mathematical operator describing the system's energy, possesses a set of allowed energy eigenvalues. The lowest of these values is the ground-state energy. Determining this energy accurately is important for understanding molecular stability, electronic interactions, and chemical reactivity. Quantum algorithms attempt to estimate these eigenvalues by preparing electronic quantum states and examining how they evolve. One established approach is quantum phase estimation (QPE). QPE extracts energy information from the phase accumulated during quantum time evolution. However, conventional implementations can require deep quantum circuits and substantial computational resources. These requirements are difficult to satisfy on present-day quantum processors, where errors accumulate as additional gates are executed. An alternative approach, quantum prolate diagonalization (QPD), uses a hybrid strategy involving quantum measurements and classical signal processing. Rather than extracting energy information entirely within a quantum circuit, QPD measures a quantity known as the autocorrelation function. The autocorrelation function describes how closely a quantum state resembles its original state after evolving for a particular amount of time. It can be expressed as: C(t) = ⟨Φ|e−iHt|Φ⟩ Here, Φ represents the initial quantum state, H is the electronic Hamiltonian, and t represents the evolution time in the chosen units. Different electronic energy eigenstates contribute oscillations with characteristic frequencies to this signal. Consequently, the autocorrelation function contains information about the electronic energies of the molecular system. A useful analogy is identifying musical notes from a recording. Different notes produce oscillations at different frequencies. By analyzing the recorded sound, one can identify the frequencies present without directly observing the instruments that produced them. Similarly, quantum algorithms can infer molecular electronic energies from the oscillatory behavior of a measured autocorrelation signal. QPD employs special mathematical filter functions known as prolate spheroidal wave functions. These filters concentrate information within a selected energy range while suppressing contributions from unwanted frequencies. The filtered information is then used to construct and solve a generalized eigenvalue problem. This allows the researchers to estimate molecular energy eigenvalues from the measured quantum signals. However, conventional QPD still requires a substantial number of measurements. The autocorrelation function is sampled at many distinct time points. Each time point generally requires a corresponding quantum circuit that simulates molecular time evolution for that duration. As the desired time window becomes longer and the sampling grid becomes denser, the number of distinct circuits increases. This creates a measurement bottleneck. Even when each circuit is relatively shallow, executing many different circuits repeatedly can consume considerable quantum computing resources. The researchers therefore asked whether every time point needed to be measured directly. Their solution was to combine QPD with compressed sensing. Compressed sensing is a signal-reconstruction method that can recover information from a relatively small number of measurements when the underlying signal possesses a suitable structure. For example, a signal containing only a few important frequency components may be reconstructed without measuring every point in its time evolution. The researchers exploited a similar property of molecular autocorrelation functions. If the prepared initial state has most of its weight concentrated on only a few electronic energy eigenstates, the measured signal is dominated by a small number of frequencies. The corresponding data can be organized into a Hankel matrix. A Hankel matrix is a structured matrix in which elements along each anti-diagonal share the same value. For a signal dominated by relatively few independent frequency components, the associated Hankel matrix can be approximated by a low-rank matrix. Low rank means that the matrix contains substantially fewer independent information components than its full dimensions might suggest. This property makes it possible to reconstruct missing data from a limited collection of measured values. The researchers implemented this reconstruction using a method called Hankel-structured Newton-like descent (HSNLD). Instead of measuring the autocorrelation function at every time point, sparse QPD randomly selects a subset of measurement times. The quantum processor executes circuits only for these selected points. The resulting measurements are then transferred to a classical computer. HSNLD reconstructs the missing parts of the autocorrelation signal by exploiting its approximate low-rank structure. Finally, the completed signal is processed using the original QPD procedure to estimate the electronic energies. The theoretical advantage concerns the number of distinct measurement points. For a time grid containing Ns positive-time sampling points, conventional QPD requires a number of measured points proportional to O(Ns). Under the assumptions used in the proposed compressed-sensing approach, sparse QPD reduces this requirement to O(log Ns). This means that the number of directly measured points can grow much more slowly than the size of the complete time grid. However, the improvement is not guaranteed for every molecular system. Successful reconstruction depends on the spectral properties of the initial state and the accuracy of the measurements. In particular, the method works most favorably when the initial state has a large overlap with the target ground state. The researchers used the Hartree–Fock state as the initial state. Hartree–Fock theory approximates the electronic wavefunction using a single Slater determinant. For many weakly correlated molecular systems, this state provides a relatively good approximation to the true electronic ground state. In the small molecular models used in the study, the squared overlap between the Hartree–Fock state and the ground state was approximately 0.99. This meant that the ground-state contribution dominated the autocorrelation signal. The researchers therefore used a rank-one approximation for signal reconstruction. However, molecules with strong electronic correlation may require several electronic configurations to describe their ground states accurately. title: Regulation of Quantum Communications in the Republic of Singapore
authors: Aleksey Minbaleev, К. С. Евсиков
abstract: The Republic of Singapore is a global leader in the adoption of digital innovations. This makes its legal system an important subject of study for domestic specialists in the field of information law. The paper analyzes the legal mechanisms used in this country to support quantum communication technologies. Having examined the influence of Singapore's legal institutions on this technology, the authors identified a unique combination of strict legal regulation with the search for a balance between human rights and the interests of digital technology developers. This approach is reflected, among other things, in regulatory legal acts on personal data protection, information security, and cryptography. In implementing quantum communications, the Republic of Singapore has followed a path typical for most countries by adopting a National Quantum Strategy and stipulating in it the need to prepare the public and private sectors for the quantum threat. To develop the quantum communications infrastructure, the state has subsidized the creation of the National Quantum-Secure Network, which, to date, lacks clear legal regulation at the national level. Singapore has adopted numerous official instruments that encourage the experimental implementation of quantum communications in various fields. For the financial sector, Singapore's regulator has introduced a regulatory sandbox that enables banks to implement quantum-secure data protection technologies. These actions by public authorities are accompanied by official reports, made publicly available, which enhances business and societal trust in the technology. In Russia, similar measures are not being implemented, which undoubtedly affects the development of this innovation. The conducted analysis shows that Singapore's experience can become an integral part of the legislation of any country seeking to succeed in the field of quantum communications technologies.

title: Quantum Computing Is Coming: All Encryption Is at Risk
authors: Şevki Işıklı
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Quantum computers, drawing on properties such as superposition and entanglement, have the potential to outperform classical computers on certain computational problems. This capability threatens widely used systems such as RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography while opening new possibilities for secure communication through quantum key distribution and quantum-resistant encryption. The prospect that encrypted data collected today could be decrypted in the future makes it necessary for individuals, companies, and governments to strengthen their security measures now. The article argues that if access to quantum technologies becomes concentrated in the hands of a few large companies or countries, it could deepen the existing digital divide and create a quantum divide. For Türkiye, investing in quantum research and participating in international initiatives are therefore important both for safeguarding its cybersecurity and for maintaining a voice in global competition.

title: Ensemble Basis-Free Coherence for Quantum Communication
authors: Aleksei Kodukhov
abstract: The resource theory of coherence quantifies the quantum properties of states and their role in quantum information processing. Extending coherence theory to ensembles, the natural objects in quantum communication, remains an active research direction, with their operational potential still being explored. In this work, we establish a maximally coherent ensemble in every finite dimension: the continuous ensemble of pure states distributed according to the normalized Haar measure attains the tight upper bound on basis-free relative entropy ensemble coherence. We then prove that, for two equiprobable pure states, ensemble coherence bounds the conditional informational advantage of unambiguous state discrimination over the Holevo quantity, weighted by the probability of a conclusive outcome. Finally, for a family of Bob’s symmetric USD measurements in qubit B92 QKD, we show that Alice’s initial ensemble coherence upper-bounds the asymptotic secret key rate when Bob’s conclusive outcomes are error-free. These results give ensemble coherence a quantitative operational meaning in quantum communication and cryptography.

title: Protein Language Models Improve Quantum Annealing-Based Protein Sequence Search
authors: inquantio
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: By combining protein sequence representations from a pretrained protein language model with a binary variational autoencoder, the researchers improved the accuracy of encoding protein variants into 64 binary variables and reconstructing their amino acid sequences. Using a real D-Wave Advantage System 6 quantum annealer, the researchers optimized three protein sequence design tasks and generated more novel candidates with high computational scores than the conventional method. For AAV capsid variants, the number of candidates exceeding the predefined score threshold increased from 19 with the conventional bVAE to 2,761 with the hyperparameter-optimized pLM-bVAE. However, these results were based on computational predictions and did not experimentally establish improved protein function or a quantum computational advantage. [Quantum Biology Society] One of the greatest challenges in protein design is the enormous number of possible amino acid combinations. Even changing a small number of residues can rapidly expand the sequence space that researchers must explore. Quantum annealing (QA) is one approach to solving such combinatorial optimization problems. However, applying it to protein design presents a fundamental challenge: amino acid sequences must first be converted into binary variables consisting of zeros and ones, which can be processed by a quantum annealer. If this conversion loses important information about how protein sequences are related, even an extensive computational search may fail to identify useful protein candidates. A research team from Kitasato University, RIKEN, the University of Tokyo, Tohoku University, the National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS), and the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST) in Japan proposed an artificial intelligence-based binary representation method to address this challenge. The researchers, Hiromi H. Ueda, Andrejs Tučs, Koji Tsuda, Mitsuo Umetsu, and Yutaka Saito, developed pLM-bVAE, a model combining a pretrained protein language model with a binary variational autoencoder. They then evaluated its performance in protein sequence optimization using a D-Wave quantum annealer. Yutaka Saito served as the corresponding author. The study was posted to bioRxiv on November 6, 2026, as a preprint that has not yet undergone peer review. ■ Encoding Protein Sequence Information into 64 Binary Variables Previous approaches to quantum annealing-based protein design have used binary variational autoencoders (bVAEs) to convert amino acid sequences into binary representations. A bVAE consists of two principal components. The encoder compresses an amino acid sequence into a shorter binary vector containing zeros and ones. The decoder then reconstructs an amino acid sequence from the binary vector produced or optimized during computation. This process can be compared to representing locations on a map using compact coordinates. However, the important requirement is not simply to reduce the size of the representation. Sequences that are biologically or evolutionarily related should ideally retain meaningful relationships within the compressed binary space. If similar protein sequences become arbitrarily separated in the binary representation, the optimization algorithm may struggle to explore the sequence space effectively. To improve this mapping, the researchers introduced a protein language model (pLM) before the conventional bVAE architecture. Protein language models are artificial intelligence systems pretrained on large collections of amino acid sequences. They learn statistical patterns associated with amino acid context, sequence relationships, and evolutionary information. The principal model used in the study was ESM2_650M, which contains approximately 650 million parameters. The researchers used this model to generate residue-level representations of protein sequences. These representations were then provided to the bVAE, which converted them into 64-dimensional binary vectors and reconstructed the corresponding amino acid sequences. Importantly, the pretrained protein language model was not further trained during this process. Its parameters were frozen, while the bVAE component was trained to generate binary representations and reconstruct sequences. The optimization also focused on designated variant regions rather than necessarily redesigning an entire protein. The researchers evaluated the method using three publicly available protein variant datasets. The first contained 12,160 peptides with experimentally measured binding affinities to the HLA-A*02:01 major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecule. The second contained 9,591 variants of the complementarity-determining region 3 of the heavy chain (CDRH3) in the single-chain variable fragment (scFv) of trastuzumab, an antibody targeting HER2. The third contained 16,743 variants of the surface region of the adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid. These datasets represented three distinct protein sequence design problems: peptide binding, antibody engineering, and viral capsid engineering. For each dataset, the researchers divided the sequences into training, validation, and test sets. They evaluated how accurately the models could reconstruct the original sequences after binary encoding and how well the encoded vectors preserved the relationships between different protein sequences. The results showed that pLM-bVAE outperformed the conventional bVAE on all three datasets. The researchers measured reconstruction accuracy using Levenshtein distance and BLOSUM62 similarity scores. Levenshtein distance describes the minimum number of insertions, deletions, or substitutions required to transform one sequence into another. BLOSUM62 is an amino acid substitution matrix commonly used to evaluate sequence similarity while accounting for evolutionary relationships. A smaller Levenshtein distance between the original and reconstructed sequences indicates more accurate reconstruction. The researchers also examined whether differences between amino acid sequences were reflected in their binary representations. To do this, they compared pairwise Levenshtein distances between protein sequences with Hamming distances between their corresponding binary vectors. Hamming distance counts the number of positions at which two binary vectors of equal length differ. A stronger positive correlation between these distances indicates that the binary representation better preserves the relationships among protein sequences. For the MHC-I binding peptide dataset, the Spearman correlation coefficient increased from 0.30 with the conventional bVAE to 0.41 with pLM-bVAE. After additional hyperparameter optimization, the coefficient increased further to 0.50. Hyperparameter optimization refers to the systematic adjustment of model settings, such as learning rates, network structure, and regularization parameters, to improve model performance. The researchers used Bayesian optimization to identify favorable training settings for pLM-bVAE. The resulting model was designated pLM-bVAE (HPO). Similar improvements in reconstruction accuracy and preservation of sequence relationships were observed for the trastuzumab CDRH3 and AAV capsid datasets. These findings suggest that incorporating representations learned by a protein language model helps preserve biologically relevant sequence information when converting amino acid sequences into binary variables. However, the results do not imply that the 64-bit representation captures every structural or functional property of a protein. Instead, the experiments demonstrate improved sequence reconstruction and better preservation of the sequence-distance and similarity relationships examined in the study. ■ At Which Stage Was the Actual Quantum Annealer Used? The study did not rely exclusively on simulated quantum annealing. The researchers explicitly reported using a D-Wave Advantage System 6 quantum annealer accessed through the D-Wave Leap cloud platform. However, the quantum hardware did not train the protein language model or directly process amino acid sequences. Its role was to perform combinatorial optimization over the 64 binary variables generated by the artificial intelligence models. The overall computational workflow combined several distinct components. First, the researchers trained three bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) neural networks to predict scores associated with the protein variant sequences. A BiLSTM is a neural network architecture capable of learning contextual relationships within sequential data. The predictors were trained using experimentally measured values available in the original public datasets. However, when new sequences were generated during optimization, their scores were calculated by these trained predictors rather than measured experimentally. Next, the researchers used a factorization machine (FM) as a surrogate model. The factorization machine approximated the relationship between a binary vector and its associated optimization score. This surrogate model was then converted into a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem. QUBO is a mathematical formulation in which an objective function involving binary variables and their pairwise interactions is minimized. The QUBO problem was subsequently converted into an Ising model, allowing it to be processed by the quantum annealer. In an Ising model, a candidate solution can be represented by a configuration of binary spin variables, and the optimization task is to identify configurations with low energy. The D-Wave quantum annealer searched for binary configurations that minimized the corresponding objective function. The optimized binary vectors were then decoded back into amino acid sequences using the trained bVAE or pLM-bVAE decoder. The resulting sequences were evaluate

title: Artificial Flavoproteins Redirect Photochemical Pathways by Repositioning Tryptophan
authors: inquantio
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The researchers incorporated a flavin cofactor into a previously developed de novo protein scaffold and created two highly thermostable proteins, with or without a heme-binding module. X-ray crystallography confirmed that their structures closely matched the computational designs at near-atomic resolution. In a redesigned variant containing two tryptophan residues positioned around the flavin, the absorption spectrum and redox properties changed substantially, while fluorescence and photoreduction were strongly suppressed. Ultrafast spectroscopy supported the formation of a rapidly relaxing flavin–tryptophan charge-transfer state. The study demonstrates how quantum chemical calculations can be integrated with protein design to control excited-state relaxation pathways. However, it does not establish a fully functional photocatalyst or provide direct evidence of long-lived quantum coherence or spin entanglement. [Quantum Biology Society] A light-sensitive protein is more than a molecular container that absorbs light. The arrangement of amino acids surrounding its chromophore can determine which electronic excited states become accessible, whether the absorbed energy is released as fluorescence, transferred through electron movement, or dissipated through nonradiative relaxation. Natural proteins such as cryptochromes and other flavin-based photoreceptors exploit these molecular environments to control their photochemical functions. However, designing comparable properties from the ground up remains a major challenge. Rather than modifying an existing natural photoreceptor, researchers must construct a stable protein scaffold capable of holding a chromophore in a precisely defined position. They must also understand how the surrounding molecular environment influences the electronic states and relaxation pathways that emerge after light absorption. A collaborative research team led by the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom, with researchers from the Universities of Portsmouth, Essex, and East Anglia, combined computational protein design with structural biology, quantum chemistry, and ultrafast spectroscopy to address these challenges. The study was conducted by Ethan L. Bungay, Juno Underhill, Meiyue Liu, Alexandra N. Stuart, Catherine R. Back, Jessica C. Berrones-Reyes, Paulina Dubiel, James A. Birrell, Aditya G. Rao, Christopher Williams, Rob Barringer, Philip Hinchliffe, Bruce R. Lichtenstein, Basile F. E. Curchod, Julea N. Butt, Thomas A. A. Oliver, Adrian J. Mulholland, and J. L. Ross Anderson. Ethan L. Bungay and Juno Underhill contributed equally as co-first authors, while Thomas A. A. Oliver, Adrian J. Mulholland, and J. L. Ross Anderson served as corresponding authors. The researchers developed three related artificial flavoprotein designs. They experimentally determined the crystal structures of the first two and used electrochemistry, electron paramagnetic resonance, and ultrafast spectroscopy to investigate their molecular properties and photochemical behavior. The study, titled "De Novo Design of Flavoproteins with Controlled Excited State Dynamics," was posted to bioRxiv on October 10, 2026. It is a preprint that has not yet undergone peer review. ■ From an Artificial Protein Scaffold to Atomic-Scale Placement of Flavin The researchers began with the 4D2 family of de novo protein scaffolds, which had previously been developed as a modular platform for constructing redox-active proteins. Unlike proteins derived directly from natural sequences, de novo proteins are designed using computational principles to form specific three-dimensional structures and perform selected molecular functions. The 4D2 platform is based on a four-alpha-helix bundle, a structure in which four helical segments are arranged together to create a stable protein framework. For the present study, the researchers developed an extended scaffold containing 140 amino acid residues and three functional modules. The first module contained a binding site for heme B, an iron-containing cofactor capable of participating in electron-transfer reactions. The second module provided additional structural stability. The third module contained a binding site for a flavin chromophore, which absorbs light and can undergo electron-transfer reactions. Rather than using ordinary biological flavin directly, the researchers incorporated 8-demethylriboflavin (8-dMeRF), a modified flavin cofactor. The chromophore was covalently attached to a cysteine residue within the protein through a thioether linkage. This linkage allowed the researchers to anchor the flavin at a defined location and reduce structural variability around the chromophore. However, merely attaching a flavin molecule to a protein does not guarantee that the surrounding structure will be sufficiently stable or precisely organized. The researchers initially attempted sequence redesign using Rosetta-based methods, but the resulting proteins exhibited structural disorder around the flavin-binding site. They therefore adopted an iterative, machine-learning-assisted design strategy. The workflow combined LigandMPNN, which designs amino acid sequences while considering the local environment of a bound ligand, with ESMFold, which predicts protein structures from amino acid sequences. The researchers repeated this sequence-design and structure-prediction process over five iterations. During the iterations, the predicted structural quality improved substantially. The mean predicted template modeling score (pTM) increased from approximately 0.822 to 0.897, while the mean predicted local distance difference test score (pLDDT) increased from 85.4 to 91.7. These metrics provided computational indications that the redesigned sequences were increasingly compatible with the intended protein structure. The resulting highest-scoring design was named FC-4D2, a flavocytochrome containing both heme B and flavin. The researchers also developed Fl-4D2, a related design in which the heme-binding module was removed or repacked through nine amino acid substitutions, leaving the flavin as the principal redox-active cofactor. Importantly, this process was not simply the reproduction of a naturally occurring flavoprotein sequence. It involved adapting an existing artificial protein architecture to accommodate different combinations of cofactors while preserving the intended structural framework. Both proteins were successfully expressed in Escherichia coli and purified for experimental characterization. Circular dichroism spectroscopy indicated that the designed proteins retained their characteristic helical structures over a wide temperature range. Neither FC-4D2 nor Fl-4D2 exhibited a clear cooperative unfolding transition during heating up to 95°C. This result demonstrated high thermal stability under the tested conditions, although it does not imply that the proteins would remain indefinitely functional at such temperatures. The researchers then used X-ray crystallography to determine the three-dimensional structures of the proteins. The FC-4D2 crystal structure was resolved at 1.35 Å, while the Fl-4D2 structure was resolved at 1.8 Å. One ångström is equivalent to 0.1 nanometers. The experimentally determined structures closely matched the computational models. When the positions of the alpha-carbon atoms in the protein backbones were compared, the root-mean-square deviations (RMSDs) were approximately 0.844 Å for FC-4D2 and 0.840 Å for Fl-4D2. These small structural deviations indicated that the proteins had adopted conformations close to those intended by the design process. The structural data also supported the predicted positions of the bound cofactors. In FC-4D2, the experimentally observed heme–flavin separation was approximately 19.8 Å, consistent with the computational prediction of approximately 19.3 Å. This agreement demonstrated that the modular scaffold could position different redox cofactors within a relatively well-defined structural environment. However, the presence of two cofactors at a particular distance does not itself establish that rapid or efficient electron transfer occurs between them. The researchers initially estimated that the heme–flavin separation could support relatively slow electron transfer on a millisecond timescale. The significance of the crystallographic results was therefore structural: the designed proteins largely reproduced the intended arrangements of their cofactors. This precision is essential because a chromophore's photochemical behavior is not determined by the chromophore alone. Charged amino acid residues, hydrogen bonds, aromatic rings, and local electrostatic interactions can change the electronic energy levels of the same flavin molecule. By first establishing a stable scaffold with a precisely positioned chromophore, the researchers created a platform in which the surrounding protein environment could subsequently be modified to control photochemical behavior. ■ Flavin Accepts Electrons One at a Time: Redox States Change with Light and pH Flavins are versatile biological cofactors because they can access several oxidation and protonation states. An oxidized flavin can accept one electron to form a semiquinone radical. It can then accept another electron to reach a fully reduced hydroquinone state. The semiquinone and hydroquinone forms can also exist in different protonation states, giving the same chromophore different electronic structures and chemical properties. These processes are important in natural flavoproteins involved in electron transfer, oxidation–reduction reactions, and light-driven chemistry. To investigate whether their designed proteins could support similar behavior, the researchers performed protein film electrochemistry and optical absorption measurements. title: A Conceptual Framework for Hybrid Quantum Computing-Enabled Smart Sustainable Cities: Integrating AI, IoT, Digital Twins, and Urban Sustainability
authors: Dillip Kumar Das
abstract: Rapid urbanisation and growing environmental, economic, and social pressures are increasing the need for intelligent and sustainable urban management. Artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and digital twins support real-time monitoring, prediction, simulation, and decision-making, but increasingly complex urban systems can exceed the capabilities of conventional computing. Quantum computing offers new possibilities for complex optimisation and simulation, yet its integration with smart sustainable city technologies remains underexplored. This paper develops a theoretically grounded conceptual framework for Hybrid Quantum Computing-Enabled Smart Sustainable Cities through an integrative review of research on AI, IoT, digital twins, hybrid quantum computing, and urban sustainability. The framework positions IoT as the data-acquisition layer, AI as the analytical and predictive engine, digital twins as the representation and simulation layer, and hybrid quantum–classical computing as an advanced capability for optimisation, simulation, and quantum machine learning. It also identifies enabling conditions, including data governance, interoperability, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure, regulation, workforce readiness, ethics, and citizen trust. The framework highlights applications across transport, energy, water, waste, healthcare, and public safety, providing a foundation for empirical validation and policy development towards more intelligent, resilient, resource-efficient, and sustainable cities.

title: Spintronics in Lead‐Free Hybrid Perovskites: Mechanisms, Materials, and Prospects for Room‐Temperature Devices
Energy-filtered readout preserves gap-enhanced sensing in interacting quantum dots
Memory-dependent operating windows for photonic teleportation from a laser-driven spin–photon interface
authors: Mukhtar Y. Y. Abdalla, Naglaa Mohammed, Osman Osman, Ines Hilali Jaghdam, Muntasir Suhail, Muhammad Javed
abstract: Generating entangled photons from a laser-driven spin provides a promising resource for quantum communication, but their usefulness can depend on how the surrounding nuclear environment evolves during photon generation. We investigate a spin–photon interface driven by finite laser pulses while retaining nuclear-spin dynamics across successive emission cycles. Measurements on the intermediate photons produce conditional endpoint states, whose entanglement, Bell correlations, teleportation fidelity, and expected detection rates are evaluated. By comparing dynamically evolving, frozen-field, and reset nuclear environments, we find that simplified noise models can predict different operating windows for useful teleportation. In particular, the frozen-field approximation may overestimate performance under the conditions studied. Optical branching, imperfect feedforward, and nuclear-register size further constrain these windows. The results establish a task-oriented framework for evaluating photonic resources while highlighting the need for accurate environmental modeling and device-specific calibration.

title: Smart soft matter: from high-resolution fabrication to physical intelligence
Enhancing quantum metrology with high-order Fisher information and experiments
authors: Xin-Zhu Liu, Junli Jiang, Yan-Han Yang, L Zhao, Xiaomin Yang, Shao‐Ming Fei, Ming-Xing Luo
abstract: Fisher information plays a central role in statistics and quantum metrology, providing the basis for the celebrated Cramér–Rao bound. In this work, we introduce a new information measure based on higher-order Fisher information and show that it naturally leads to a generalized uncertainty relation for parameter estimation, which can be regarded as an extension of the Cramér–Rao bound. As an application, we analyze the case of quantum phase estimation and compare our theoretical bounds with the well-known established hierarchical bounds. Finally, we experimentally validate the proposed framework using a photonic platform.

title: Architectures of Sovereign AI in the Neural Age: Epistemic Agency, Managed Interdependence, and an Empirical Stress-Test of the 2027 Horizon
authors: Syed Muntasir Mamun
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical formalization, comparative institutional analysis, and late-2026 empirical stress-test of operational doctrines for sovereign artificial intelligence (AI), synthesizing and critically extending the KSCCN corpus developed by Syed Muntasir Mamun. Rejecting both territorial autarky and passive absorption into planetary platform monopolies, the study conceptualizes AI sovereignty as the sustained capacity of a political community to retain autonomous control over the epistemic and ontological foundations of its strategic existence. Across seven interlocking domains—local capability formation, enterprise resilience, privacy-preserving cross-border collaboration, regulatory coherence, innovation safeguards and cognitive protection, cross-jurisdictional accountability, and regional shared infrastructure—the analysis evaluates the Triple-Lock Architecture (binding material, civic, and public triads), Dual-Core Fractal Statecraft, and Sovereign Interoperability in dialogue with contesting paradigms, including open-weight maximalism, European regulatory sovereignty, Chinese vertical state control, data-colonialism critiques, and Hakkı Tan's ontopolitical theory of the Onopticon. Grounded in market concentration telemetry, small language model (SLM) and distributed training benchmarks, cryptographic attack surfaces, and enacted statutes as of November 2026 across the European Union, United States, China, India, Southeast Asia, and Africa, the empirical audit establishes two core findings alongside three structural caveats. First, capital-light pathways—combining parameter-efficient fine-tuning, Governance-Aware Retriever middleware, low-communication training, and modular Digital Public Infrastructure—offer a technically viable "Third Way" for middle powers and Global South polities facing an estimated 580-fold fiscal asymmetry against US hyperscalers, yet remain highly vulnerable to execution lags, agent-runtime lock-in, and authoritarian co-optation. Second, stress-testing the KSCCN 2027 horizon forecast strongly corroborates its trajectories regarding agentic proliferation, compute chokepoints, and statutory cognitive safeguards, while refuting its projection of a hardware "Q-Day" around August 2027: late-2026 fault-tolerant hardware (48 small-code logical qubits) remains an order of magnitude or more below RSA-2048 factoring requirements, even though collapsing theoretical qubit overheads and active Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later exposure validate immediate architectural migration toward crypto-agile, post-quantum signed AI memory. KSCCN article, Series on Critical AI and Digital Sovereignty Studies, 26 November 2026 (44 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables, 205 references). Full-colour expanded research edition and empirical stress-test of the KSCCN Teaching Note Architectures of Sovereign AI in the Neural Age: Epistemic Agency, Managed Interdependence, and the 2027 Horizon (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24547226). Draws on Fractal Statecraft under Permanent Systemic Instability (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24298608), Cognitive and Semantic Sovereignty as the New Westphalian Pillar (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24298653), The Algorithmic Leviathan as Constitutional Form, Volume II (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24299263), Sovereign AI for Jute (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24218888), Governing AI Without Governing Speech (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24239711) and Sovereign AI in the Developing Global South (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23543853).

title: Quantum Search Identifies Shared Connections in Lung Cancer Gene Networks
authors: inquantio
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: By comparing 28,390 regulatory interactions inferred from genomic and gene-expression data from lung cancer patients, the researchers identified 4,943 shared connections between two sample sets within the same cohort using quantum circuit simulations, matching the results of classical computation. In a separate comparison involving 7,063 regulatory interactions from two patient cohorts, the researchers identified 24 shared connections. They also tested the core search procedure on a real IBM quantum processor using a reduced 11-qubit circuit. The reported 100% accuracy in large-scale simulations refers to detecting matching connections in previously inferred networks. It does not represent lung cancer diagnostic accuracy or demonstrate faster end-to-end processing than classical computers. [Quantum Biology Society] Understanding lung cancer requires examining not only which genes have changed but also how different genes interact with one another. When certain regions of DNA are amplified or deleted in cancer cells, the expression levels of other genes may also change. These alterations can propagate through complex networks of molecular regulatory relationships. Multi-omics analysis integrates different types of molecular information, such as genomic and transcriptomic data, to represent these relationships as gene regulatory networks (GRNs). A major challenge is identifying connections that consistently appear across large networks constructed from different patient populations. When statistical stability is evaluated through bootstrapping, a procedure that repeatedly resamples data, the number of required network comparisons and the computational burden increase further. Abdul Mannan Kitab and Yiming Zeng of Binghamton University in the United States, Qing Ye of Sostos Inc., and Nancy Lan Guo, who is affiliated with both institutions, developed QuBIN, a quantum computing-based pipeline designed to address this search problem. The researchers designed quantum circuits based on Grover's search algorithm to identify overlapping connections in lung cancer gene regulatory networks. They evaluated the approach using large-scale quantum circuit simulations and experiments on an actual quantum processor. Nancy Lan Guo served as the corresponding author. The study was published online on November 16, 2026, in npj Genomic Medicine. The paper has undergone peer review but is currently available as an accepted Article in Press. Its final bibliographic information and some editorial details may change when the Version of Record is published. ■ Conserved Connections Across Patient Cohorts Matter More Than Individual Genes The central task addressed in this study was not searching individual gene sequences or discovering new regulatory networks from scratch. Instead, the researchers investigated how to identify common regulatory relationships between networks that had already been inferred from biological data. They used DNA copy number variation (CNV) and gene-expression measurements from patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Copy number variation occurs when a region of DNA is present in more or fewer copies than usual. For example, an increase in the copy number of one gene may be statistically associated with increased or decreased expression of another gene. The researchers represented statistically supported directional relationships between these molecular variables as connections, or edges, within gene regulatory networks. These connections had previously been constructed using a framework known as Prediction Logic Boolean Implication Networks (PLBINs). PLBINs identify relationships between molecular variables by evaluating implication rules and their statistical support. For example, if increased DNA copy number of one gene is repeatedly associated with increased expression of another gene, the relationship may be retained as a candidate regulatory interaction when it satisfies predefined statistical criteria. Each connection contains information about the implication-rule type, source gene, target gene, and regulatory direction. However, such a connection does not necessarily demonstrate that the source gene directly causes the observed change in the target gene. The relationships are inferred from molecular data and require additional biological investigation before direct causal mechanisms can be established. The researchers performed two types of network comparisons. The first was an intra-cohort comparison using the publicly available NSCLC dataset GSE31800. This dataset included 271 tumor samples, of which 49 had corresponding gene-expression measurements. The researchers compared two sets of regulatory connections derived from these sample groups. One contained 21,363 edges, while the other contained 7,027 edges. Together, the two sets comprised 28,390 regulatory interactions. Importantly, these were not completely independent patient cohorts. The smaller group of 49 samples was nested within the larger GSE31800 cohort. The second analysis involved an inter-cohort comparison between GSE31800 and an independent NSCLC patient cohort, GSE28582. For this comparison, the researchers examined selected subnetworks associated with a previously investigated seven-gene prognostic signature. The two subnetworks contained 2,014 and 5,049 regulatory interactions, respectively, giving a combined total of 7,063 edges. An interaction was considered conserved between cohorts only when its implication-rule type, source gene, target gene, and regulatory direction matched. Identifying such shared connections can help researchers prioritize molecular relationships for subsequent biomarker investigations. A relationship that appears repeatedly in different patient datasets may be more useful for follow-up research than one identified in only a single dataset. However, recurrence across cohorts does not automatically establish clinical significance or biological causality. The purpose of QuBIN was to improve the computational search for these shared relationships, rather than independently validate their biological functions. ■ The Quantum Circuit Searches for Matching Connections Rather Than Building New Networks The first step in QuBIN is converting each regulatory connection into binary information that can be compared within a quantum circuit. The researchers represented each connection using 33 bits. Of these, 3 bits encoded the regulatory rule type, 15 bits identified the source gene, and another 15 bits identified the target gene. This representation preserved the information needed to determine whether two connections referred to the same regulatory relationship. The researchers then designed a quantum oracle that compared pairs of connections from different networks. A quantum oracle is a component of a quantum algorithm that determines whether a candidate satisfies the conditions of a search problem. In this study, the oracle used exclusive OR (XOR) operations to compare the binary fields of two regulatory connections. An XOR operation returns zero when two compared bits are identical. Therefore, when all the relevant fields of two connections matched, the oracle could identify the pair as a shared regulatory interaction. The corresponding quantum state was marked for amplification by Grover's search algorithm. For intra-cohort comparisons in which all connections within a batch shared the same source gene, the researchers omitted the redundant comparison of that field. This simplified the quantum circuit without changing the matching conditions for the relevant data. Grover's algorithm differs from a conventional sequential search. Instead of examining possible answers one at a time, it uses quantum superposition and interference to increase the probability of measuring states corresponding to valid solutions. The process can be compared to searching a library. Rather than opening every book in sequence, the algorithm progressively increases the probability of selecting books that satisfy the search criteria. However, this is only an analogy. The algorithm does not literally inspect every connection simultaneously and immediately reveal all correct answers. It uses quantum operations to amplify the probability amplitudes of marked states, after which measurements provide candidate results. The researchers divided the large regulatory networks into small batches and applied quantum searches to the individual batch pairs. The results were then collected and combined. This approach differs fundamentally from loading tens of thousands of regulatory interactions into a single quantum computer and searching the entire dataset at once. For the large-scale evaluations, the researchers did not execute the complete circuits on physical quantum hardware. Instead, they used matrix product state (MPS) tensor network simulations running on classical high-performance computing infrastructure. MPS is a mathematical representation that can efficiently simulate certain quantum states when their entanglement structure remains sufficiently constrained. This makes it possible to simulate quantum circuits that would require impractically large memory if represented using full quantum state vectors. The researchers used Qiskit and its MPS simulation backend to evaluate the circuits. For the intra-cohort comparison, the networks were divided into batches containing eight edges each. The corresponding circuit contained 90 qubits. For the inter-cohort comparison, the researchers used batches of four edges and a 104-qubit circuit. These qubit counts describe the sizes of the simulated quantum circuits. They do not mean that the full 90-qubit or 104-qubit experiments were executed on real quantum processors. The distinction is important because quantum circuit simulation and physical quantum computation have different limitations. A simulator uses conventi

title: Predicting and Interpreting Quantum Circuit Reliability: An Integrated Machine Learning and XAI Framework
authors: Duong Van Hieu
abstract: Quantum computing promises exponential advantages for classically intractable problems but remains severely bottlenecked by hardware noise.Accurately predicting quantum circuit reliability prior to execution is crucial for effective compilation and error mitigation, yet exact fidelity estimation is computationally prohibitive.While recent machine learning (ML) approaches have attempted to predict circuit reliability, they often suffer from topological blindness and operate as uninterpretable "black boxes."In this study, we propose an Integrated Machine Learning and Explainable AI (XAI) framework for pre-execution quantum circuit analysis.Using the QUASAR Quantum Reliability Dataset v1 (50,000 synthetic circuits), we evaluate tree-based ensemble models for both continuous reliability regression and categorical classification.Our results demonstrate that HistGradientBoosting achieves superior predictive performance (R 2  0.945 for regression; 88.86% accuracy for classification) under rigorous grouped cross-validation.Furthermore, unsupervised clustering reveals four distinct "reliability archetypes," proving that circuit reliability is driven by a multidimensional interplay of qubit count, depth, and gate composition rather than a single metric.Post-hoc explainability techniques (SHAP, Permutation Importance, and Partial Dependence Plots) identify qubit count, circuit depth, and measurement-related features as primary drivers of reliability degradation.Finally, we critically examine the methodological caveats of synthetic data, target determinism, and feature multicollinearity, establishing a foundational baseline for interpretable quantum software engineering while highlighting the necessity for future hardware-level validation.

title: 17th Conference on Data Analysis Methods for Software Systems
Benchmarking quantum feature encoding strategies for binary classification with QSVM
authors: Murat Kurt
journal: Frontiers in Quantum Science and Technology
abstract: Quantum feature maps determine the mapping of classical data into quantum states and the similarity structure induced by quantum kernels. This study investigates the effects of incorporating statistical relationships between features into quantum encoding on classification performance and circuit resources. Five quantum feature maps based on Pearson correlation, Spearman correlation, Kendall correlation, mutual information, and distance correlation were compared with Angle-RY, H + RY, Z, and ZZ maps with three different connectivity topologies. Classical SVM results with an RBF kernel were also computed for comparison. Experiments were conducted on 500 samples selected from each of five binary classification datasets. Performance was evaluated using class-wise metrics, macro and weighted averages, ROC-AUC, log-loss, and confidence intervals; Holm correction was applied to paired comparisons. The findings showed that no feature map consistently outperformed the others across all tasks and metrics. The numerical gains achieved by dependency-based maps on some tasks did not translate into an overall statistically significant advantage over Angle-RY or classical SVM. Quantum Encoding Feature Score (QFES) scores, defined independently of execution times and combining macro F1 and AUC with the training–test gap and decomposed circuit resources, were computed. The results indicate that quantum feature maps should be selected by jointly considering predictive performance, class balance, uncertainty, and circuit resources.

title: Emulating non-Markovian system-bath dynamics with parametrically driven cavities
authors: Valentin Boettcher, Félix Pellerin, Philippe St-Jean, W. A. Coish
abstract: We introduce and characterize a scheme for emulating non-Markovian quantum system-bath dynamics using the discrete electromagnetic field modes of a parametrically driven cavity. In this scheme, the character of a bosonic bath (the form of the bath spectral density) is tied directly to the shape of the real-time waveform describing periodic parametric cavity modulation. As an explicit example, we demonstrate the feasibility of this scheme for a fiber-loop experiment with currently achievable parameters, supported by numerical simulations and analytical estimates. In particular, we show that a localization transition of the spin-boson model can be accurately emulated in this fiber-loop cavity system. This localization effect is characterized by a sharp transition from partial decay to complete decay for a two-level system coupled to a bosonic bath as the bath spectral density J ( ω ) ∝ ω s is continously tuned from the sub-ohmic ( s < 1 ) to the super-ohmic ( s > 1 ) regime. The transition is only exactly realized in the thermodynamic limit (for an infinite number of bath modes) and for sufficiently weak system-bath coupling. We highlight a competition between the weak-coupling and thermodynamic limits in this problem and show that challenges in approximately realizing the transition can nevertheless be overcome. Finally, we provide bounds on the systematic error introduced when emulating non-Markovian dynamics for arbitrary system observables. The scheme presented here can enable the realization of a modular platform for engineering custom non-Markovian baths, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics, thermalization of many-body systems, and resource-efficient quantum simulations of open quantum systems.

title: Automated construction and verification of unextendible product bases
authors: Zicheng Han, Wanchen Zhang, Fei Shi, Xiande Zhang
journal: Journal of Physics A Mathematical and Theoretical
abstract: Unextendible product bases (UPBs) are important structures in quantum information theory, with applications to completely entangled subspaces, bound entanglement, and local indistinguishability. Since many properties and applications of UPBs are closely related to their sizes, one of the central problems in the study of UPBs is to determine whether UPBs of prescribed sizes exist in a given multipartite system. In this paper, we introduce a SAT-assisted framework based on decompositions of the N-dimensional hypercube. We define O_N-tile decompositions and prove a tile-to-UPB theorem: every O_N-tile decomposition induces a UPB through a construction based on tile-wise Fourier product bases and a global stopper state. We then encode the search for such decompositions as a Boolean satisfiability (SAT) problem and use SAT solvers to generate explicit instances. In terms of verification, we also implement a UPB verification algorithm based on local orthogonality graphs and unsaturated subspaces. The algorithm can be used to determine whether an arbitrary finite set of product states forms a UPB. Using this framework, we obtain UPBs of several sizes in some tripartite and quadripartite systems, including sizes 7, 11, 12, ..., 23 in C^3 ⊗ C^3 ⊗ C^3. Moreover, the small-dimensional instances obtained here can serve as seed UPBs for recursive constructions, leading to further examples in larger multipartite systems.

title: Fast pulses for high-fidelity circularization of interacting Rydberg atoms
authors: Matthias Hüls, Aurore-Alice Young, C. Sayrin, M. Brune, J. M. Raimond, Tommaso Calarco, Felix Motzoi, Robert Zeier
abstract: Circular states in Rydberg atoms offer a promising platform for quantum computation, quantum simulation and quantum sensing. However, the final step of their preparation - termed as circularization, a process that involves the transfer of a large amount of angular momentum quanta to the valence electron by means of radio-frequency (RF) pulses - remains as a major bottleneck for all technological applications based on interacting circular Rydberg atoms. Even though successfully implemented to circularize an atom cloud in the dilute regime, previous efforts to speed up the circularization process have focused on the single-atom case, thereby neglecting the interactions which constitute one of the main resources for quantum simulation and computation. In this theoretical work we show how interactions between two atoms disturb the efficiency of pulses designed for single atoms and identify shifts induced by the interactions on relevant transition energies as the dominant disturbance. We demonstrate that the initial efficiency of single-atom pulses can be restored by adapting them to these shifts. Our approach is based on a simple functional form depending only on two linear parameters determined by the pair arrangement, which we derive analytically. The adapted pulses prepare two ⁸⁷Rb atoms after 65 ns in a n = 52 circular state with a fidelity of at least least 95 % for interatomic distances down to 6.3 μm and for all angular configurations, while also complying experimental amplitude and frequency constraints. Finally, we show that when combining our adapted pulses with Krotov's pulse-shaping algorithm we obtain high-fidelity pulses for any pair arrangement with interatomic distances larger than 5.9 μm. This work demonstrates that fast RF pulses can circularize interacting Rydberg atoms, paving the way toward their technological application.

title: Long-range nonstabilizerness of topologically encoded states from mutual information
authors: David Aram Korbany, Tyler D. Ellison, David T. Stephen, Lorenzo Piroli
abstract: We study long-range nonstabilizerness (LRN), namely the obstruction to remove nonstabilizerness with shallow-depth local quantum circuits. In one-dimensional settings, the mutual information between disconnected spatial regions has proven to be a powerful tool to diagnose LRN. In this work, we focus on encoded states of two-dimensional topologically-ordered systems, and explore the ability of the mutual information to serve as a diagnostic of LRN. Focusing on the concrete setting of lattice models defined on a torus, we show that information about LRN can be gained from the analysis of the mutual information between non-overlapping regions containing non-contractible loops, and of the change of such mutual information under modular real-space transformations. We exemplify this idea in the toric code and the non-abelian string-net model with doubled Fibonacci topological order. In the former case, we show that the mutual information provides a full classification, certifying LRN for all encoded non-stabilizer states. In the latter case, instead, our approach does not lead to a full classification, as it detects LRN for all states except from a finite subset with special transformation properties under the modular group. Finally, we discuss how our results on LRN constrain the logical gates that can be implemented fault-tolerantly on the torus.

title: Optical quantum teleportation with known amplitude distorting factors of teleported qubits
authors: Mikhail S. Podoshvedov, Sergey A. Podoshvedov
abstract: We develop a quantum teleportation protocol of an unknown optical single-rail qubit using a hybrid quantum channel consisting of continuous variable (CV) states of certain parity and photonic states. The quantum channel is characterized by two parameters: a squeezing parameter of single-mode squeezed vacuum (SMSV) state and the beam splitter (BS) parameter, which can be appropriately tuned to improve the protocol efficiency. The CV part of the hybrid state interacts with the single-rail qubit on balanced BS at Alice's location, while discrete variable (DV) half of the quantum channel is controlled by Bob. In half the cases, Bob receives the original qubit, and in almost half the remaining cases, he obtains the input qubit with distorted amplitudes, with both participants knowing the values of the distortion coefficients. As the amount of classical information transmitted by Alice increases, they both gain greater access to partial information about the unitary transformations undergone by the teleported qubits, allowing Bob to continue using them or attempt to recover them to improve the efficiency of the protocol. The proposed probabilistic method for restoring the original qubit from an amplitude distorted one allows increasing the overall probability of the protocol to more than 0.5. The proposed method is a generalization of quantum teleportation, in which a nonlocal photon serves as the quantum channel for transmitting a single-rail qubit.

title: Efficient construction of time-invariant process tensors for simulating high-dimensional non-Markovian open quantum systems
authors: Émile Cochin, Jonathan Keeling, Brendon W. Lovett, Alex W. Chin
abstract: Numerical methods for obtaining exact dynamics of non-Markovian open quantum systems are mostly limited to either small systems or to short-time evolution only. Here, we propose a new algorithm for computing process tensors—matrix product operator (MPO) representations that capture the environment influence—which achieves greatly enhanced computational scalings with system size, while maintaining linear scaling with simulation length. We build on recent developments in the field which allow for long-time evolutions through process tensors which have a time-translational invariance. These can be built for general Gaussian environments and generic coupling operators with the system using infinite time-evolving block decimation (iTEBD). We introduce a modified iTEBD algorithm using intermediate compression steps which bring down the computation time scaling with system size d d from \mathcal{O}(d^8) 𝒪 (d 8) to \mathcal{O}(d^4) 𝒪 (d 4), as well as significantly lowering the required memory. To illustrate the power of this method, we apply it to the problem of dispersive qubit readout in circuit QED, which was previously out-of-reach numerically. The full treatment of the measurement resonator, which requires a large system space, combined with the long simulation times precipitated by the separation of timescales between the measurement drive and the environment dissipation, is now possible. The algorithm we introduce not only allows for capturing non-Markovian dynamics in large open quantum systems, but also further extends all the existing capabilities of process tensors, for example in quantum optimal control, or in computation of multi-time correlations or of steady states, to more complex systems with tens of levels.

title: A Quantum Computing Framework for VLBI Data Correlation
authors: Lei Liu
abstract: This work presents a quantum computing framework for very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) data correlation. It is shown that a classical baseband time series data of a length N can be embedded into a quantum superposition state using amplitude encoding with only log2N qubits. The basic VLBI correlation and fringe fitting operations, including fringe rotation, a Fourier transform, delay compensation, and cross correlation, can be implemented via quantum algorithms with significantly reduced computational complexity. A single-baseline quantum pipeline for geodetic VLBI data processing is constructed, and its feasibility and accuracy are validated through direct comparison with a classical pipeline. Amplitude encoding of large data volumes remains the primary bottleneck in quantum computing. However, the quantized nature of VLBI raw data helps reduce the state preparation complexity. This investigation demonstrates that quantum computation offers a promising paradigm for VLBI data correlation and is likely to play a role in future VLBI systems.

title: Topology aware quantum circuit cutting via reinforcement learning
authors: Abhishek Sadhu, Aritra Sarkar, Akash Kundu
abstract: Simulating molecular systems on quantum processors has the potential to surpass classical methods in computational resource efficiency. The limited qubit connectivity, small processor size, and short coherence times of near-term quantum hardware constrain the applicability of quantum algorithms like quantum phase estimation and variational quantum eigensolver. Quantum circuit cutting has the potential to address these constraints by partitioning large circuits into smaller subcircuits, enabling execution on resource-limited devices. However, standard graph-theoretic partitioning often fails to account for the entanglement structure of the quantum state, leading to partitions that minimize wire cuts at the cost of increasing the simulation error. To address these limitations, in this article, we propose CutQAS, a framework that integrates quantum circuit cutting with quantum architecture search (QAS) to enhance quantum chemistry simulations. Our framework primarily contains two steps. First, an RL agent explores all possible topologies to identify an optimal circuit structure. Subsequently, a second RL agent refines the selected topology by determining optimal circuit cuts, ensuring efficient execution on constrained hardware. We demonstrate that CutQAS implicitly optimizes the Schmidt spectrum truncation, identifying partitions that yield higher accuracy by mapping a 4- and 6-qubit quantum chemistry problem onto a 3-qubit processor. This approach presents an improved solution for quantum chemistry applications, offering a systematic pathway to overcoming hardware constraints in near-term quantum computing.

title: Optimal recoil-free state preparation protocols in an optical atom tweezer
authors: Lia Kley, Nicolas Heimann, Aslam Parvej, Lukas Broers, Ludwig Mathey
abstract: Quantum computing in atom tweezers requires high-fidelity implementations of quantum operations. Here, we demonstrate the optimal implementation of the transition $\ket{\downarrow} \rightarrow \ket{\uparrow}$ of two levels, serving as a qubit, of an atom in a tweezer potential, driven by a single-photon Rabi pulse. The Rabi pulse generates a photon recoil of the atom, due to the Lamb-Dicke coupling between the internal and motional degree of freedom, driving the system out of the logical subspace. This detrimental effect is strongly suppressed in the protocols that we propose. Using pulse engineering, we generate optimal protocols composed of a Rabi pulse protocol and a force protocol, corresponding to dynamically displacing the tweezer.
