We generate these for a large parameter space, from small to large values of the Rabi frequency, and a range of pulse lengths. We identify three main regimes for the optimal protocols, and discuss their properties. In all of these regimes, we demonstrate infidelity well below the current technological standard, thus mitigating a universal challenge in atom tweezers and other quantum technology platforms.

title: Secure IoT communication architecture using lattice-based cryptography and quantum randomness
authors: G. Vennira Selvi
abstract: The rapid expansion of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has revolutionized sectors such as healthcare, agriculture, transportation and smart cities. However, the exponential growth of connected devices has increased security threats with limited computing resources, heterogeneous architectures and vulnerability to cyberattacks. The threat landscape is evolving as a result of quantum computing and traditional cryptographic methods are facing an increasing challenge. Quantum computing represents both a threat and an opportunity for IoT security. Algorithms such as Shor’s algorithm that run on quantum computers, threaten the security of classic cryptographic methods such as RSA and ECC. In contrast, post quantum quantum cryptography (PQC) provides cryptographic approaches designed to resist quantum attacks. To address the vulnerability of IoT systems to quantum attacks, this work proposes a lattice-based post quantum secure IoT architecture using NTRUEncrypt combined with AES-256-GCM. NTRUEncrypt provides post-quantum protection, while AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption to ensure confidentiality and data integrity. A quantum random number generator (QRNG) and SHA3-256 are used for secure session key generation. The proposed architecture applies NTRUEncrypt at the device level and gateway level, followed by AES-256-GCM protection of the NTRU ciphertext. The approach is designed to protect sensor data and control messages while maintaining low computational and communication overhead for resource-constrained IoT devices. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture provides enhanced security with reasonable encryption/decryption latency and communication overhead. The performance is compared with conventional approach RSA-2048, ECC-256 and PQC approach ML-KEM-512, demonstrating the suitability of the proposed architecture for secure and quantum resistant IoT communication.

title: Learning adaptive unravelings for efficient quantum-trajectory simulations
authors: Xing‐Liang Dong, Yun-Feng Xiao
abstract: Different unravelings of the same Lindblad dynamics can generate markedly different levels of trajectory entanglement, with direct consequences for the efficiency of quantum-trajectory simulations of open many-body systems. This makes adaptive, state-dependent unraveling appealing, but in practice it requires online evaluation of short-time entanglement growth for candidate unravelings along every sampled trajectory. Here, we amortize this overhead by learning adaptive unraveling from a small set of optimized trajectories, typically one to two orders of magnitude fewer than the trajectories used for Monte Carlo averaging, while retaining comparable entanglement suppression. Using local observables and tensor-network-aware features of the conditional state, the policy sets parameters in physically motivated unraveling manifolds that extend photon counting and field-quadrature measurements. We benchmark the approach on locally dephased Brownian circuits, Dicke superradiant decay, and dissipative preparation of correlated spin states, which probe local, collective, and quasi-local forms of dissipation, respectively. Our results identify adaptive unraveling as a learnable, reusable component for more efficient quantum-trajectory simulations.

title: Q-ClassicalNN: A Four-Qubit Hybrid Neural Network for Binary Image Classification
authors: Paksha Bhamare, Sakshi Singh, Nidhi Gangurde, Sakshi Chaudhari
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Q-ClassicalNN: A Four-Qubit Hybrid Neural Network for Binary Image Classification This research presents Q-ClassicalNN, a hybrid quantum-classical neural network architecture designed to investigate the integration of quantum computing with conventional machine learning for image classification. The proposed framework combines classical feature extraction, parameterized quantum circuits, quantum measurement, and classical classification within a unified computational architecture. The model employs a four-qubit quantum circuit incorporating angle embedding, parameterized rotation gates, CNOT entangling operations, and Pauli-Z expectation-value measurements. The framework is implemented using Python, PyTorch, and PennyLane, with quantum operations executed through the default.qubit simulator. Experimental evaluation is conducted using the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, comprising 2,000 training samples and 1,000 testing samples for binary classification. Across three experimental runs, the proposed Q-ClassicalNN achieves a reported mean classification accuracy of 99.93%, compared with 99.87% achieved by a classical neural network baseline. The study further examines computational overhead, quantum circuit scalability, mathematical foundations, measurement mechanisms, statistical evaluation, and the limitations of simulator-based quantum machine learning. While the experimental findings demonstrate the feasibility of hybrid quantum-classical architectures, they do not establish a definitive quantum computational advantage. This research contributes an implementation-focused investigation of hybrid quantum-classical learning systems and provides a foundation for future studies involving multiclass classification, quantum circuit optimization, and physical quantum hardware.

title: AI-driven inverse design of quantum materials: From crystal structures to quantum states
authors: Ganlin Xiang, Ze-Feng Gao, Zhong-Yi Lu
abstract: Quantum materials exhibit emergent phenomena arising from quantum coherence, topology, magnetism, and many-body interactions and are increasingly important to fundamental quantum science and emerging quantum technologies. Machine learning, a branch of artificial intelligence (AI), supports materials discovery through property prediction, candidate screening, and target-driven structure generation or optimization, thereby accelerating the theoretical search for materials with target properties. This review examines machine learning for quantum-materials discovery at three interconnected levels: crystal structures, quantum properties and electronic Hamiltonians, and low-energy effective Hamiltonians, distinguishing prediction, screening, and target-driven design. Inverse design provides a framework that can connect generative models for candidate generation with foundation models for transferable representation and evaluation. Future progress should focus on data expansion, representation transfer, multi-objective optimization, and experimental validation, with autonomous laboratories offering a possible route toward large-scale synthesis and feedback.

title: A deep-learning-boosted framework for quantum sensing with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond
authors: Changyu Yao, Haochen Shen, Zhongyuan Liu, Ruotian Gong, Md Shakil Bin Kashem, Stella Varnum, Liangyu Li, Hangyue Li
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a versatile quantum sensing platform for high sensitivity measurements of magnetic fields, temperature, and strain with nanoscale spatial resolution. A common bottleneck is the analysis of optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, where target quantities are encoded in resonance features. Conventional nonlinear fitting is often computationally expensive, sensitive to initialization, and prone to failure at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Here we introduce a robust, efficient machine learning (ML) framework for real-time ODMR analysis based on a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN). The model performs direct parameter inference without initial guesses or iterative optimization, and is naturally parallelizable on graphics processing units (GPU) for high-throughput processing. We validate the approach on both synthetic and experimental datasets, showing improved throughput, accuracy, and robustness than standard nonlinear fitting, with the largest gains in the low-SNR regime. We further validate our methods in two representative sensing applications: diagnosing intracellular temperature changes using nanodiamond probes and widefield magnetic imaging of superconducting vortices in a high-temperature superconductor. This deep-learning inference framework enables fast and reliable extraction of physical parameters from complex ODMR data and provides a scalable route to real-time quantum sensing and imaging.

title: TensorCircuit-NG: A universal, composable, and scalable platform for quantum computing and quantum simulation
authors: Shi-Xin Zhang, Yu-Qin Chen, Weitang Li, Jiace Sun, Wei-Guo Ma, Pei-Lin Zheng, Yu-Xiang Huang, Qi-Xiang Wang
abstract: We present TensorCircuit-NG, a next-generation quantum software platform designed to bridge the gap between quantum physics, artificial intelligence, and high-performance computing. Moving beyond the scope of traditional circuit simulators, TensorCircuit-NG establishes a unified, tensornative programming paradigm where quantum circuits, tensor networks, and neural networks fuse into a single, end-to-end differentiable computational graph. Built upon industry-standard machine learning backends (JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch), the framework introduces comprehensive capabilities for approximate circuit simulation, analog dynamics, fermion Gaussian states, qudit systems, and scalable noise modeling. To tackle the exponential complexity of deep quantum circuits, TensorCircuit-NG implements advanced distributed computing strategies, including automated data parallelism and model-parallel tensor network slicing. We validate these capabilities on GPU clusters, demonstrating a near-linear speedup in distributed variational quantum algorithms. TensorCircuit-NG enables flagship applications, including end-to-end QML for CIFAR-100 computer vision, efficient pipelines from quantum states to neural networks via classical shadows, and differentiable optimization of tensor network states for many-body physics. CONTENTS I. Introduction 2 A. The Evolution of TensorCircuit 3

title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference
authors: Yixiong Chen
abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.

title: Structure theorem for quantum limit cycle attractors: A geometric path-integral approach
authors: Nana Siddhartha
abstract: We show a Structure Theorem for an arbitrary separable quantum system (\(\dim\mathcal{H}\leq\aleph_0\)) that is coupled, through a symmetric bidirectional phase interface, to a self-sustaining phase-oscillator environment. Under the assumptions of \(U(1)\) covariance, instantaneous Lindblad bounded positivity, and the existence of an entrainable periodic attractor, the reduced generator is forced into a universal operator structure consisting of a state-dependent coherent recoil together with single-quantum feedback. Positivity further imposes a sharp dimensional dichotomy: purely dissipative gain saturation is forbidden in finite dimensions by trace-norm contraction, so coherent feedback is mandatory for qubits and qudits, whereas unbounded ladder algebras permit purely dissipative saturation. Expanding the general feedback functionals to leading order in the coupling recovers a canonical polynomial master equation that remains completely positive and trace-preserving in every dimension and combines additively with ordinary linear Lindblad channels. An accompanying Inverse Coupling Theorem shows that an autonomous periodic orbit can be sustained only when the interaction manifold has non-trivial fundamental group \(π_1(\mathcal{M})=\mathbb{Z}\), thereby isolating the sinusoidal \(U(1)\)-covariant phase coupling as the generic mechanism. The resulting implementation is realized explicitly for a single qubit, a bipartite two-qubit system, and a bosonic Fock space.

title: Reproducible distributions of energy-relaxation times in superconducting qubits from broadband SWAP spectroscopy
authors: Joaquin Minguzzi, John Clai Owens, Maximilien F. Debbas, Ana Valdés-Curiel, Ming-Han Chou, Haifeng Qiao, Shahriar Aghaeimeibodi, Oskar Painter
abstract: The distribution of the qubit energy-relaxation time (T1) in a superconducting quantum processor affects its logical error rates. However, reports on qubit fabrication quality focus on the median or best-case T1 from measurements that are not reproducible due to resonant coupling to two-level system (TLS) defects whose frequencies fluctuate in time. Here, we sweep the frequency f01 of a flux-tunable qubit over several GHz with SWAP spectroscopy, quoting the quality factor Q = 2 pi f01 T1 to make T1 comparable across frequencies. We show that the cumulative distribution of Q pooled over the sweep is reproducible across four thermal cycles spanning 326 days, up to the reshuffling of strongly coupled TLSs. In contrast to repeated measurements at a single frequency, the medians of the broadband Q distributions spread by an order of magnitude less over 3 days. The distance between the cumulative distributions of repeats comes close to its sampling floor only for the broadband sweeps. The broadband Q distribution further resolves small coherence differences between identically designed qubits on two dies of the same wafer. These results establish the broadband Q distribution as a reproducible metric for qubit fabrication quality.

title: How Many Autonomous Encoded Qubits Force an Isotropic Noise Response?
authors: Xu Chen, Xue Ma
abstract: Depolarizing noise scales trace distances by a common factor. An encoded qubit is autonomous if its reduced input state determines its output. For $D=2^n\ge4$, autonomy forces this isotropy at a sharp threshold of $(D^2+5)/3$ generic encodings, two more than state tomography requires. For Pauli noise, one generic encoding suffices. With one-bit readouts and no quantum memory or reference, switching encodings cuts the worst-case cost for the Pauli test by a factor of $D$, up to logarithms. For any family, a channel with leakage $O(D^{-3/2})$ can transmit one bit perfectly and erase another.

title: Phonon-Aware Electron-to-Nuclear Spin Quantum Memory in NV Centers
authors: Manjith Baby Sarojam Chellam
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a promising solid-state platform for quantum memory: the electron spin can be optically initialized and read out, while nearby nuclear spins have long coherence times and can serve as storage qubits. In this work, we develop a phonon-aware open quantum system model for electron-to-nuclear spin state transfer in a single NV center. The model includes the NV electron spin, a coupled 13C nuclear spin, the hyperfine interaction, an effective microwave/radio-frequency-assisted SWAP interaction for writing and reading, a single effective phonon mode with longitudinal spin-phonon coupling, and Lindblad relaxation and dephasing channels. The dynamics are simulated with the Lindblad master equation in QuTiP, using the secular approximation and a hyperfine-resonant drive in the rotating frame. Without spin-phonon coupling and electron decoherence, the write-store-read protocol recovers the stored state with a fidelity above 0.9999. With the default decoherence rates, increasing the spin-phonon coupling from 0 to 0.06 MHz lowers the worst-case retrieval fidelity from 0.9994 to 0.9884, and the fidelity oscillates with the phonon-mode period because electron-phonon entanglement generated during the write step is partially undone during the read step. With a phenomenological temperature-dependent rate model, the fidelity decreases monotonically from 0.9997 at 1 K to 0.9938 at 300 K, while storage-time losses follow the assumed nuclear-spin decoherence rates. The storage-time plots, temperature sweep, and parameter maps identify operating regimes for NV-center quantum memory, and the accompanying open-source code provides a reproducible framework for studying phonon-limited quantum memory.

title: Quantum Advantage in Privacy-Preserving Hypothesis Testing via Entanglement-Assisted Classical Communication
authors: Ji-Ho Jung, Seung-Hyun Nam, Si-Hyeon Lee
abstract: Quantum mechanisms satisfying quantum local differential privacy (QLDP) have been shown to achieve a quantum advantage over classical local differential privacy (LDP) mechanisms in certain hypothesis-testing problems. While previous demonstrations have considered the transmission of quantum states from users to a server, we investigate whether this advantage can persist under entanglement-assisted classical communication (EACC), where users and the server share entanglement in advance and communicate only classical messages. We formulate an EACC-based hypothesis-testing framework and introduce measurement local differential privacy (MLDP) to protect private inputs against arbitrary shared quantum states and server-side measurements. We establish that QLDP classical-to-quantum channels admit MLDP-compliant EACC simulations and that, in the high-privacy regime, certain optimal QLDP mechanisms can be realized with one-bit classical communication, albeit using high-dimensional entanglement. We then demonstrate that a strict quantum advantage persists even when the pre-shared entanglement is restricted to a single qubit pair and each user communicates only one classical bit. Using EACC protocols based on the geometry of qubit measurements, we establish this advantage for both asymmetric and symmetric hypothesis testing and every input alphabet of size $v \geq 3$ in the high-privacy limit. The ratio of the achieved error exponent to the optimal one under the LDP constraint is at least $5/4$ for all such alphabets and approaches $3/2$ as $v$ grows. These results demonstrate that quantum advantage in locally private hypothesis testing can persist under simultaneous constraints on entanglement dimension and classical communication.

title: Geometry, masking and selection in Differential Evolution and SOMA on quantum state manifolds
authors: Vojtěch Novák, Ivan Zelinka
abstract: Differential Evolution (DE) and the Self-Organizing Migrating Algorithm (SOMA) generate new candidates through vector arithmetic: they subtract population members, scale the difference, and mask coordinates. Many practical search spaces are not vector spaces, however. Rotation angles are periodic, normalized states lie on spheres and projective spaces, and circuit parameters are coupled through the quantum states they produce. We present a systematic study of how such geometry affects the core operations of DE and SOMA. Keeping the operators and selection rules fixed, we replace only their geometric primitives and separate the effects of difference construction, masking, and selection in a large paired numerical study covering textbook manifolds and variational quantum problems. Geometry-consistent differences make full-crossover (CR = 1) DE significantly better on 16 of 31 non-Euclidean configurations, with no significant deterioration, and the advantage persists when the measured computational cost of each variant is taken into account. The effect is largest where ordinary subtraction misrepresents distances between candidates: success on periodic synchronization rises from 44% to 100%, and on a positive-definite matrix problem from 1% to 99%. On six- qubit variational eigensolvers, shortest-path angular differences reduce the mean final loss by 90% for about 3% extra runtime. The improvements come with two contrasting diversity patterns, more effective population contraction or preserved population diversity, so higher acceptance rates do not necessarily indicate better search. Crossover masks interact with geometry: they can favor cheaper retractions and can increase the distance moved in quantum-state space when circuit parameters are coupled. These results give practical rules for designing population-based optimizers on non-Euclidean and quantum search spaces.

title: Ancilla-Assisted Accelerated Readout of Transmon Qubits
authors: Christopher Corlett, Noah Linden, Paul Skrzypczyk
abstract: We present a scheme for accelerating dispersive readout of superconducting transmon qubits. Dispersive readout works by weakly coupling the target transmon to a resonator, such that the resonator experiences a state-dependent frequency shift, which can then be read out. Our scheme introduces an ancillary transmon coupled to the same resonator. By appropriately correlating its state with that of the target transmon (using a fast CNOT gate), we show that the resonator frequency shift is approximately doubled, halving the required measurement duration to maintain the same quality. We present analytical results within the dispersive approximation, before employing and extending the recently introduced technique of branch analysis to account for ionization and other nonlinearities. Using this, and taking into account realistic noise and gate times, we show that our scheme allows measurement durations smaller by a factor of approximately 0.6, demonstrating that it offers a viable route for accelerating measurements of transmon qubits.

title: Intrinsically nonlinear nanomechanical resonator toward the single-phonon Kerr regime
authors: S. Klingel, T. Althuon, C. Wassmer, C. Sürgers, T. Cubaynes, W. Wernsdorfer
abstract: Manipulating a physical system at the single-quantum level typically requires an anharmonic energy spectrum. Nanomechanical resonators, however, are commonly admitted to be linear objects in the single-phonon regime, thus motivating most efforts to employ external sources of nonlinearity at the cost of added relaxation and decoherence channels. Here, we take a radically different approach by directly exploiting strong intrinsic mechanical nonlinearities. We quantify this nonlinearity using a novel method based on the coupling between bending modes. Using this technique, we establish an upper bound of 34.0 +/- 9.7 phonons for the onset of intrinsically mechanical bistability. In addition, we highlight a new tuning mechanism based on a mechanical polarization angle of an upward-buckled nanotube resonator allowing us to reach an optimal working point. Extrapolating this level of intrinsic nonlinearity to realistically shorter resonators shows that the single-phonon Kerr regime is within reach, allowing for the realization of purely mechanical Schrödinger-cat states and highly coherent mechanical qubits.

title: Experimental characterisation of compilation-dependent Grover--Rudolph probability distribution loading on a three-qubit NMR processor
authors: Antonio Falcó, Daniela Falcó-Pomares, Juan-Carlos Latorre, Yuefeng Lin
abstract:
Exact state-preparation circuits are normally judged by how closely the measured output distribution reproduces the target. Using the ancilla-free Grover-Rudolph construction compiled into {Ry, X, CNOT}, we ask instead how much the accuracy of a probability-distribution loading depends on which of several logically equivalent compilations is executed.
  Two Gray-code realisations of the level-2 uniformly controlled rotation, A and B, differ only in the order of their CNOT controls: same unitary, same angles. On a three-qubit liquid-state NMR processor they do not perform identically. Across 700 runs over seven targets the A/B contrast is significant for 3 of them under Holm, with no fixed sign.
  Two further campaigns isolate the effect within one unit. Removing the circuit's identity-equivalent gates, which changes the executed schedule but not the unitary, affects the two realisations differently: a ladder x intervention interaction of +0.0625 (95% CI [+0.0306, +0.0944], paired p = 4.8e-4), reversing the sign of the A/B advantage. Across five acquisitions of this one logical circuit the contrast runs from +0.0395 to -0.0229. Not every compilation choice matters: commanding the two level-1 inverse rotations as 720 deg - theta rather than -theta, with the gate list unchanged, moves the mean fidelity by -0.0006 ([-0.0157, +0.0146]) on one target in one session. We offer the order and timing of the executed pulses as the hypothesis these observations favour, without identifying a mechanism.
  The metric does not certify coherences, and the measured correlators are inconsistent with any global depolarising description: on the uniform target, at a classical fidelity of 0.962, a two-body correlation of +0.217 appears where the target has none. Run-level data and code are deposited for every campaign run on our own unit; the pulse-level campaign is reported from summary tables.

title: Noise threshold for learning with quantum memory
authors: Miaojiang Chen, Wenjing Xiao, Haiqiang Chen, Jiarong Liang, Anfeng Liu, Zhenrong Zhang, Athanasios V. Vasilakos, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: A quantum memory can reduce exponentially the number of experiments needed to learn a physical process, but real memories are noisy. Here we show that, for Pauli memory noise with eigenvalues $λ_X,λ_Y,λ_Z$, the advantage is governed by $λ_X^2+λ_Y^2+λ_Z^2$. We prove that no protocol with an entangled probe gains an exponential advantage when this sum is at most one, reduce the general case to the additivity of a Rényi-2 coherent information, and find coded memories that retain a growing advantage within 1% of this threshold. On a superconducting processor, nine simultaneously operated Bell pairs show an advantage that grows or shrinks exponentially with system size, reversing where a parameter-free model predicts. A three-qubit repetition code turns a shrinking advantage into a growing one with all processor and readout errors included, and under dephasing its memory performs better than Bell sampling in any memory frame on a perfect processor.

title: Experimental Quantum Hardware Benchmarks of Flat Non-Clifford Hypergraph States, Antipodal Obstructions, and Nonlocal Games on IBM Heron r2
authors: Filipe Martins Vono, Valéria Gonzaga Santos, André Oliveira Naufel de Toledo
abstract: Real-hardware demonstrations of quantum contextuality have reached high precision on superconducting processors, exemplified by Google Quantum AI's Mermin-Peres magic square and stabilizer games on Willow (Science, 2026). Extending such benchmarks beyond the Clifford regime requires non-Clifford hypergraph states |ψ_f> = 2^{-n/2} \sum_x (-1)^{f(x)} |x> governed by discrete algebraic invariants. Building on our Lean 4-verified framework of Modular Walsh Rigidity and Antipodal Obstructions, we present an experimental study on two 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors (ibm_fez, ibm_kingston) across 3 to 50 qubits and 11 auditable jobs (2.13 RUs total). First, we verify antipodal obstructions and mod-17 Walsh rigidity for degree-3/4 states (n=6,8,10), observing 5.4x-11.6x X-basis flatness separation between bent states, obstructed controls, and a degree-4 mod-3 fooler (W = +-1 mod 3), plus n=7 nonlinearity extraction (54.83 vs. 56.00). Second, barrier-protected Loschmidt echoes confirm non-Clifford coherence up to genuinely entangled 16-qubit degree-4 states (1,488x above random on ibm_fez; 17,296x on ibm_kingston for 2x8q, a 2.87x cross-chip gain) and locate a Heavy-Hex depth-513 coherence cliff. Third, calibration-aware layout raises the raw Mermin-Peres win rate on ibm_fez to 96.85 +- 0.09% raw (+87.4 sigma above 88.89% classical; 1.45 pp below Willow's 98.30% raw), while a tensored SPAM diagnostic reaches 98.35%. Uniformly random even-weight GHZ parity games beat the classical bound up to n=30 (89.44% [+79.4 sigma] at 6q to 59.46 +- 0.54% [+17.4 sigma] at 30q). Finally, 3-qubit CCZ rotated Mermin-3 (83.95 +- 0.29%, +31.2 sigma) and Hardy/Guhne-Cabello (77.15 +- 0.33%, +6.5 sigma) games strictly violate the exhaustive 75.00% LHV ceiling, and degree-3/4 antipodal parity witnesses achieve up to +45.87 pp (n=12) and +35.79 pp joint advantage on connected 16-qubit degree-4 states.

title: Unitary Synthesis with a Unary Tracker
authors: Fred Sun
abstract: This manuscript studies general unitary synthesis using unary-encoded ancillary register. Our first construction focuses on the $T$-cost of unitary synthesis. We maintain a unary register that coherently tracks the computational-basis label of the data. This allows Boolean lookups to use only CNOTs and shares the precision-dependent synthesis cost across the branches of each cosine-sine decomposition (CSD) factor. For a classically specified $n$-qubit unitary with $K$ mixing branches in its CSD, we obtain $T$-count $O(K+NL)$ using $N+O(L)$ clean ancillas, where $N=2^n$ and $L=n+\log(1/ε)$. We also give a related construction that directly applies the unitary onto a unary register to implement disjoint branches in parallel. Combining this with the quantum Shannon decomposition gives space-depth volume $O(N^2)$ using arbitrary single-qubit gates and CNOTs, which matches the asymptotically optimal bound.

title: Fewer Parameters, Longer Runtimes: The Wall-Clock Cost of Hybrid Quantum Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Leyan Lyu, Shabnam Jabeen
abstract: While hybrid quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks (QCPINNs) are often described as efficient because they have fewer trainable parameters than classical PINNs, parameter count does not measure wall-clock cost. To examine this gap on a one-dimensional seawater temperature diffusion benchmark, with the quantum circuits simulated on a CPU, we time the four cumulative stages a PINN needs (the forward pass, the first- and second-order input gradients, and the PDE-loss parameter gradient) for a classical PINN, four hybrid configurations that differ in qubit count and circuit depth, and size-matched classical controls that share the hybrids' classical layers. We find that the hybrids are 14-56x slower than the classical PINN for the forward pass and 10-97x slower for the PDE-loss parameter gradient, and even against the size-matched controls, they remain 9-85x slower. Further, over the tested ranges, runtime increased approximately exponentially with qubit count, approximately linearly with circuit depth, and sub-linearly with batch size, while for the circuit-only forward pass, a second simulator backend was 10-165x slower under the same calling pattern. Although the hybrids have 38-44% fewer parameters than the classical PINN, this reduction comes from their smaller classical layers, as the quantum circuit accounts for at most 2.5% of each hybrid's parameters. Yet parameter count failed to predict runtime even among the classical networks, since the size-matched controls, despite having fewer parameters than the classical PINN, run slower than it. Our conclusion is that fewer parameters did not mean lower cost: every hybrid took at least ten times longer than the classical PINN at every stage, and the gap grew quickly with the number of qubits.

title: $\mathsf{AC}^0 \not\subseteq \mathsf{BQAC}^0/\mathsf{qpoly}$ via Sublinear-Degree Pauli Approximation
authors: Xiaoming Sun, Jingheng Wang
abstract:
We prove $\mathsf{AC}^0 \not\subseteq \mathsf{BQAC}^0/\mathsf{qpoly}$ in the single-copy, single-output model via an explicit $\mathsf{P}$-uniform family of linear-size monotone depth-2 CNFs. Every $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuit with arbitrary quantum advice achieves only an inverse-polynomial worst-case advantage over random guessing on this family. To prove this, we approximate the acceptance operator of any such circuit in operator norm by an advice-independent Hermitian operator of sublinear Pauli degree on a designated register alone, with degree exponent independent of width. Product-projection localization and Pauli twirling produce an auxiliary-register spectral cutoff that folds into contractions during backward peeling.
  The same approximation yields two stretched-exponential bounds against $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits on $m$-qubit states. First, given polynomially many copies and input-independent quantum advice, single-output circuits distinguish exact or exponentially approximate state $2$-designs from Haar-random states with advantage at most $e^{-m^α}$. Second, any state prepared from fewer than $k$ arbitrary input qubits and remaining $|0\rangle$ inputs has spectral weight at most $2e^{-m^α}$ in a constant-energy-density band of an Anshu--Breuckmann--Nirkhe NLTS Hamiltonian encoding $k$ logical qubits. Both bounds hold for every fixed $α\in(0,1)$.

title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More
authors: Masayuki Miyamoto
abstract:
The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. For general edge weights, the classical dynamic programs of Bellman and of Held and Karp solve TSP on $n$ cities in $O^*(2^n)$ time. To date, no $\Oh(c^n)$-time classical algorithm is known for any $c<2$. Combining Grover search with the dynamic programming technique, Ambainis et al. (SODA 2019) introduced a quantum algorithm with running time $O^*(1.7274^n)$, which is still the best known quantum time bound.
  In this work, we improve the running time to $O^*(1.70961^n)$. The core idea of our algorithm is to combine the framework of Ambainis et al. with the extremal set-system framework, which was recently used for classical space-time tradeoffs of TSP by Jabal Ameli, Nederlof and Wang (FOCS 2026) and Dallant and Kozma (FOCS 2026). To obtain our upper bound, we decompose the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of different sizes, for which, based on the idea of set-systems, the optimal values are computed using dynamic programming with small success probability and use amplitude amplification. Using the same idea, we also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP, improving the previous results of Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant (arXiv:2607.12374). Finally, we obtain the same quantum upper bounds for several other related problems.

title: Unified preparation of exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scars from Dicke states
authors: Yuki Asari, Masaya Kunimi, Tetsuro Nikuni
abstract: We propose a unified quantum algorithm for preparing exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scar (QMBS) states in the spin-1 {\it XY}, domain-wall-conserving, and Onsager scar models. Model-dependent isometries map the exact scar states to Dicke states and the target asymptotic QMBS states to gapless magnon excitations of the spin-1/2 ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain. Exact QMBS states are prepared by applying the inverse isometries to Dicke states. For asymptotic QMBS states, block encoding first prepares the magnon excitations from Dicke states to a prescribed fidelity, after which the inverse isometries map the prepared states back to the physical chains. At fixed target fidelity, the block-encoding success probability has a positive lower bound independent of system size and scar index, implying that a constant number of amplitude amplification rounds suffices. Our algorithm enables systematic studies of nonergodic dynamics on programmable quantum simulators.

title: Search-for-Gradient: Search-Based Restarts for Optimisation in Structured Flat Landscapes of Variational Quantum Algorithms
authors: Subham Das, Bikash K. Behera, Andrés Camilo Granda Arango, Giuseppe Sergioli, Roberto Giuntini
abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are a promising class of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms that involve parameterised quantum circuits and classical optimisation. VQAs have found applications in simulation, optimisation, and machine learning. However, their scalability is hindered by flat landscapes-regions in the parameter space where gradients vanish exponentially small. In such regimes, gradient-based optimisation methods fail because parameter updates become ineffective in the absence of informative gradients. In this work, we propose a search-based restart framework to escape flat regions in structured flat landscapes, in which small trainable regions exist within a large flat landscape. This framework approaches the plateau escape as a search problem and locates trainable regions. The optimiser's parameters stop updating when the gradients vanish, and the method then searches over-sampled points to identify landscapes with nonzero gradients. We provide theoretical estimates of the number of jumps and the probability of escape from flat landscapes. This restarts the local optimisation process and avoids stagnation. We tested this framework on synthetic functions that mimic structured flat landscapes and a real quantum circuit cost landscape. Theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that Search-for-Gradient improves optimisation performance in structured flat landscapes. The proposed framework assumes the existence of a trainable region with nonzero measure and will not work if it has zero measure. Our framework can be integrated with existing VQAs to improve trainability and robustness.

title: High-Throughput GPU Decoding of Quantum Bivariate Bicycle Codes under Circuit-Level Noise
authors: Aditya Sodhani, Keshab K. Parhi
abstract: Bivariate bicycle (BB) codes reduce the physical-qubit overhead of quantum error correction compared to other codes such as Surface codes, but circuit-level faults create dependencies across measurement rounds that limit decoding throughput. We present a parallel-window GPU decoder that combines reusable fault patterns, compact shared-memory state, and persistent GPU workers using min-sum with Relay-BP recovery. On an RTX 5090, the proposed decoder keeps pace with one syndrome round every 1 $μ$s across all four evaluated codes, up to [[144,12,12]] with 63-144 $μ$s median commit delays. This rate has not been demonstrated in prior circuit-level GPU decoding studies and it provides $120\times$ higher decoding throughput than sequential sliding-window decoding. Checking neighboring detector rounds before accepting a decoding result reduces failure rates by up to 65%. For [[144,12,12]] at $p=0.002$, our proposed decoder achieves $7.58\times 10^{-6}$ failures per round, 36% lower than the published belief propagation (BP) with syndrome flipping (BP-SF) result.

title: LatentRL-QAS: Transfer via Latent Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Architecture Search
authors: Maria Ilektra Plakitsi, Sebastian Feld, Akash Kundu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) emerges as a prominent approach to quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits. However, transferring what an agent has learned from one number of qubits to another is still weakly explored: the state, the action space and the neural network of a state-of-the-art RL-QAS agent all grow with the number of qubits, which makes transfer learning across qubit counts prohibitive. We make this transfer possible by introducing LatentRL-QAS, a latent space transfer and refresh framework for RL-based QAS. At its core, a circuit variational autoencoder encodes a circuit as one token per gate and maps circuits on any number of qubits into the same latent space. An RL agent navigates this space instead of adding gates, so its state, actions and network have the same size at every qubit count. The latent space is periodically refreshed with the agent's new discoveries and, for a larger system, grown from the solutions of the smaller one, so what is transferred is the representation of circuits, not network weights or past experience. To show transfer, we consider absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, a resource for quantum error correction. LatentRL-QAS discovers the five- and six-qubit AME states without being shown them and prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes, whereas the baseline RL-QAS fails to find them with the same budget, even with a network 10 to 17 times larger. LatentRL-QAS remains robust under depolarizing noise with single-qubit gate errors amplified 10x and two-qubit gate errors 5x compared with IBM quantum hardware. By decoupling the RL agent from the number of qubits, LatentRL-QAS lets quantum architecture search reuse circuit representations learned on smaller problems, providing a foundation for the transferable design of circuits across quantum optimization problems.

title: A scalable dense silicon qubit architecture with logical operations
authors: Masahiro Tadokoro, Tetsuo Kodera
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires a large number of physical qubits to encode logical qubits with sufficiently low error rates. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform because of their small footprint, compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing technologies, and demonstrated high-fidelity operations. However, realizing a scalable architecture that supports quantum error correction, qubit transport, wiring, and logical gate operations remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture designed to support large-scale FTQC. The architecture consists of qubit memories, data qubit lanes, and cross junctions. Qubit memories store logical qubits encoded using the rotated surface code and support logical single-qubit operations. Data qubit lanes enable high-speed one-dimensional spin shuttling for connectivity between logical qubits, while cross junctions provide routing functionality and implement transversal logical CNOT gates. Using experimentally demonstrated silicon spin qubit parameters, we evaluate logical error rates as a function of code distance and estimate that a code distance of at least 21 is required to achieve logical error rates below $10^{-10}$ per syndrome cycle. We further analyze wiring constraints based on CMOS-compatible multiplexed control schemes and show that, with optimized wiring efficiency, more than 120,000 logical qubits could be integrated on a 100 mm $\times$ 100 mm chip. These results provide a practical roadmap toward large-scale FTQC based on silicon spin qubit technology.

title: Amatlas: A 2D Array Architecture for Union-Find Decoding Without Global Coordination
authors: Takuya Kasamura, Leo Itoh, Seita Tsuboi, Hidetsugu Irie, Junichiro Kadomoto
abstract: Real-time decoding of the surface code is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and scaling the decoder to large code distances in hardware remains a challenge. The locality of Union-Find (UF) decoding makes it a leading candidate for such a decoder in distributed hardware. Prior distributed UF decoders, however, map the three-dimensional decoding graph onto an array of processing elements (PEs) under a central controller that synchronizes all PEs at every stage, and a three-dimensional array of PEs scales poorly on planar hardware. This paper presents Amatlas, a two-dimensional PE array for UF decoding that operates without a central controller. Amatlas assigns one PE to each stabilizer on the two-dimensional qubit lattice and stores the states of all measurement rounds in the local memory of the PE, so every link connects adjacent PEs in the array. Every PE advances on every clock cycle without array-wide synchronization, and the clock is the only global signal of the array. Under circuit-level noise, the RTL implementation of Amatlas fits a VCU129 FPGA up to a code distance of 25, where the average decoding time is 462 ns per round at a physical error rate of 0.1%. Amatlas achieves a threshold of 0.72%, compared with 0.78% reported for UF decoding under the same noise model.

title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm for the Generalised Geography Game
authors: Mriganka Sandilya, Shibdas Roy
abstract: The Generalized Geography Game ($GGG$) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a directed graph, where players alternately move a token along edges without revisiting previously visited vertices. In the existing literature, determining whether an arbitrary position in a graph is a winning position for either player is a well-known $PSPACE$-complete decision problem. Certain formulations of $GGG$ have been shown to fall outside the $PSPACE$-complete complexity class. While $PSPACE$-complete problems are believed to take exponential time for classical computation, quantum computation offers new possibilities. In this work, we present a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time ($BQP$) algorithm for solving the $GGG$ problem. The proposed algorithm runs in time $O(N^{2}/ε^{6})$, which is polynomial in the input size $N$, and achieves bounded error with $ε= O(1/\mathrm{poly}(N))$. This result demonstrates the potential of quantum algorithms to efficiently solve combinatorial game problems that are traditionally considered computationally hard in the classical setting.

title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
authors: Xiaoran Li, Zhi Yin, Zhupeng Han, Zhengquan Pan, Kangyu Zheng
abstract:
Quantum computational chemistry is often framed around a hybrid quantum solver. In practical applications, however, bottlenecks to adoption also lie in the surrounding multiscale workflow. A molecular problem may combine classical molecular mechanics and dynamics, conventional electronic-structure calculations, and a quantum solver for selected orbitals or embedded fragments. This division of work is particularly relevant when a chemically important electronic subspace is strongly correlated. The size of the electronic Hilbert space and the qubit, noise, and circuit-depth constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices make active-space and embedding choices central to a feasible quantum calculation. The resulting energies and gradients must remain consistent with the surrounding classical simulation.
  We present TyxonQ, a workflow layer that connects these levels of treatment rather than addressing only the hybrid quantum algorithm. Four integration interfaces link PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, simulator and hardware backends, and classical consumers. The implementation combines QM/MM and fragment embedding with conventional CCSD/FCI fragment solvers, variational and sampling-based quantum methods, and adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS (through i-PI), and MDI. We describe the contracts and audit coverage, and evaluate correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support. The purpose of TyxonQ is to support incremental integration of quantum calculations into existing computational chemistry workflows, including those used in industry, while retaining appropriate classical treatments elsewhere.

title: Quantum Algorithm for Direct Estimation of Energy-Level Differences via Quantum Dynamics Simulation
authors: Norifumi Matsumoto, Yuya O. Nakagawa, Shota Kanasugi, Yuichiro Hidaka, Kazunori Maruyama, Hirotaka Oshima
abstract: We present a quantum algorithm for the early fault-tolerant quantum computing (early-FTQC) era that estimates minute energy-level differences, such as energy gradients and molecular forces, at a lower sampling cost than existing phase-estimation methods. Such energy derivatives, accessed as the small energy difference induced by an infinitesimal parameter shift, are central to quantum simulation in chemistry and materials science. Although Statistical Phase Estimation (SPE) is well-suited to energy estimation in this era, applying it to an energy difference demands a sampling complexity that scales with the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian, which grows with system size. Our algorithm overcomes this by incorporating two time-evolution operators, corresponding to the Hamiltonians before and after the parameter shift, into a single quantum circuit, which is combined with a non-adaptive, statistically sampled reconstruction in the energy-difference domain. This reduces the relevant scale from the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian to that of the operator norm of the Hamiltonian derivative and the parameter shift, thereby lowering the sampling complexity. We further propose the joint estimation of energy eigenvalues and their differences, giving a holistic view of the energy landscape. Numerical simulations and resource estimations on prototypical systems, such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, demonstrate the resulting reductions in required resources without compromising precision. This positions energy-difference estimation as a practical task for early-FTQC devices, opening a route to molecular forces, response properties, and excited-state energy differences.

title: Native higher-order optimization with entropy quantum computing
authors: Narendra N. Hegade, Pranav Chandarana, Sebastian Wagner, Bahman Qawami, Wesley Dyk
abstract: Higher-order interactions are common in applied optimization: parity checks, radar-code sidelobes, portfolio skewness and kurtosis, and marketing-channel synergies all yield cubic or quartic objectives. Quantum annealers and most Ising machines accept only quadratic objectives, and gate-based quantum processors build every higher-order term from two-qubit gates. Entropy quantum computing, realized in the hybrid photonic-electronic Dirac-3S system, accepts polynomials of degree up to five with all-to-all coupling over binary, integer or simplex-constrained continuous variables. No user-supplied quadratization or circuit compilation is needed. We formulate four industrial use cases as six cubic and quartic instances, run them on Dirac-3S with 30 samples each, and score every sample against a certified optimum or a classical best-known value. We also estimate their cost on quantum annealers, superconducting grids and trapped-ion registers under standard mappings. For the two densest instances, a portfolio with about 80,000 terms and a budget allocation with 360,000 terms, the quadratized problems need embeddings far beyond current annealers, over $10^5$ physical qubits for the portfolio alone, and one phase-separation layer costs over $10^6$ two-qubit gates before optimization. Dirac-3S ran all six natively and returned feasible, distinct solutions. All samples of the binary instances are single-flip local minima. The best portfolio sample lies within 0.32% of the best-known value and the best budget sample 15% above it, but no sample reached its reference. Classical solvers reach the references within minutes at these sizes, and random starts followed by a local polish reach comparable or better values, so the advantage established here is one of expressibility and mapping cost, not of solution quality. Whether it extends to time to solution at larger sizes remains open.

title: Magic Moments: An Operational Approach of Certifying Nonstabilizerness from Few Copies
authors: Kunal Sharma, Sudip Chakrabarty, Saheli Mukherjee, Bivas Mallick, Ananda G. Maity
abstract: Magic is the key resource enabling universal fault-tolerant quantum computation beyond classically simulable stabilizer circuits. Certifying it, however, usually requires either full state tomography or an optimization over the set of stabilizer states, both of which rapidly become prohibitive as the system grows. Here, we introduce a moment-based criterion that certifies magic from a few moments of the discrete Wigner function, without fully reconstructing the distribution itself. For pure states of any number of qudits the criterion is necessary and sufficient, while for mixed states we construct a hierarchy of higher moments conditions that reaches the exact negativity threshold. We also derive lower bounds on sum negativity and mana from low-order moments, and use them to bound the negativity factor in quasiprobability simulation. Each moment can be evaluated as the expectation value of a two-outcome observable on a few copies of the state, measurable with a constant-depth Clifford circuit and a number of rounds independent of qudit number, providing efficient, experimentally accessible tools for certifying and quantifying nonstabilizer resources.

title: The integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition for nonlinear dynamics: Efficient Hamiltonian simulation of the Stepanoff flow
authors: Ilon Joseph, Ivan Novikau, Michael R. Montgomery, Joanna Slawinska, Dimitrios Giannakis
abstract: We propose an efficient unitary numerical time integration strategy for nonlinear dynamical systems: the integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition (I-LTS). First, express the generator as a sum of integrable parts. Second, approximate the full evolution operator using a Lie-Trotter-Suzuki (LTS) decomposition of the desired approximation order in time step. The I-LTS construction ensures that the full evolution operator can be represented as a product of terms that each have an efficient explicit tensor product factorization that can be handled efficiently with tensor network and/or quantum block-encoding methods. Next, we apply this method to an important non-integrable point example of a dynamical system: the Stepanoff flow on the torus. First, we derive an efficient unitary quantum algorithm for simulating the Stepanoff flow that can be thought of as a unitary classical version of a quantum map. Then, we provide a detailed description of the encoding of the two-dimensional system into an efficient quantum circuit, including an efficient block-encoding for all required operators. An efficient Hamiltonian simulation algorithm is constructed using a sequence of alternating quantum Fourier transforms (QFT) and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) circuits. Finally, the circuit is simulated using a numerical emulator of fault-tolerant quantum computers, and the results are found to be consistent with several alternative classical computational methods. While efficient, the need for Trotterization introduces fundamental complexity in requiring small enough time step for an accurate approximation and solving for the transfer operator requires one to confront the linear scaling of the advection operator with grid size.

title: Enhancing the Stationary Optomechanical Entanglement and Cooling of a Rotating Mirror in a Laguerre–Gaussian Optomechanical System via Coherent Feedback
authors: Keru Zhu, Sumei Huang, 邓立 Li Deng, Aixi Chen
abstract: Optomechanical entanglement generation and near‐ground‐state cooling of macroscopic mechanical resonators play important roles in probing fundamental physics and develop new quantum applications. Here, we investigate how a coherent feedback loop affects the stationary optomechanical entanglement and the cooling of a rotating mirror in a Laguerre–Gaussian (LG) optomechanical system. By implementing a coherent feedback loop with a beam splitter and three mirrors outside the cavity, a fraction of the output field is fed back into the optical cavity. In the unresolved‐sideband regime, by adjusting the beam‐splitter reflectivity and the feedback phase, the coherent feedback can significantly enhance the entanglement between the LG cavity field and the rotating mirror due to the feedback‐induced reduction in the effective cavity decay rate, and the optomechanical entanglement is shown to persist for ambient temperatures above 150 K. Furthermore, the coherent feedback can effectively suppress the thermal decoherence effect; even in a 50 K environment, the rotating mirror can be brought close to its quantum ground state by tuning the beam‐splitter reflectivity and the feedback phase to suitable values. Moreover, the effect of optical losses in the feedback loop on entanglement and cooling is discussed. We find that these losses degrade both entanglement and cooling performance.

title: Optical gas thermometry with parts-per-million accuracy
authors: Jin Wang, Yan Tan, Qi Huang, Jin-Ke Li, Cun-Feng Cheng, An-Wen Liu, Shui-Ming Hu
abstract: Optical gas thermometry provides a quantum-based route for primary thermodynamic temperature measurement. This work reports advances in Doppler broadening thermometry (DBT) and line-intensity ratio thermometry (LRT) achieved by implementing cavity mode dispersion spectroscopy (CMDS). The CMDS technique, which relies solely on frequency measurements of cavity-mode dispersive shifts induced by molecular absorption, effectively circumvents the limitations of traditional absorption spectroscopy, such as detector nonlinearity and long-term intensity drifts. We demonstrate record-setting accuracies, with combined standard uncertainties of approximately 12 ppm for DBT and 7 ppm for LRT, establishing the most precise optical thermometry measurements achieved to date. These results validate DBT and LRT as robust, primary thermometry methods grounded in fundamental molecular physics and open new avenues for quantum metrology and precision spectroscopy.

title: Matrix phase-space representations for quantum symmetries
authors: Alexander S. Dellios, M. D. Reid, P. D. Drummond
abstract: We introduce a general phase-space representation that includes global quantum symmetries in the basis expansion. This method, called matrix phase-space, projects the basis onto a reduced Hilbert space, which can greatly reduce sampling errors of many-body quantum simulations when there is a symmetry, and unifies several previous phase-space methods. The purpose of this paper is to provide detailed proofs of basic theorems and operator identities. We also treat several different types of symmetries, corresponding to parity, number, and momentum conservation laws. To illustrate these methods, we give a detailed derivation of previous applications to the topical problem of validating the outputs of Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) quantum computers (QCs) with photon-number-resolving (PNR) detectors. Exact evaluation of GBS PNR output probabilities has exponential classical complexity. Fortunately, special cases of output GBS grouped probabilities have tractable solutions, providing a way to check the results. Using matrix phase-space with parity symmetry, we observe a reduction of over two orders of magnitude in sampling errors compared with earlier methods in low-loss cases. Additional nonlinear examples are also treated. These include the dynamical evolution of a nonlinear damped one-dimensional lattice and the periodic Bose-Hubbard model. More details will be given elsewhere. As well as direct application to experiments, this scalable first-principles method may be useful for validating other QC calculations on large Hilbert spaces.

title: Adaptive quantum metrology with large dynamic range using short one-axis twists
authors: Tyler G. Thurtell, Akimasa Miyake
abstract: Phase estimation with potentially large phase values, i.e., with large dynamic range, has many applications in quantum metrology, for example to atomic clocks. A recently proposed phase estimation scheme approaches the Heisenberg scaling in this global setting using sequences of increasingly squeezed Gaussian states as probes and adaptively chosen, potentially mid-circuit, measurements. In this work, we first observe that the pattern of increase in the squeezing of the probes is applicable even to states with some non-Gaussian features. We then propose an experimentally feasible version of this phase estimation scheme, based on the alternating application of one-axis twist (OAT) operations and rotations. Our protocols are explicitly described in terms of multiple OAT angles whose durations decrease polynomially with system size and spin-squeezing parameters that decay as N − μ , with μ > 2 / 3 in most cases. Using numerical computation of the system-size dependence N − ν of the Bayesian mean-squared error of an estimator, we show that these states are suitable for use in the phase estimation scheme, and highlight the protocols to achieve ν = 17 / 9 and 53 / 27 using two and three OAT operations respectively in the last adaptation stage. We also analyze the limited non-Gaussianity of the resulting probe states and discuss the role of non-Gaussianity in this protocol more generally. Finally, we analyze how robust these protocols are with respect to imperfections such as particle number fluctuations and coherent control fluctuations.

title: Digital Twin Networks for 6G Wireless Systems: Architecture, Enabling Technologies, AI-Driven Control, and Open Challenges
Quantum timekeeping and the dynamics of scrambling in critical systems
authors: Devjyoti Tripathy, Federico Centrone, Sebastian Deffner
abstract: Interacting quantum many-body systems can rapidly scramble quantum information, raising the question of how precisely local subsystems can track the passage of time during this evolution. In this work, we develop a quantum metrological framework for quantum chaos by showing that local subsystems of information scrambling systems naturally function as quantum stopwatches. The reduced quantum state of a subsystem encodes the passage of time through its local temporal distinguishability along its dynamical trajectory. Treating time as the estimation parameter, we then derive a generalized quantum Cramer-Rao bound that directly relates the precision of time estimation to the decay of out-of-time ordered correlators (OTOCs) and subsystem quantum Fisher information (QFI). For a single qubit subsystem, we obtain an exact relation between the incoherent component of subsystem QFI and the decay rate of OTOCs in quantumly chaotic dynamics, while the total subsystem QFI provides an upper bound to the corresponding decay rate. Furthermore, using a scaling analysis based on imaginary-time correlators, we investigate under what conditions the incoherent subsystem QFI exhibits critical amplification near quantum phase transitions. Our results are demonstrated and verified by a numerical analysis of the dynamics of a chaotic Ising chain.

title: Superposed quantum evolutions across chaotic and regular regimes
Resolving topological obstructions to vectorial structured field control
Reconstructing the unitary part of a noisy quantum channel
High-resolution image-projection fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy
Co-optimization of Spin Coherence and Valley Splitting in Si/SiGe Heterostructures
authors: Peihong Zhang, Xuedong Hu, Saif Ullah, J. R. Petta
abstract: Single electron spins can be used to encode and process information in semiconductor quantum devices. Progress has been hindered by materials challenges, such as the small energy splitting between low-lying valley states and hyperfine coupling to nuclear spins. Here we use density functional theory to optimize the valley splitting and spin dephasing time in realistic Si/SiGe heterostructures. Reductions in the Si quantum well width generally increase the valley splitting. However, in narrow quantum wells, a larger fraction of the electronic wavefunction resides in the SiGe buffer layers, which increases the hyperfine coupling with spinful [73]Ge. Our work shows that Si/SiGe heterostructures with 3 – 4 nm wide quantum wells and [73]Ge and [29]Si concentrations of 50 ppm should support average valley splittings Ev > 500 µeV and spin dephasing times T2[∗] [exceeding 15][ µ][s] assuming an effective quantum dot area of 700 nm[2]. In addition, sharper Si/SiGe interfaces in general result in larger valley splittings and longer spin dephasing times.

title: Logarithmic-depth quantum state preparation of polynomials
authors: Baptiste Claudon, Alexis Lucas, Jean-Philip Piquemal, César Feniou, Julien Zylberman
abstract: Quantum state preparation is a central primitive in many quantum algorithms, yet it is generally resource intensive, with efficient constructions known only for structured families of states. This work introduces a method for preparing quantum states whose amplitudes are given by a degree − d polynomial, using circuits with logarithmic depth in the number n of qubits and only O (n) ancilla qubits, improving previous approaches that required linear-depth circuits. The construction first relies on a block-encoding of an affine diagonal operator based on its Pauli-basis decomposition, which involves only n terms. A modified linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) technique is introduced to implement this decomposition in logarithmic depth, together with a novel circuit for the EXACT-one oracle that flags basis states in which exactly one qubit is in the state | 1 ⟩. It then uses a generalized quantum eigenvalue transformation (GQET) to promote this affine operator to an arbitrary degree polynomial. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations are reported along with a proof-of-principle implementation on a Quantinuum System Model H2 trapped-ion quantum processor using 14 qubits and more than 500 primitive quantum gates. Because polynomial approximations are ubiquitous in scientific computing, this construction provides a scalable and resource-efficient approach to quantum state preparation, further improving the potential of quantum algorithms in fields such as chemistry, physics, engineering, and finance.

title: Atomic interface for high-dimensional temporal mode quantum networks
authors: Shicheng Zhang, Aonan Zhang, Ilse Maillette de Buy Wenniger, Paul Burdekin, Jerzy Szuniewicz, Steven Sagona-Stophel, Sarah E. Thomas, Ian A. Walmsley
abstract: Photonic temporal modes are an attractive encoding basis for high-dimensional quantum networks due to their high channel capacity and fiber compatibility. However, realizing their full potential requires devices capable of synchronizing, processing and interfacing these modes across photonic and atomic bandwidths. Here, we demonstrate a programmable high-dimensional temporal mode processor based on a Raman quantum memory in warm cesium vapor. Exploiting the single-mode nature of the Raman interaction kernel, we dynamically shape the control field to synthesize a tunable coherent filter that selectively addresses user-defined temporal waveforms. Operating with 50 ns pulses, we characterize the mode-selectivity of the filter across 30 orthogonal Hermite-Gaussian modes, with five-dimensional process tomography yielding an efficiency-normalized filtering fidelity of 0.955(7). Independent shaping of the read control field further enables programmable temporal-mode conversion with uniform efficiencies comparable to those of mode-preserving storage and retrieval. Moreover, we demonstrate tenfold bandwidth compression and expansion of 10~ns pulses, offering a coherent interface between GHz- and MHz-bandwidth network nodes. These results establish the potential of Raman quantum memories as active nodes for scalable quantum information processing.

title: Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing
Coherent manipulation of interacting electron qubits on solid neon
authors: Xinhao Li, Yizhong Huang, Xu Han, Xianjing Zhou, Amir Yacoby, Dafei Jin
abstract: Electrons trapped on solid neon surfaces serve as low-noise charge qubits with long coherence times and high operational fidelities. Such charge qubits offer full electrical control and compact device footprints, convenient for scaling up with quantum circuits. Realizing two-qubit gates on this platform is a critical step towards practical quantum information processing. In this work, we report the first experimental demonstration of coherent manipulation of multiple interacting electron-on-solid-neon (eNe) charge qubits. By exploiting the electrons naturally confined in close proximity by the surface structures of solid neon, we have achieved a direct qubit-qubit coupling strength of up to 62.5 MHz, as well as implemented cross-resonance (CR) and bSWAP two-qubit gates using global microwave drives. The natural electron confinement by solid neon mitigates the high-density-wiring challenge, simplifies the multi-qubit control, and establishes a unique path to scale up the eNe qubit platform.

title: Optimal Calibration of Qubit Detuning and Crosstalk
authors: David Shnaiderov, Matan Ben Dov, Yoav Woldiger, Assaf Hamo, Eugene Demler, Emanuele G. Dalla Torre
abstract: Characterizing and calibrating physical qubits is essential for maintaining the performance of quantum processors. A key challenge in this process is crosstalk, which complicates the estimation of individual qubit detunings. In this work, we derive optimal strategies for estimating detuning and crosstalk parameters by optimizing Ramsey interference experiments using Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound. We compare several calibration protocols, including measurements of a single quadrature at multiple times and of two quadratures at a single time, for a fixed number of total measurements. Our results predict that the latter approach yields the highest precision and robustness in both cases of isolated and coupled qubits. We validate our approach experimentally using both a single NV center and superconducting transmon qubits. Our approach enables accurate parameter extraction with significantly fewer measurements, resulting in up to a 50% reduction in calibration time while maintaining estimation accuracy.

title: Machine learning models in FinTech for sustainable innovation: a comprehensive empirical evaluation with the S.A.F.E. framework
Performance evaluation of a photon-based quantum router network for Kathmandu Metropolitan City
authors: Chitran Pokhrel, Babu Ram Dawadi, Bishnu Prasad Gautam
abstract: Deploying quantum communication networks in dense cities is challenging because photon loss, noise, and inefficient entanglement distribution degrade fidelity and increase latency. Conventional repeater chains add intermediate nodes along each fiber span, and housing quantum memories at such mid-span sites in a dense city is operationally demanding. This study evaluates a photon-based quantum router network for Kathmandu Metropolitan City in which entanglement buffering and swapping are performed only at quantum router (RTR) nodes co-located with existing network sites. On an infrastructure-derived topology of 12 routers and 14 fiber links, the simulated network achieves a mean fidelity of 0.925 (95% CI 0.916–0.934), a mean throughput of 1159.5 ebps, and a mean latency of 15.28 ms over 83 completed requests. A closed-form multi-hop model, consistent with the simulation for single links, shows that end-to-end fidelity is limited mainly by hop count and by memory and detector efficiency rather than by urban fiber loss, that mid-span repeaters lower the rate on spans shorter than about 9 km, and that the router-only design remains viable for spans up to about 50 km. A simulation of the Illinois Express Quantum Network topology gives fidelity and latency of the same order as reported experimentally.

title: Quantum Algorithms for Computational Fluid Dynamics
authors: Mario Guillaume Cecile, Nis-Luca van Hülst, Tomohiro Hashizume, Pia Siegl, Anonymous, José Diogo Da Costa Jesus, Paul Over, Sergio Bengoechea
abstract: We present a comprehensive review of quantum approaches for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) arising in computational fluid dynamics (CFD). We examine fully quantum approaches, including quantum linear system algorithms (QLSAs), ranging from the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd (HHL) algorithm to quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), Hamiltonian simulation, and quantum lattice Boltzmann methods (QLBMs), while emphasizing hybrid quantum–classical approaches, including quantum-physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) and amplitude-encoded variational PDE solvers. We focus on hardware-agnostic algorithms compatible with present noisy processors and emerging fault-tolerant architectures. For each framework, we analyze the mathematical formulation, algorithmic structure, and principal limitations. We also examine tensor-network (TN) representations, since CFD fields, differential operators, and geometrical information can often be encoded efficiently in low-rank form. The TN formalism bridges CFD discretizations and quantum states, operators, and circuits, enabling compact representations to be translated into tensor-programmable variational quantum algorithms (TP-VQAs). We further review benchmark problems, including Poisson, reaction, diffusion, and nonlinear model equations, and assess how well quantum algorithms capture key features of fluid dynamics. Our analysis highlights that potential quantum advantage is highly problem dependent and governed by condition number, representational complexity, state preparation, and measurement constraints. We outline capabilities, limitations, and challenges toward scalable quantum algorithms for CFD.

title: Non-Gaussianity in cat codes: global incompatibility and local geometric alignment with the magic resource
authors: Yuwei Zhu, Seungbeom Chin, William J. Munro, Kae Nemoto
abstract: Non-Gaussianity is an essential resource for genuine quantum advantages in continuous-variable quantum systems and is regarded as a counterpart of the magic resource in discrete-variable systems. Recently, an exact correspondence between non-Gaussianity (NG) and the magic resource was identified within the Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) encoding framework. Whether such a relation persists beyond GKP encoding, however, remains unclear. Here, we address this question in the cat-code setting. By comparing the Wigner logarithmic negativity (WLN) and a magic measure defined from a phase-operator basis, we analyze the resource geometry of non-degenerate $d$-peaked cat states. We find that cat codes do not inherit the global value-preserving GKP magic--NG equivalence, but their asymptotic WLN geometry allows a constructive local alignment with the magic-measure geometry. Specifically, the sector-adapted asymptotic cat construction has the same local phase-rotation invariance as the magic measure for general $d$, while the qubit construction establishes an explicit local alignment of their complete level-set contours. We also examine how thermal attenuation changes the finite-code contour geometry and the surviving WLN contrast. These results identify both the global incompatibility and the locally constructive relation between magic and non-Gaussian resources in cat codes, suggesting a geometry-based approach to resource correspondences beyond the GKP framework.

title: Logical entangling by qubit permutations in hypergraph products
authors: Keming He, Ziao Tang, Zetong Li, Ge Bai, Xin Eric Wang
abstract: Logical entangling gates are a major source of physical spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Phantom codes reduce this cost by implementing every ordered in-block logical CNOT through physical qubit permutations and Pauli-frame updates. Whether this mechanism can coexist with qLDPC structure is a central question for low-overhead fault-tolerant architectures. We give a complete answer within binary CSS hypergraph product (HGP) codes. Up to natural equivalences, phantomness singles out the simplex–repetition family. The same symmetry further extends to the full in-block logical Clifford group. We evaluate this family under circuit-level noise in logical GHZ-state preparation and Trotterized many-body quantum simulation. With ideally prepared Steane ancillas, the HGP code yields lower observable mismatch rates than the rotated surface-code baseline at distance eight. Reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays offer a natural setting for this approach, supporting nonlocal qLDPC operations while enabling in-block logical CNOTs without additional physical operations. Together, these results connect code symmetry, logical-gate overhead, and qLDPC design, and motivate phantom families with improved asymptotic parameters.

title: Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains
Quantum-Accelerated Self-Consistent Field: A Hybrid Algorithm
authors: Alexis Ralli, Tim Weaving, Thomas M. Bickley, Peter V. Coveney, Peter J. Love
journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
abstract: We present the Grover adaptive search self-consistent field (GAS-SCF) algorithm. GAS-SCF leverages quantum arithmetic to construct an efficient oracle that marks target states (Fock states) which improve upon some initial classical energy estimate. Amplitude amplification then increases the probability of measuring these states. This approach offers a theoretical quadratic speed-up for the optimization problem encountered in SCF quantum chemistry and establishes a baseline against which structured optimization algorithms, such as QAOA and DQI, may be compared. In this work, we classically simulate three examples as proofs of concept of the algorithm, the largest consisting of 26 qubits. We then extend our analysis to two larger systems, with O3 representing the largest case at 330 qubits. These examples are chosen to probe classically challenging SCF regimes. Achieving chemically relevant applications of GAS-SCF will require large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: Quantum in biology, quantum for biology, and biology for quantum: mapping the evidence and the road ahead
authors: Lea Gassab, Betony Adams, Yashine H. Goolam Hossen, Abbas Hassasfar, Onur Pusuluk, Nirosha J. Murugan, Iannis K. Kominis, Özgür Esat Müstecaplıoğlu
abstract: Quantum science and biology now intersect in three complementary directions: quantum in biology, quantum for biology, and biology for quantum. This review provides a structured narrative evidence map of that interface rather than an exhaustive catalogue or formal systematic review. For each topic, we ask what the mechanistic or technological claim is, which quantum resource is invoked, what the strongest experiments and models establish, which classical alternatives or engineering confounds remain competitive, and which tests or benchmarks would most strongly change confidence.
