A compact mathematical framework relates Hamiltonian couplings, environmental decoherence, barrier penetration, spin-dependent reaction yields, and matched perturbations to biological observables. The most mature quantum-in-biology cases remain mechanistically constrained tunneling in some enzymatic hydrogen-transfer reactions and radical-pair spin chemistry as a viable framework for magnetoreception, whereas several higher-visibility topics remain suggestive but unresolved under physiological conditions. In quantum for biology, the central issue is whether quantum-enabled tools improve biological inference relative to strong classical baselines under realistic calibration, dose, throughput, and uncertainty constraints. In biology for quantum, the strongest claims arise when biomolecular structure or self-assembly measurably improves fabrication, integration, or robustness in quantum devices. Summary tables in the Appendix provide a compact cross-map view of the current evidence, major confounds, and the experiments or benchmarks most likely to discriminate between competing explanations.

title: Minimum weight decoding in the colour code is NP-hard
authors: Mark Walters, Mark L. Turner
abstract: All utility-scale quantum computers will require some form of Quantum Error Correction in which logical qubits are encoded in a larger number of physical qubits. One promising encoding is known as the colour code which has broad applicability across all qubit types and can decisively reduce the overhead of certain logical operations when compared to other two-dimensional topological codes such as the surface code. However, whereas the surface code decoding problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time by finding minimum weight matchings in a graph, prior to this work, it was not known whether exact and efficient colour code decoding was possible. Optimism in this area, stemming from the colour code’s significant structure and well understood similarities to the surface code, fanned this uncertainty. In this paper we resolve this, proving that exact decoding of the colour code is NP-hard – that is, there does not exist a polynomial time algorithm unless P=NP. This highlights a notable contrast to some of the colour code’s key competitors, such as the surface code, and motivates continued work in the narrower space of heuristic and approximate algorithms for fast, accurate and scalable colour code decoding.

title: Recursive Clifford noise reduction
authors: Aharon Brodutch, Gregory Baimetov, Edwin Tham, Nicolas Delfosse
abstract: Clifford noise reduction CliNR is a partial error correction scheme that reduces the logical error rate of Clifford circuits at the cost of a modest qubit and gate overhead. The CliNR implementation of an n -qubit Clifford circuit of size s achieves a vanishing logical error rate if s n p 2 → 0 where p is the physical error rate. Here, we propose a recursive version of CliNR that can reduce errors on larger circuits with a relatively small gate overhead. When n p → 0, the logical error rate can be vanishingly small. When s p > 2 this can be achieved with (2 ⌈ log ⁡ (s p) ⌉ + 1) n + 1 qubits and at most 24 s ⌈ (s p) 3.6 ⌉ gates. For s p ≤ 2 we recover the original CliNR. Using numerical simulations, we show that the recursive method can offer an advantage in a realistic near-term parameter regime. When circuit sizes are large enough, recursive CliNR can reach a lower logical error rate than the original CliNR with the same gate overhead. The results offer promise for reducing logical errors in large Clifford circuits with relatively small overheads.

title: Directional codes for quantum LDPC error correction on square and hexagonal grid architectures
authors: György Pál Gehér, David Byfield, Archibald Ruban
abstract: Utility-scale quantum computing requires quantum error correction to protect quantum information against noise. Superconducting hardware is a promising platform for fault-tolerant computation, but its typically two-dimensional nearest-neighbour connectivity restricts the variety of quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes that can be implemented efficiently. Here we introduce directional codes, a family of qLDPC codes compatible with square-grid and, in some cases, hexagonal-grid architectures. The key idea is to use the iSWAP gate to measure long range stabilisers using only local interactions, without requiring additional connectivity. We evaluate directional codes using a superconducting-inspired circuit-level Pauli noise model and compare them to the rotated toric code and bivariate bicycle codes. The best directional code family considered matches the logical error rate of the rotated toric code at physical error rate p = 10 −3 but requires only a quarter to a third of the number of physical qubits to encode a given number of logical qubits.

title: Designing fault-tolerant blind quantum computation
authors: Gefen Baranes, Iria W. Wang, Francisco Machado, Aziza Suleymanzade, Pieter-Jan Stas, Yan-Cheng Wei, Susanne F. Yelin, Johannes Borregaard
abstract: Blind quantum computing (BQC) allows a client with limited quantum capabilities to delegate quantum computations to a more powerful server while hiding the computation. Existing protocols face significant challenges when scaling to large-scale fault-tolerant computations due to large communication overhead, photon losses, and low efficiencies. We use a recently demonstrated hybrid light-matter approach [PRL 132, 150604 (2024); Science 388, 509-513 (2025)] to develop a scalable architecture for blind quantum computation. By combining high-fidelity local gates on the server’s matter qubits with delegated rotations using photons, we construct loss-tolerant blind gates that enable new algorithmic design possibilities. Using these tools, the client can compile the algorithm to meet specific privacy goals while using fewer communication resources. We then present a scalable approach for fault-tolerant blind logical algorithms that improves the error-correction threshold and increases the speed and depth of blind logical circuits. Finally, we outline how this architecture can be implemented on state-of-the-art quantum hardware, including neutral atom arrays and solid-state spin defects. These new capabilities open up opportunities for deep circuit blind quantum computing.

title: Sequential decoding of the XYZ 2 hexagonal stabilizer code
authors: Basudha Srivastava, Yinzi Xiao, Anton Frisk Kockum, Ben Criger, Mats Granath
abstract: Quantum error correction requires accurate and efficient decoding to optimally suppress errors in the encoded information. For concatenated codes, where one code is embedded within another, optimal decoding can be achieved using a message-passing algorithm that sends conditional error probabilities from the lower-level code to a higher-level decoder. In this work, we study the XYZ 2 topological stabilizer code, defined on a honeycomb lattice, and use the fact that it can be viewed as a concatenation of a 2, 1, 1 phase-flip parity check code and the surface code with Y Z Z Y stabilizers, to decode the syndrome information in two steps. We use this sequential decoding scheme to correct errors on data qubits, as well as measurement errors, under various biased error models using both a maximum-likelihood decoder (MLD) and more efficient matching-based decoders. For depolarizing noise we find that the sequential matching decoder gives a threshold of 18.3 %, close to optimal, as a consequence of a favorable, effectively biased, error model on the upper-level YZZY code. For phase-biased noise on data qubits, at a bias η = p z p x + p y = 10, we find that a belief-matching-based decoder reaches thresholds of 24.1 %, compared to 28.6 % for the MLD. With measurement errors the thresholds are reduced to 3.4 % and 4.3 %, for depolarizing and biased noise, respectively, using the belief-matching decoder. This demonstrates that the XYZ 2 code has thresholds that are competitive with other codes tailored to biased noise. The results also showcase two essential components in optimizing the performance of concatenated codes: (1) tailoring the upper-level code to the effective noise profile of the decoded lower-level code, and (2) using an upper-level decoder that is adapted to this noise profile.

title: Full Structure Recovery of Linearized Reed-Solomon Codes
authors: Valentina Astore, Martino Borello, Alain Couvreur
abstract: Linearized Reed-Solomon codes (LRS) are optimal sum-rank-metric codes that generalize both Reed-Solomon and Gabidulin codes, and benefit from excellent decoding capabilities, making them potentially interesting candidates for post-quantum code-based cryptography. Previous works have investigated the underlying geometric structure of LRS codes, identifying geometric invariants that distinguish them from random codes. Other works have proposed approaches to recovering the LRS structure from an arbitrary generator matrix, together with additional data. However, both the distinguishers and the recovery techniques proposed so far are either not fully general, or have a prohibitive computational complexity. In this paper, we propose a polynomial-time procedure for the full structure recovery of LRS codes from the sole knowledge of an arbitrary generator matrix. Our results show that, like their Hamming and rank metric counterparts, LRS codes cannot be used as they are for McEliece-like encryption. Our approach combines Overbeck-type attacks with suitable matrix manipulations and shortening techniques to recover the evaluation parameters across different ranges of code dimensions.

title: Monotonic probes of asymmetry and robustness of the quantum Mpemba effect
authors: Riccardo Travaglino, Michele Mazzoni, Pasquale Calabrese
abstract: Entanglement asymmetry has emerged as a powerful probe of symmetry restoration and the quantum Mpemba effect. However, its conventional Rényi generalizations, defined as differences of Rényi entropies, are not monotones in the resource-theoretic sense. Here, we investigate an alternative family of asymmetry quantifiers based on sandwiched Rényi divergences, which satisfy monotonicity under symmetry-preserving quantum channels. Developing a two-parameter replica approach, we show how these quantities can be computed from charged moments and establish a remarkable correspondence with conventional Rényi asymmetries under the inversion of the Rényi index, $α\leftrightarrow 1/α$. This relation, exact for pure states, holds at leading order in the relevant scaling limits for homogeneous quantum quenches, including interacting integrable systems, and for Haar-random states. Applying these results to quenches from tilted ferromagnetic states, we demonstrate that the quantum Mpemba effect is remarkably robust, occurring throughout the entire family of sandwiched Rényi asymmetry monotones. We identify dynamical regimes in quenches from spatially inhomogeneous initial states where conventional Rényi asymmetries and genuine monotones exhibit qualitatively different behaviours. We also investigate a solvable toy model illustrating the possible dependence of Mpemba crossings on the Rényi index. Our findings establish a connection between conventional Rényi asymmetries and quantum resource theory, explaining their effectiveness in broad classes of nonequilibrium protocols while highlighting the additional information provided by genuine asymmetry monotones.

title: State convertibility in quantum-state texture from a general form of free operations
authors: Jose Alfredo de Leon
abstract: State convertibility specifies which transformations between states a quantum resource theory allows. In quantum-state texture, deterministic conversion criteria are known for qubits and pure sources in arbitrary dimension, but a general criterion for mixed states in higher dimensions is missing. We derive this exact criterion from a complete characterization of free operations in arbitrary finite dimension. Because the unique free state is pure, every free operation splits into a quantum filter and a residual completely positive map. Using this decomposition, we show that every allowed conversion admits a two-outcome measurement that retains the filtered state after one outcome and prepares a fixed state after the other. Conversion thus reduces to finding such a filter whose unnormalized output leaves a positive semidefinite remainder when subtracted from the target, a search we show to be solvable by semidefinite programming. Beyond deterministic conversion, the characterization of free operations can be used to study probabilistic and assisted manipulation of quantum-state texture. More broadly, since the construction relies on a pure fixed state, it also applies to other resource theories defined by free operations fixing such a state.

title: Simultaneous computation of multiple excited states via double bracket flows
authors: Reyhaneh Aghaei Saem, Mehrad Sahebi, Zoë Holmes, Yudai Suzuki
abstract: Efficient computation of excited states is essential for studying strongly correlated many-body systems and molecular electronic structure. In this work, we propose a framework for simultaneously simulating multiple excited states based on dynamical flows. The main idea is to exploit a common double bracket flow that drives different pure initial states toward different target excited states without such prior information. We establish a necessary condition for convergence and a sufficient condition for exponential convergence. We further develop two scheduling strategies: Chebyshev scheduling, which achieves optimal convergence near a fixed point but requires prior spectral information, and adaptive scheduling, which achieves comparable performance in numerical simulations without spectral information. Our results enable new classical and quantum algorithms for excited-state computation without prior preparation of lower-energy eigenstates.

title: Bound magic in multi-qubit systems
authors: Jonas Kitzinger, Jens Eisert, Ravi Kunjwal
abstract: Magic captures nonstabilizerness, a resource required for quantum computational speedups. We prove the existence of multi-qubit nonstabilizer states from which no pure magic can be distilled, even with arbitrarily many copies and rounds of stabilizer operations. Such bound magic states have previously been only known to exist in odd Hilbert-space dimensions, where positivity of discrete Wigner functions can be used analogously to the positive partial transpose (PPT) criterion for bound entanglement. We introduce a PPT analogue for magic in multi-qubit systems that is closed under tensor products and stabilizer operations and reduces to the stabilizer polytope for one and two qubits. This enables the proof of multi-qubit bound magic and the explicit construction of bound magic states for $n \geq 3$ qubits.

title: ProbFaS: Probabilistic Video Frame Selection for MLLMs via Multi-Fidelity Calibration
Memory Is Not Ground Truth: Revising Navigation Authority under Unreliable VLM Evidence for Persistent Semantic Navigation
$μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
One Ocean, Many Tasks: A Data-Grounded Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Marine Robotics
Exact monogamy of steering and remote Wigner negativity for multimode Gaussian nodes
authors: Sudip Chakrabarty
abstract: Optical quantum networks route correlations through nodes that hold several modes and are linked to many neighbors. Steering is the correlation behind one-sided device-independent tasks and behind the remote preparation of non-Gaussian states. It is monogamous for a single mode, which can be steered by only one party, but how many neighbors can steer a node with $k$ modes was not known. We show that for Gaussian states the answer is exactly $2k-1$ when the neighbors use Gaussian measurements, with any number of measurement settings. The limit follows from a simple bound. To every neighbor we assign a share, computed from the covariance matrix, and we prove that the shares of all neighbors add up to at most $k$, irrespective of the amount of squeezing, amplification or noise the network contains. A neighbor steers the node by Gaussian measurements exactly when its share exceeds one half, and a network built from a harmonic tight frame reaches the limit. The same number governs remote Wigner negativity. A heralded non-Gaussian operation at the node can make at most $2k-1$ neighbors Wigner negative, and in our network a single heralded projection makes all of them negative in the same run. With $n$ settings of arbitrary measurements, at most $nk-1$ neighbors can steer the node or violate a Bell inequality with it. More than $2k-1$ neighbors can therefore steer the node or violate a Bell inequality with it only if they use non-Gaussian measurements with at least three settings, whereas entanglement can reach any number of neighbors. These results determine exactly how many neighbors one multimode node can serve with steering and with remote Wigner negativity.

title: Transition Path Sampling for Rare Events in Non-Markovian Open Quantum Systems
authors: Ritesh Pant, Kai Müller, Tarun Gera, Doran I. G. B. Raccah
abstract: Rare transitions govern the dynamics of many open quantum systems, but their probabilities and rates are difficult to calculate. Transition path sampling (TPS) of quantum systems has so far been limited to Markovian, perturbative descriptions. Here, we formulate TPS for non-Markovian quantum state diffusion, which is exact for Gaussian baths, extending it to non-Markovian and strongly coupled open quantum systems. For normal-to-superradiant tunneling in the unbalanced open Dicke model, we determine probabilities down to $10^{-8}$ and rates beyond the reach of brute force.

title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning
The Price of Quantum Advantage in Computational Chemistry
authors: Haejung Koh, Katerina Gratsea, Hao Zhang, Matthew Otten
abstract: As the fault-tolerant era approaches, the question shifts from ``is it possible'' to ``is it worthwhile.'' To assess practical quantum advantage against reliable classical baselines, we examine 26 benchmark instances including FeMoco, iron-sulfur clusters, cytochrome P450, and ruthenium catalysts using two selected configuration interaction solvers, SHCI and TrimCI. Comparing classical workloads with fault-tolerant resource estimates, we calculate the break-even whole-QPU hourly price. Even at an optimistic price of US\$7{,}000 per whole-QPU hour, and with mid-range CPU clusters, classical computation remains cheaper for six of seven systems. FeMoco alone remains sensitive to the classical method and extrapolation strategy. Wavefunction analysis further reveals how orbital choice affects the determinant support required for target-state overlap in quantum phase estimation (QPE). Our results highlight the importance of reliable classical references and trial-state characterization, and quantify the economic conditions under which quantum computing can become competitive with classical alternatives.

Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations

Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
Neural Network Decoders For Qubit Loss
authors: J. Wilson Staples, Winston Fu, Yihe Dong, Jeff D. Thompson
abstract: Qubit loss is a significant source of error in many quantum hardware platforms, requiring circuits that periodically replace or reset qubits to maintain fault-tolerance. When the reset process includes loss-resolving measurements, this information can improve decoding and substantially reduce overhead compared to the case where this information is not available. Prior work has demonstrated loss-tolerant circuits for the surface code that show significantly improved thresholds and subthreshold scaling by incorporating loss information. However, the computational complexity of loss simulation and decoding, which falls outside of the usual stabilizer framework, has limited extending these studies to high-rate qLDPC codes, which are already challenging to decode in the absence of loss. In this work, we present a loss-aware convolutional neural-network (CNN) decoder framework that circumvents this challenge. Training is enabled by a novel sampler, \texttt{slim}, which achieves a throughput for circuits with Pauli noise and loss that is comparable to the state-of-the-art for pure Pauli noise. On the surface code with loss, the decoder matches the accuracy of computationally expensive most-likely error (MLE) decoders at much lower latency. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle (Gross) code, we study a walking syndrome extraction circuit with Pauli and loss errors. For physical error rates $p<1\%$, we observe a more than $10^3$-fold lower logical error rate for a pure loss model, relative to a pure Pauli error model at the same physical error rate, along with significantly enhanced sub-threshold error rate scaling. This demonstrates that loss-dominated error models can also significantly improve performance in a high-rate qLDPC code, and provides a simulation and decoder training platform that can be extended to other codes and algorithmic gadgets.

What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video

The thermodynamic budget of objectivity
authors: Wonyong Chung
abstract: An event becomes a fact when enough independent records of it exist such that no operation is possible that leaves all observers ignorant of it again. Records are physical, and creating, keeping, and destroying them have thermodynamic costs. We compute these costs exactly in a minimal broadcast model with a driven central qubit writing records into $N$ initially thermal registers, with work sources and baths at temperature $T$. The basic arguments for the operations are outlined here, with full treatment in the text. Creation of one event record at redundancy $R$ and information deficit $δ$ requires work $W \ge R\, k_\mathrm{B}T \ln 2\, (1-δ) H(\varepsilon)$, linear in redundancy at the Landauer coefficient. Recording in a basis misaligned by $θ$ with the einselecting interaction fails at a critical angle, $θ_c = 2\arcsin\sqrt{H_2^{-1}(δ)}$, beyond which objectivity is unreachable at any work, and below $θ_c$ the optimal work is a closed form in the pointer basis that minimizes the work of objectivity. Reducing objectivity is impossible at any work with access to fewer than $R - R_{\min} + 1$ records, while work protects nothing if given access. Inter-record redundancy is extractable free energy and erasing the accessed records yields a net gain of work beyond the first copy. The second law constrains the destruction of the correlation: erasing a fact from a sector an adversary controls dissipates at least the mutual information erased, but a consolidation dissipates nothing. Records in re-thermalizing media are nonequilibrium steady states, and the minimal power to maintain a record at $(R,δ)$ is the known two-state driving bound evaluated at the record-quality boundary.

title: Linear Single-Source Shortest Path, Almost
LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
Complementary mechanisms of critical quantum metrology
authors: Nikita Leppenen, Shaked Levy, Ephraim Shahmoon
abstract: Critical metrology conventionally exploits enhanced susceptibility to a system parameter near a phase transition. Here we identify a complementary mechanism for critically enhanced estimation of intrinsic system parameters via suppressed quantum noise rather than enhanced response. We demonstrate both mechanisms in coherently radiating spin states (CRSS)-correlated states of $N$ spin-$1/2$ particles defined as asymptotic eigenstates of the collective-spin lowering operator with complex eigenvalue $r e^{-i\varphi}$. At the critical value $r=1$, CRSS exhibit a second-order transition. We show that near criticality, estimation of $r$ benefits from enhanced susceptibility despite increased noise, whereas estimation of $\varphi$ benefits from suppressed quantum noise without enhanced response. Remarkably, both yield the same estimation error $\sim N^{-2/3}$, improving over the standard quantum limit $N^{-1/2}$. For $\varphi$, this establishes quantum-enhanced metrology of phases intrinsic to the critical system, rather than phases externally encoded by interferometry. We demonstrate these results for CRSS realizations in both dissipative (superradiant) and Hamiltonian (Ising) systems relevant to cavity QED and trapped ions, where fast preparation of CRSS is shown possible thanks to gap opening. Applications to metrology of coupling rates and phases or optical lengths are discussed.

title: Monoidal analog of cluster-tilting theory and monoidal reachability of acyclic cluster algebras
Bound Entanglement with Negative Partial Transpose Exists
authors: Islam Faisal
abstract: We show that the Werner state $ρ= (23 I - 3\,\mathrm{SWAP})/1448$ on $\mathbb{C}^8 \otimes \mathbb{C}^8$ has a negative partial transpose and is bound entangled: no LOCC protocol can distill entanglement from any number of copies of $ρ$, and even with separable operations the fidelity of a two-qubit output with a Bell state never exceeds $(1+\sqrt{2})/4 \approx 0.604$. It follows that distillable entanglement is neither additive nor convex.

Tokenisation is not in APX
LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies
Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
Quantum-Resistant Communication System
authors: Abdulazeem M H, Manu H, Karibasavanagowda B M, Abdul Razak, Nayanashree D
abstract: Long-term confidentiality over public networks is threatened less by real-time quantum cryptanalysis today than by harvest-now, decrypt-later adversaries recording classical elliptic-curve and RSA handshakes for future decryption via Shor's algorithm.This paper reports a working six-stage hybrid post-quantum communication pipeline (Q-AEGIS) that establishes quantum-resistant sessions without relying on proprietary hardware accelerators: an antiamplification cookie gate filters spoofed connection floods, X25519 elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman is combined with NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM-768 for hybrid key encapsulation, NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65 authenticates the full SHA-384 handshake transcript, dictionary-based certificate compression reduces handshake wire footprint from 9,842 bytes to 2,894 bytes, and ChaCha20-Poly1305 provides authenticated encryption with epoch-based forward-secure key ratcheting.Across an 18-scenario evaluation catalogue comprising 10 adversarial or impaired network profiles and 8 nominal links, the system achieves 100% session establishment and authentication accuracy with zero downgrade acceptances, and classifies 240 of 240 test sessions correctly under leave-profiles-out evaluation.Removing transcript binding costs 22.22 percentage points of security accuracy, identifying it as the enabling safeguard.Wire optimization reduces handshake latency 2.9-fold, and MTU-aware framing sustains 100% handshake completion up to 6% packet loss.Because evaluations run on a user-space emulated testbed, the results characterize protocol correctness and cryptographic overhead rather than line-rate appliance throughput.

title: Authentication of IoT Nodes in Tactical Networks under the Quantum Threat: A Comparative Analysis of Post-Quantum Primitives and Zero-Knowledge Proof
authors: Roman Maliarchuk, Oleh Basystiuk
abstract: The paper addresses the problem of authenticating Internet-of-Things nodes in tactical networks — self-organizing radio networks of military units, sensor fields and unmanned platforms built on microcontroller-class devices with hundreds of kilobytes of RAM, battery power and intermittent radio channels — under the emerging quantum threat. Classical authentication protocols for constrained devices rely on elliptic-curve or RSA cryptography, whose security collapses once a scalable quantum computer becomes available. The threat is physical in nature: its time horizon is determined not by advances in classical cryptanalysis but by the pace of quantum computing platforms — the growth in the number and quality of physical qubits and the scaling of quantum error correction; for tactical infrastructure with a decades-long life cycle, the harvest-now-decrypt-later strategy means that the threat is already relevant today. Six categories of attack scenarios specific to the tactical environment, systematized by the adversary's channels of access to the node, are formulated: physical node capture with key extraction and cloning, active electronic warfare (jamming, spoofing and message relaying), degraded and intermittent communication channels, passive side-channel attacks based on timing and power analysis, a quantum adversary, and network-level protocol attacks. A verifiable protocol requirement is derived from each category. Thirteen cryptographic schemes of three families — lattice-based (Module-LWE/SIS, NTRU), hash-based, and zero-knowledge proof constructions — are then compared under a unified set of criteria: public-key size, proof or signature size, RAM requirements on the ARM Cortex-M4 platform, and overall suitability for tactical-grade embedded platforms. Classical schemes (Schnorr, Groth16, Bulletproofs) are included as compactness baselines that quantify the cost of quantum resistance. It is shown that no standardized scheme satisfies all requirements simultaneously: the standardized lattice primitives, while efficient on the target platform, do not by definition provide zero-knowledge of the authentication transcript; stateful hash-based schemes fail under node cloning and rollback scenarios; floating-point Gaussian sampling conflicts with constant-time implementation on microcontrollers; and transparent hash-based proof systems produce proofs of tens to hundreds of kilobytes, which exceed the resource budget of a tactical radio channel. A research gap is identified: no open RAM measurements of lattice-based zero-knowledge proofs and hash-based proof systems on microcontrollers are available in the open literature. A lattice-based sigma-protocol construction with the Fiat-Shamir-with-Aborts transform and Module-SIS commitments is justified as the target direction for protocol synthesis, since it combines quantum resistance, transparent setup, constant-time integer arithmetic, and a shared computational base with the standardized ML-KEM and ML-DSA primitives. Future work includes numerical modelling of the chosen construction, game-based formalization of the threat model, and a reference implementation in Rust for embedded targets.

title: Engineering Quantum Emitters Through the Presence of Two-Dimensional Materials: Coupling with Surface Modes
authors: Leonardo A. Lugarini, Ana Beatriz Monteiro dos Santos, V. G. M. Duarte, Danarah Ariel Pires Gomes Brito, A. J. Chaves
journal: Aplicações Operacionais em Áreas de Defesa
abstract: Quantum emitters, systems capable of emitting one photon per cycle, are one of the fundamental building blocks for establishing quantum communication, which has great potential to improve cryptography and make the transmission of information through free space more secure.The information rate transmitted by a quantum emitter depends on the average time for spontaneous emission to occur, being one of the main figures of merit in single-photon sources. It is possible to alter the photon emission rate using the Purcell effect. In this work, we explore how the presence of surface plasmon-polaritons can increase the photon emission rate, and we study the effect of the presence of a graphene sheet. Finally, we present perspectives for future work.

title: A state-of-the-art review on cryptographic approaches to secure vehicle identification systems
authors: Dilip Kumar Barman, Dushmanta M. Kalita, Abhijit Boruah, Rabinder Kr Prasad, Sudipta Majumder, Nomi Baruah
abstract: Connected and autonomous vehicles depend on Vehicle Identification Systems (VIS) to authenticate vehicles, authorise access and protect vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication. As these systems become connected to the cloud and the Internet of Things, they are exposed to relay, replay, man-in-the-middle and key-cloning attacks. Quantum computers are also expected to break the RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC) that they rely on. This paper is a state-of-the-art review of cryptographic methods for VIS, combined with a simulation-based feasibility study of one hybrid construction. The review asks which methods can provide low-latency authentication that remains secure against quantum attacks. We compare symmetric encryption (AES), asymmetric encryption (RSA and ECC), neural cryptography based on Tree Parity Machine (TPM) key synchronisation, lattice-based post-quantum cryptography and blockchain-based authentication. The comparison covers key management, computational cost, quantum resistance and suitability for automotive electronic control units (ECUs). We then combine TPM key synchronisation with AES-256 and study it in a SUMO/OMNeT++ vehicular network simulation. We also measure the cost of cryptographic operations on a server-class ARMv8 processor and verify the secrecy and mutual-authentication goals of the protocol with ProVerif. The construction is compared with recent (2024–2026) lattice-based and physically unclonable function based schemes. The main open problems are computational-model proofs, energy measurement on real ECUs, hardware-in-the-loop testing and robustness against adversarial machine learning. No single method is sufficient. Secure VIS will need layered designs that combine adaptive key updates, standardised post-quantum methods and decentralised trust.

title: Robust critical metrology in noisy quantum systems
authors: Ruo-Qi Li, Yi-Xiao Ren, Shang-jing Liu, Yongyuan Jiang, Jie Song
abstract: Critical quantum metrology exploits the divergent susceptibility of quantum systems near phase transitions. However, the long adiabatic evolution required near criticality inevitably causes severe decoherence in open systems. Here, we utilize a fully differentiable quantum-control approach to optimize transient metrological performance. Using numerical gradient descent through the Lindblad master equation, we discover nonintuitive driving strategies. Under weak dissipation, the optimal trajectory deliberately breaks adiabaticity and harnesses weak coherent nonadiabatic excitations as an interferometric resource. The resulting non-Gaussian states interfere constructively, generating a strong transient peak in the signal-to-noise ratio with exponential, super-Heisenberg-like scaling. Under strong dissipation, the control instead steers the system toward the shifted dissipative critical boundary to extract enhanced susceptibility before relaxation to the vacuum state. Our results demonstrate an increase in the magnitude of the measurement indicators under the conditions of a limited parameters range and open quantum system, provide a practical path to criticality-enhanced sensing in noisy quantum platforms.

title: Quantum enhanced multi-parameter estimation with multi-mode entangled Fock state
authors: Zhongjian Zhang, Kaimin Zheng, Ben Wang, Hao Zhan, Baichuan Yang, Lijian Zhang
abstract: The precision of parameter estimation critically depends on the choice of the probe state, making the identification of high-performance quantum states a central task in quantum metrology. Although the multi-mode NOON state (MNS) can saturate the ultimate precision limit in multi-parameter estimation for specific sensing schemes and cost functions, it is notoriously difficult to prepare and highly vulnerable to photon loss. In this work, we propose a multi-mode entangled state for multi-parameter estimation. The state is generated by injecting the entangled Fock state into a parallel array of beam splitters, and we derive the corresponding quantum Cramér–Rao bound (QCRB). In the lossless regime, the proposed state surpasses the standard quantum limit and approaches the precision achievable with MNS. We further analyze the effect of loss on the precision of different probe states under various configurations, and show that the proposed state is more robust than the MNS. Combined with its experimental feasibility in the four-mode, four-photon configuration, our proposed state serves as a promising candidate for practical multi-parameter estimation.

title: Quantum sensing through bosonic-fermionic Bell-state transitions in two-photon interference
authors: Chahat Kaushik, Vimlesh Kumar, G. K. Samanta
abstract: Hong–Ou–Mandel (HOM) interference has become a central resource for quantum sensing and metrology owing to its sensitivity to temporal delay and photon indistinguishability. However, existing HOM-based sensing schemes generally rely on inserting a sample into one arm of the interferometer, making the measurement vulnerable to optical loss, alignment instability, and bandwidth-dependent distortion of the interference profile. Here, we demonstrate a symmetry-controlled quantum sensing scheme based on continuous transitions between symmetric (bosonic-like) and antisymmetric (fermionic-like) Bell states in two-photon interference. By imprinting a geometric phase onto the classical pump beam and transferring it to polarization-entangled photons generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, we coherently tune the exchange symmetry of the entangled state without altering the temporal or spectral indistinguishability of the photons. The HOM response evolves continuously from bunching to antibunching with a sine square phase dependence, producing a coincidence modulation of ∼ 10 × 10 4 counts/second. In contrast to conventional HOM sensing, the phase-modulation linewidth remains fixed at π/2, independent of photon bandwidth. As a proof-of-concept verification of Bell-state transition for quantum sensing, we placed a birefringent PPKTP crystal in the pump beam, and measured the thermo-dispersive birefringence with a response scale of the order of 10 -6 over a broad temperature range. Our results establish exchange symmetry as a controllable resource for robust quantum sensing and symmetry-engineered photonic quantum information processing.

title: Efficient quantum circuits for coherent conversion between general first-and second-quantized many-body representations
authors: Jack S. Baker, Gaurav Saxena, Thi Ha Kyaw
abstract: Quantum simulation at fixed particle number admits two equivalent descriptions, a first-quantized (particle) representation and a second-quantized (occupation-number) representation. Their quantum resource costs differ sharply across computational tasks, so the ability to convert coherently between them is valuable. We construct an explicit unitary $Q$, with inverse $Q^\dagger$, that maps a first-quantized state to its fixed-$N$ occupation-number form while diagnosing the input's particle-exchange symmetry. The conversion is therefore symmetry-agnostic at the input yet fully resolved at the output, and it applies uniformly to bosonic, fermionic, and parastatistical sectors. At its foundation lies a structural identification that we place at the center of this work: the quantum Schur transform supplied by Schur--Weyl duality is the non-abelian Fourier transform of the commuting pair $(S_N,U(d))$, and the occupation-number representation is its weight basis, retaining only the labels shared by both factors, the irrep $\lambda$ and the $\mathfrak{u}(d)$ weight. This reduction is lossless for bosons and fermions, while a canonical Gelfand--Tsetlin promise renders it one-to-one for the remaining sectors. Algorithmically, $Q$ composes the strong Schur transform with reversible arithmetic that computes occupations as successive row-sum differences of the Gelfand--Tsetlin pattern, yielding gate complexity $\mathrm{poly}(N,d,\log(1/\epsilon))$. The converted state is prepared efficiently in quantum memory. Any classical algorithm that outputs it explicitly, however, must in the worst case pay a cost set by the sector dimension, which is polynomial of degree $N$ in $d$ at fixed $N$ and exponential in $N$ when $d=\Theta(N)$. Finally, a classical polynomial-time sampler that approximates the occupation-number distribution of the converted state for every promised input would imply $\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}$.

title: Photon efficiency-coherence time product rule for NV-centre and trapped-ion quantum repeater chains
authors: Samir Thapa, Nanda Bikram Adhikari
abstract: The fidelity of a first-generation quantum repeater is controlled by a single hardware quantity, whose identification explains a striking equivalence between the two leading qubit platforms. By simulating nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre and trapped-ion (171 Yb +) repeater chains over an identical 200 km fibre channel—anchored to optical time-domain reflectometry field measurements of a deployed single-mode link and statistically extended to 66.08 dB total loss—we find that the two platforms deliver statistically indistinguishable raw fidelity at three segments (NV: F tel = 0.605; trapped ion: F tel = 0.589), despite five-fold opposite photon-efficiency and coherence-time specifications. A two-dimensional sensitivity analysis reveals why: at fixed channel loss, repeater fidelity is controlled by the product η photon ⋅ T 2 of photon efficiency and coherence time, not by either quantity alone. Both platforms share η photon ⋅ T 2 = 0.20 s and therefore perform identically; any two platforms on the same iso-product line will likewise coincide. This design rule yields a concrete hardware target: reaching the BB84 key-distribution threshold at three segments requires η photon ⋅ T 2 ⩾ 2.44 s, a twelve-fold improvement, and at the throughput-optimal segment count gate and measurement errors cap fidelity near 0.806 regardless of memory quality. The comparison is built on the NetSquid discrete-event simulator with experimentally validated parameters, full three-basis state tomography, and density-matrix DEJMPS purification; the last reveals that realistic dephasing-biased chain states purify substantially better than the Werner-state recurrence predicts. Trapped ions purify more effectively (Bell fidelity 0.608 versus 0.509 after one round) owing to superior gate and readout fidelity, while NV centre generate entangled pairs 4–5 × faster. The photon–memory interface, captured by the η photon ⋅ T 2 product, is the universal bottleneck limiting both platforms.

title: Transmon qutrit-based simulation of spin-1 AKLT systems
authors: Keerthi Kumaran, Faisal Alam, Norhan M. Eassa, Kaelyn Ferris, Xiao Xiao, Łukasz Cincio, Nicholas T. Bronn, Arnab Banerjee
abstract: Qutrit-based quantum circuits could help reduce circuit depths, and hence the effect of noise, when the system of interest has a local dimension of three. Accessing second excited states in superconducting transmons provides a straightforward hardware realization of qutrits useful for such ternary encoding. In this work, we successfully calibrate microwave pulse gates to a low error rate to operate transmon qutrits. We use these qutrits to simulate one-dimensional spin-1 AKLT states (Affleck, Kennedy, Lieb, and Tasaki), which exhibit a multitude of interesting phenomena, such as topologically protected ground states, string order, and a robust Berry phase. We demonstrate the efficacy of qutrit-based simulation by preparing high-fidelity ground states of the AKLT Hamiltonian with open boundaries for various chain lengths. We then prepare perturbed periodic-boundary AKLT ground states to compute the Berry phase and illustrate non-trivial ground state topology. To establish the advantage of qutrits over qubits under the compilation strategy and the noise model used here, we present scalable tensor network simulations for AKLT state preparation and Berry phase computation. Our work provides a pathway toward more general spin-1 physics simulations using transmon qutrits, with applications in chemistry, magnetism, and topological phases of matter.

title: Quantum Community Detection for Data Analysis
authors: Vicente P. Soloviev, Brian Coyle, Stefano Scali, Michal Krompiec
abstract: Community detection offers an alternative to conventional methods for data analysis tasks such as feature selection and clustering, and detecting communities with quantum algorithms is a promising avenue for quantum speedup. We investigate quantum spectral community detectors, such as the modularity-matrix algorithm deteQt, in pipelines for both tasks. We first generalise deteQt to multiple communities by recursive bisection, and show that it recovers planted communities, and hence redundant features, in synthetic and small datasets. We then propose projeQt, which applies a spectral filter to the encoded modularity matrix through the quantum singular value transformation, retaining higher-order eigenvectors that deteQt does not use. projeQt acts on the generalised modularity matrix and extracts several communities at once, without recursion, by k-means clustering of a Gram matrix built from quantum state overlaps. On MNIST we demonstrate both pipelines, selecting informative pixels and classifying images directly by clustering, and find them competitive with standard community detectors.

title: Prospects and limitations of adaptive variational quantum algorithms for lattice field theories: a case study in 2+1 dimensions
authors: Nico Dichter, Andrea Bulgarelli, Lena Funcke, Stefan Kühn
abstract: The variational quantum algorithm ADAPT-VQE has previously been used to prepare the vacuum of lattice gauge theories in $1+1D$. In this paper, we study whether it extends to higher dimensions. We identify two general limitations of ADAPT-VQE. First, if the qubit Hamiltonian and the initial state are real, i.e., invariant under qubit-level time-reversal, all real-valued pool operators have vanishing gradients and are never selected. Second, the algorithm can converge to excited eigenstates. We illustrate both limitations, also providing examples from literature, and present a first application of ADAPT-VQE to a lattice field theory in $2+1D$, namely free Wilson fermions, where both obstacles occur. Adding charge conjugation symmetry to the operator pool improves the results, and combining different pools with suitable initial states recovers the ground and first excited states over the full mass range. These findings give practical guidelines for applying ADAPT-VQE to lattice field theories beyond $1+1D$.

title: Using a static spacetime subsystem code to calculate Floquet code distance
authors: Ethan Egger, Milad Marvian
abstract: Dynamical codes, including Floquet codes, can capture time-dependent phenomena in quantum error correction circuits that are absent from static stabilizer or subsystem codes, such as detecting regions and error propagation. They are also capable of preserving more logical qubits than corresponding schemes in which the same syndrome-extraction measurements are performed without being distributed over time. However, evaluating the performance of dynamical codes is more complicated than for static codes because error detection depends on when an error occurs within the measurement schedule. In this work, we introduce a mapping from the measurement sequence of a Floquet code to a static spacetime subsystem code and show that calculating the distance of a Floquet code can be reduced to calculating the distance of the corresponding static subsystem code. Crucially, our mapping preserves code distance, a property that is not guaranteed for general spacetime code mappings. This reduction converts the dynamical distance problem into a static subsystem code problem, substantially simplifying the analysis of Floquet measurement schedules and facilitating the evaluation of fault tolerance for new measurement schemes.

title: Constructively Embedding Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Yucheng He, Todd A. Brun
abstract: Implementing quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) requires more than favorable algebraic parameters: the interactions among data qubits and ancillas must also fit physical hardware. Surface codes map naturally onto two-dimensional arrays, but many quantum LDPC codes have Tanner graphs with nonlocal connections. We develop a constructive pipeline that maps a QECC's Tanner graph to the targeted hardware lattice in three stages (continuous embedding, grid assignment, and path routing). Continuous embeddings reveal the geometric structure of the code, including differences between stabilizer generator sets of the same code. The discrete stages produce explicit routed layouts that we can characterize and compare using proxy metrics for footprint, communication overhead, and congestion for syndrome extraction. We examine three continuous embedding methods: multidimensional scaling (distance-based), spectral embedding (Laplacian-based), and spring layout (force-based) for the first stage. Experiments across tested codes show how routing geometry, dimension, and scale selection affect the resulting costs. In ablation studies on the radius-2 (R2) HaPPY code, graph-aware methods for continuous embedding and the choice of path-routing algorithm matter more than the grid assignment under our chosen weights in the cost function. Changing the continuous embedding reveals a trade-off: MDS incurs greater communication overhead than spectral embedding over most tested scales, while spring layout can reduce communication overhead at intermediate scales but increases congestion and is less stable across scales.

title: Low-Degree Torus Approximations of the AND Function and $\mathsf{ACC}^0$ Circuits
authors: Shuhei Osaki, Ryuhei Mori
abstract: Torus polynomials, real polynomials evaluated modulo one, were proposed by Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao as a route to $\mathsf{ACC}^0$ lower bounds. We prove degree upper bounds for torus polynomials approximating a function on every input. First, for every $ε\in(0,1/4)$, $\mathsf{AND}_n/2$ has an $ε$-approximating torus polynomial of degree $O(\log(n/ε))$, improving the previous $O(\log^2(n/ε))$. This is optimal up to constant factors for inverse-polynomial error, by a lower bound of Krishan and Vishwanathan, and refutes two superlogarithmic-degree conjectures of Krishan and Sarma. Second, for every Boolean function $g$ computed by a depth-$d$, size-$s$ $\mathsf{AC}^0[m]$ circuit, $g/2$ has an $ε$-approximating torus polynomial of degree at most $C_m^d(\log s)^{\max\{1,μ-1\}d}\log(1/ε)$, where $μ$ is the number of distinct prime factors of $m$ and $C_m$ depends only on $m$. This improves the bound $(\log s)^{O_m(d^2)}(\log(1/ε))^{O_m(d)}$ of Bhrushundi, Hosseini, Lovett, and Rao, making the exponent of $\log s$ linear in the depth and the dependence on $\log(1/ε)$ linear. Both proofs sample terms of a Fourier expansion and approximate them by low-degree torus polynomials. A torus approximation of degree $D$ can be written as a linear combination of at most $(n+1)^D$ parities, called a periodic Fourier representation, which is known to give a non-adaptive measurement-based quantum computation with linear side-processing using one qubit per parity. Hence every $\mathsf{ACC}^0$ function can be computed with quasipolynomially many qubits and inverse-polynomial error probability on every input. Conversely, we prove that a periodic Fourier representation with $r$ parities and error probability $ε$ gives a torus approximation of degree $O(\log(r/ε))$, so the two notions are equivalent.

title: Classical sampling of verifiable graph-state quantum advantage experiments
authors: Zhongpu Qiu, Yuqi Qing, Jielan Li, Hongxia Hao
abstract: Quantum computers are expected to outperform classical ones on some tasks, but a convincing demonstration must be both hard to reproduce classically and verifiable. A recent proposal achieves verifiability by preparing graph states with built-in error detection, so that the quality of the experiment can be certified without simulating it; hardness is added by measuring in a non-Clifford basis or by inserting T gates. We show that the two instances posted to demonstrate this proposal on IBM hardware can be sampled classically on eight graphics processing units, with higher quality than the hardware in comparable or shorter time. For the 70-qubit instance our samples are drawn from the ideal output distribution; for the 64-qubit instance with 314 T gates they come with a certified fidelity of at least 0.908, against 0.349 for the hardware. The reason lies in verification itself: T gates can only be placed where the error detection cannot see them, which pushes them towards the end of the circuit, where they add little classical cost. Our results identify the features that future verifiable advantage experiments must control.

title: Exploiting SU(2) Symmetry for Efficient Quantum State Preparation of Matrix Product States
authors: Etienne D'Argenlieu, Alessandro Summer, François Jamet, David P. Tew, Lachlan P. Lindoy
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising route to simulating strongly correlated systems, particularly for dynamical and spectral quantities whose classical computation can become prohibitively expensive. Fault-tolerant algorithms for these tasks, including real-time dynamics and phase estimation, assume efficient preparation of the initial many-body state, making state preparation an important bottleneck. Matrix product states obtained classically with the density matrix renormalization group can be compiled sequentially into fault-tolerant circuits. We exploit non-Abelian spin SU(2) symmetry in this compilation. By the Wigner-Eckart theorem, only the reduced tensors, which carry the variational information, need generic unitary synthesis. The magnetic structure is restored by Clebsch-Gordan transformations with analytically known angles. We benchmark the method on representative strongly correlated models, including the one-dimensional Hubbard model, quasi-one-dimensional Hubbard geometries, and Anderson impurity models, and perform fault-tolerant resource estimates using the Toffoli count as the primary cost metric. Across the systems considered, exploiting non-Abelian SU(2) symmetry reduces the Toffoli cost roughly threefold relative to U(1)-adapted compilation and by more than an order of magnitude relative to the standard dense compilation method. These results demonstrate how non-Abelian symmetries can substantially reduce the cost of transferring classically tractable many-body ground states to quantum computers, facilitating their use in quantum dynamics and energy estimation.

title: Quditology: harnessing many levels for quantum information processing
authors: Abhijit Chakraborty, Zheng Shi, Noah Goss, Irfan Siddiqi, Barry C. Sanders, Christine A. Muschik
abstract: Quantum computing offers the prospect of surpassing classical computation on certain tasks by leveraging quantum coherence and entanglement. However, a significant gap remains between current quantum hardware and the requirements to transcend what classical computers can achieve, with decoherence limiting the capacity of storing quantum information and the number of logical steps that can be executed reliably. In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.

title: Bosonic Magic Resources at Quantum Criticality
authors: Paolo Stornati, Piotr Sierant, Emanuele Tirrito
abstract: Non-Gaussianity is a resource for bosonic quantum information processing, providing a necessary ingredient for universal quantum computation in continuous-variable systems. Here we quantify non-Gaussianity in the ground state of the one-dimensional extended Bose-Hubbard model using quantum relative entropy (QRE), a measure determined solely by one-body correlations. The scaling of the QRE with system size reveals quantum phase transitions involving hidden and conventional order. We connect QRE scaling in the weakly interacting superfluid phase to Luttinger-liquid correlations and identify distinct critical signatures in its extensive and subleading contributions. At the Mott-Haldane transition, subtracting the extensive background reveals a pronounced peak in the subleading contribution, providing a clear signature of the onset of hidden string order. At the Haldane-density-wave transition, the extensive contribution to the QRE instead exhibits scaling consistent with Ising criticality. These results establish non-Gaussianity as a probe of many-body criticality, linking bosonic quantum resources to strongly correlated matter.

title: How Many Keys Must a Quantum Computer Break to Take Over a Blockchain? A Quantum Nakamoto Coefficient for Fifteen Proof-of-Stake Networks
authors: Seyyed Mohammad Hassan Halataei
abstract: Blockchains that run on proof of stake, among them Ethereum and Solana, are secured by a vote: a transaction becomes irreversible once computers holding two thirds of the deposited money have signed it. Each signature is made with a secret key whose public counterpart is permanently visible, and a large quantum computer could compute the secret from the public key. We ask a simple question: how many such keys would it have to break to take over the vote? We call the answer the quantum Nakamoto coefficient and measure it on live data from fifteen networks, collected on 15 November 2026. For fourteen of them, 2 to 18 keys are enough to break the network's security guarantee and 7 to 77 to control it outright; at one key every 12 minutes, the pace implied by recent resource estimates, a single quantum computer would defeat the guarantee of any of these networks in less than four hours and take full control in less than sixteen hours. Ethereum is far more robust, but a 2025 change that lets operators merge their deposits into fewer keys has cut the number of keys at its first threshold from about 465,000 to 7,682, a factor of 60. We derive a simple formula for this effect, and another for the small rotating committee on which wallets rely, and confirm both on the data. For fourteen of the fifteen networks, the first large quantum computer would be less than a day away from total control. Their validator signatures should therefore be migrated to post-quantum schemes before such a machine exists, since once it does, the time to respond is measured in hours.

title: A Realistic End-to-End Runtime Crossover Estimation for Quantum-Enhanced Training of Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
authors: Maximilian Alexander Wolf, Alona Sakhnenko, Florian Geissler, Andrea Matic, Jeanette Miriam Lorenz
abstract: Machine Learning (ML) is one promising application domain for Quantum Computing (QC) speedups, but asymptotic complexity considerations often mask the actual engineering costs of actual end-to-end workflows. For the use case of training a linearized Neural Network with a Quantum Linear Solver, a provably favorable quantum scaling has been suggested. We present realistic resource estimates for this problem, accounting for data access, computation, and readout. Our analysis examines three increasingly complex benchmarking scenarios, under distinct sparsity-scaling assumptions, thereby enabling progressively more realistic resource estimates. We identify crossover regimes relative to classical methods and find that crossover points emerge only for very large problem sizes, long computation times, and highly restrictive output requirements. This work provides a blueprint for evaluating quantum-enhanced ML algorithms under realistic hardware constraints and help identifying the bottlenecks that must be overcome to approach industrial quantum utility.

title: NISQ Preparation of Conditional Thermal States for Precision Thermometry
authors: Emery Doucet, Reece Robertson, Nicholas Donatelli, Shou-I Tang, Sebastian Deffner, Akira Sone
abstract: The ability to prepare thermal states on gate-based quantum computers is an important building block for quantum computation, both with regard to the implementation of certain classes of quantum algorithms as well as to the study of quantum thermodynamics in and out of equilibrium. A useful generalization of the standard notion of a thermal state which appears naturally in the study of quantum work distributions is the conditional thermal state, which is conditioned on the use of an accessible pointer basis associated with a measurement apparatus. Among other uses, it has been proven that conditional thermal states can outperform ordinary thermal states in quantum thermometry. In this work we demonstrate the preparation of conditional thermal states of few-qubit systems implemented on IonQ's cloud-based quantum computers across a range of temperatures. To validate their performance advantage in thermometry, we measure the sub-quantum Fisher information (a lower bound on the quantum Fisher information) of the prepared states, which can be computed via a constant-depth quantum circuit without tomography.

title: Reducing T gates in product formulas with agent loops
authors: Luis Mantilla Calderón, Jérôme F. Gonthier, Alex Zook, Kohei Nakaji, Taylor L. Patti, Alán Aspuru-Guzik
abstract: Quantum chemistry calculations on a fault-tolerant quantum computer usually require many $\text{T}$ gates. This cost depends on the simulation method and how precisely its rotations are implemented. In this paper, we used Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a large language model (LLM), in a coding-agent loop to optimize the structure and rotation-synthesis precision of product formulas (PFs) for quantum phase estimation (QPE). Each of five independent searches optimized a shared protocol across 115 HamLib molecular Hamiltonians spanning 4--16 qubits over 100 code mutations. The searches started from a calibrated, nested second-order PF with uniform synthesis precision. We minimized $T_{95}$, the estimated total $\text{T}$-gate cost including QPE queries and repeated attempts for $95\%$ success probability, while requiring chemical accuracy for every training Hamiltonian. We name the best protocol found error-limited optimized Trotter evolution (ELOTE). It achieves chemical accuracy for its training data and achieved median and geometric-mean $T_{95}$ reductions of $85.35\%$ and $84.82\%$, respectively. ELOTE combines contributions to the same Pauli string, uses a first-order PF, and varies synthesis precision with coefficient magnitude, Pauli support, and diagonal character. We also tested ELOTE on 76 larger Hamiltonians with 18--22 qubits, which met chemical accuracy in every case. For ten reaction energies, we further optimized a shared $δ$-ELOTE protocol. It reduced geometric-mean $T_{95}$ by $58.90\%$ relative to ELOTE while preserving chemical accuracy for every signed reaction difference. These classically verified results show cost savings from shared protocols across molecules and reactions, and motivate similar searches in which energy measurements from quantum computers guide explorations in a coding-agent loop.

title: Transient entanglement generation in driven chiral networks beyond the secular approximation
authors: Yan Xi Foo, Kian Hwee Lim, Jia-Bin You, L. C. Kwek, Davit Aghamalyan
abstract: We study transient entanglement generation between two quantum nodes coupled through a chiral one-dimensional channel. In an emitter-only Born-Markov description, we show that continuous driving and an initial ground state can raise the maximum transient concurrence above the undriven 2/e benchmark associated with the effectively single-excitation model [1]. We then consider a more microscopic XX spin-chain channel with triangular plaquette couplings and compare a nonsecular time-convolutionless master equation (TCL-ME) with matrix-product-state (MPS) simulations. In the optimal driven regime, the nonsecular TCL-2 treatment reproduces the concurrence envelope and first transient peak qualitatively, while the remaining discrepancy is mainly attributable to beyond-Born system-bath correlations. The enhancement is traced to the failure of the secular approximation under strong driving, where nearby dressed transitions are not well separated on the dissipative timescale and nonsecular terms mix dressed-state coherences. Finally, we examine within TCL-2 the sensitivity of the protocol to positional disorder, imperfect chirality, and loss into nonguided modes. These results clarify when the familiar 2/e limitation ceases to apply and separate the roles of secular breakdown, Born-factorization error, and reduced-state memory in driven chiral entanglement generation; we believe that our study contributes in being one of the first studies where the breakdown of the secular approximation is useful rather than detrimental.

title: Statistics of time and frequency-averaged spectra in gravitational-wave background searches
Intelligent control of collisional architectures for multipartite Dicke-state preparation
authors: Duc Dung Vu, Minh Tam Nguyen, Özgür Esat Müstecaplıoğlu, Fatih Özaydin
abstract: Designing robust control protocols for multipartite entanglement is a central challenge for quantum technologies. We introduce a measurement-free collision-model protocol for preparing symmetric Dicke states | D n ( m ) ⟩ using excitation-preserving partial-SWAP interactions between two qubit registers and m shuttle qubits that remain part of the final state. The intra-register and shuttle–register collision strengths are treated as control parameters and optimized using a multi-start L-BFGS-B procedure. This extends collision-based entanglement generation beyond the single-excitation W-state sector without projective measurement or postselection. We assess the protocol under missed collisions, coherent crosstalk, independent and correlated dephasing, depolarization, and amplitude damping, and additionally quantify sensitivity to uncertainty in the assumed noise parameters. For the finite Dicke-state family studied here, optimized collision strengths preserve high preparation fidelities over broad imperfection ranges. These results provide a physically transparent framework for measurement-free Dicke-state preparation in repeated-interaction architectures.

title: Scalable spin squeezing in power-law-interacting X X Z models with disorder
authors: Samuel E. Begg, Bishal Ghosh, Chong Zu, Chuanwei Zhang, Michael Kolodrubetz
abstract: While spin squeezing has been traditionally considered in all-to-all interacting models, recent works have shown that it can also occur in systems with power-law interactions, enabling direct tests in Rydberg atoms, trapped ions, ultracold atoms, and nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. For the latter, Wu et al. Nature 646 (2025) demonstrated that spin squeezing is heavily affected by positional disorder, reducing any capacity for a practical squeezing advantage, which requires scalability with the system size. In this Letter we explore the robustness of spin squeezing in two-dimensional lattices with a fraction of unoccupied lattice sites. Using semiclassical modeling, we demonstrate the existence of scalable squeezing in power-law interacting XXZ models up to a disorder threshold, above which it breaks down. We produce a phase diagram for scalable squeezing, and demonstrate the impact of critical slowing down close to the phase boundary. Our work is consistent with—and offers a plausible explanation for—the absence of scalable squeezing in the aforementioned NV experiment, while illustrating the maximum disorder allowed for realizing scalable spin squeezing in a host of quantum simulators. We highlight a regime with substantial disorder tolerance and identify controlled defect creation as a promising route for scalable squeezing in solid-state systems.

title: A room-temperature extreme high vacuum system for trapped-ion quantum information processing
authors: Lewis Hahn, Nikhil Kotibhaskar, Fabien Lefebvre, Sakshee Patil, Sainath Motlakunta, Mahmood Sabooni, Rajibul Islam
abstract: We present a room-temperature Extreme High Vacuum (XHV) system engineered to support the long-duration operation of a trapped-ion quantum processor. Background-gas collisions impose limitations on trapped-ion performance and scalability by interrupting algorithmic execution and, in some cases, ejecting ions from the trap. Using molecular-flow simulations, we optimize the chamber geometry, conductance pathways, and pumping configuration to maximize the effective pumping speed at the ion location. We perform high-temperature heat treatment of stainless steel vacuum components to achieve the desired outgassing rate, guided by quantitative relations of bulk diffusive processes, allowing us to reduce the H2 outgassing load to the 10−15 mbarls−1 cm−2 level. The final pressure in our chamber, measured by a hot cathode gauge, is 1.5 × 10−12 mbar, corresponding to the gauge’s measurement limit. We measure the local pressure at the ion location by observing collision-induced reordering events in a long ion chain of mixed-isotope Yb+. From the observed reordering frequency, we extract the average interval between collisions to be (1.4 ± 0.3) hrs/ion. This corresponds to a local pressure of (5.4 ± 1.1) × 10−12 mbar at the ion location, assuming that all collisions arise from background H2 molecules at room temperature. Our demonstration extends the continuous operation time of a quantum processor while maintaining the simplicity of a room-temperature system that does not require cryogenic apparatus.

title: Femicide in the Global Premodern
Orbit-Qubit Quantum Processor of Ultracold Atoms
authors: Ming-Gen He, Wei-Yong Zhang, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, Jian-Wei Pan
abstract: It is challenging to build scalable quantum processors capable of both parallel control and local operation. As a promising platform to overcome this challenge, optical lattices offer exceptional parallelism. However, it has been struggling with precise local operations due to relatively narrow lattice spacings. Here, we introduce a new quantum processor incorporating orbit-qubit encoding and internal states (as auxiliary degrees of freedom) to achieve spatially selective operations together with parallel control. With this processor, we generate one-dimensional and two-dimensional cluster states using minimal layers of controlled-Z gates. We experimentally detect the multipartite entanglement of a two-dimensional cluster state involving 123 orbit qubits through direct stabilizer measurements, verifying the full bipartite non-separability. Furthermore, we demonstrate measurement-based quantum computation by implementing single-qubit and two-qubit logical gates, highlighting the flexibility of orbit-qubit operations. Our results establish orbit-qubit optical lattices as a scalable quantum processing architecture, opening new pathways for quantum computation applications.

title: Detecting quantum phase transitions via shallow variational quantum circuits
authors: Ching-Yu Huang, Min-Fong Yang
abstract: Mapping quantum phase diagrams through classical simulation is notoriously resource-intensive, as even small systems far from the thermodynamic limit demand prohibitive computational effort. The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) offers a compelling alternative, exploiting approximate ground states to distinguish phases. An appealing proposal, dubbed as Delta-VQE, determines critical points by contrasting variational energies optimized from reference states of distinct phases. Intriguingly, the diagnostic sharpens as circuit depth decreases, highlighting its promise as a resource-conscious probe of quantum criticality. To probe the broader applicability and underlying mechanisms of this approach, we investigate the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model with a three-spin cluster interaction, a setting in which the Ising transitions are generally situated beyond the self-dual line. We demonstrate that, whenever dual ansätze are employed, Delta-VQE invariably detects the self-dual points rather than the true criticality. In contrast, when ansätze are carefully tailored to embody the competing phases across the boundary, the genuine Ising critical point can be successfully identified with only minor finite-size effects. Our results establish that, while Delta-VQE provides a resource-efficient probe of quantum criticality without requiring precise ground-state preparation, its diagnostic power is fundamentally contingent upon the judicious selection of physically representative ansätze.

title: Multiplexed double-transmon coupler scheme in a scalable superconducting quantum processor
authors: Tianqi Cai, Chi-Tong Chen, Kunliang Bu, Sainan Huai, Xiaopei Yang, Zhiwen Zong, Yuan Li, Zhenxing Zhang
abstract: Precise control of superconducting qubits is essential for advancing quantum simulation and error correction. Transmon qubit systems employing the single-transmon coupler scheme have demonstrated high-fidelity gate operations by dynamically tuning the effective coupling between qubits. However, this scheme increases control-line count, posing a bottleneck for chip routing and scalability. To address this challenge, we propose a control-line multiplexing scheme based on a double-transmon coupler architecture, which enables shared coupler control lines to substantially reduce wiring complexity. We experimentally verify that this multiplexed configuration efficiently suppresses static Z Z coupling while maintaining accurate two-qubit gate control. We further demonstrate the feasibility of the architecture through two gate implementations: a fast coupler Z -control-based controlled- Z gate and a parametric iSWAP gate. To validate the practical applicability of this approach, we prepare Bell and three-qubit GHZ states with fidelities exceeding 99% and 96%, respectively. This architecture offers a route to reducing wiring overhead in two-dimensional qubit arrays, enhancing the scalability of superconducting quantum processors.

title: Exact gradients for linear optics with single photons
Efficient Targeting of Arbitrary Excited States with Quantum Inverse Power Iteration through Filtering Polynomials
An iterative Ising decoder for quantum error correction codes
authors: Yuanqi Liu, Weilei Zeng, Peixiang Li, Yantong Liu, Guangyao Huang, Yingwen Liu, Dongyang Wang, Junjie Wu
abstract: The Ising framework maps the decoding problem in quantum error correction onto ground-state optimization of a classical Hamiltonian, in which X – Z error correlations enter as cross terms. Under phenomenological depolarizing noise, the exact joint formulation contains up to 8-body interactions for the toric code and 10-body for the 6.6.6 color code. These high-order terms degrade solver convergence, inflate runtime, and raise the auxiliary spin overhead when embedding into native 2-body Ising hardware. In this work, we propose the iterative low-order decoding (ILOD) algorithm, which alternates between X - and Z -type sub-Hamiltonians, approximating cross-type correlations through Bayesian priors that reweight each type’s couplings using the other type’s inferred error configuration. This halves the maximum body count of interaction terms in the Hamiltonian, accelerating the solver, restoring convergence at larger code distances, and reducing the total spin count for 2-body embedding by a factor of 2.5. For the toric code, ILOD attains a threshold of 4.73 % versus 4.83 % for the joint formulation, with the empirical runtime ratio scaling as (0.81) d. For the 6.6.6 color code, the fitted ILOD and joint thresholds agree within statistical uncertainty, and ILOD remains convergent at larger distances where the joint formulation fails to converge despite a larger annealing budget.

title: Benchmarking and resource analysis for augmented-Lagrangian quantum Hamiltonian descent
authors: Zeguan Wu, Mingze Li, Muqing Zheng, Meng Wang, Junyu Liu, Samuel Stein, Ang Li, Yousu Chen
abstract: Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) is a continuous optimization algorithm based on simulating a time-dependent quantum Hamiltonian whose potential energy encodes the objective function and whose kinetic energy promotes exploration through quantum interference and tunneling. While QHD is formulated for unconstrained optimization, many real-world optimization problems are constrained and highly nonconvex. In this paper, we benchmark AL-QHD, a hybrid framework that embeds QHD within the Augmented Lagrangian Method (ALM), thereby solving a sequence of unconstrained subproblems while using ALM to enforce constraints. We evaluate AL-QHD on standard nonconvex test functions and use iterative refinement to improve solution accuracy at fixed per-run qubit cost. A finite-shot supplement replaces exact-probability feedback by measurement outcomes and scans 100–10,000 shots per readout, quantifying the empirical tradeoff between solution quality, reliability, and measurement cost across complete adaptive runs. Separately from the optimization benchmarks, we estimate gate-level resources for AL-QHD circuit constructions using ACOPF-derived symbolic models extracted from the synthetic Texas7k network dataset. These models contain 2–198 buses and 6–538 active variables and are used solely for resource estimation; we do not execute AL-QHD optimization on these models or solve the full Texas7k network. Resource estimates on Texas7k-derived ACOPF instances show steep hard-gate scaling, reaching ∼ 4.46 × 10 7 entangling gates in a NISQ-oriented model and ∼ 9.42 × 10 8 T gates in a fault-tolerant model at ∼ 5.3 × 10 2 active variables. These results suggest that AL-QHD is a useful framework for studying constrained nonconvex optimization with QHD, but that practical ACOPF-scale applications under the implementation analyzed here would likely require large-scale fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: Sequential measurements as a resource in ancilla-assisted quantum metrology
authors: Koray Mentesoglu, Rahul Trivedi, Sara Mouradian
abstract: We present a protocol for simultaneous estimation of both quadratures of a displacement channel on a quantum harmonic oscillator using a single ancilla qubit, without complex state preparation or adaptive control. The qubit is coupled to the quantum harmonic oscillator via controlled displacements of strength A and undergoes N rounds of measurement and reset, while the oscillator coherently accumulates the displacement signal. Energy is injected and the non-commuting displacements imprint an order-dependent geometric phase at each round, giving a quantum Fisher information that scales as 𝒪 ( A 2 N 3 ) .
