Although the measurement record space grows as 2 N , we show that exact likelihoods for any individual measurement record can be computed in 𝒪 ( N 2 ) time. We show that measurement in the computational basis approximately saturates the quantum bound and maintains the 𝒪 ( A 2 N 3 ) scaling. Furthermore, the periodic information extraction makes the protocol robust to decoherence. Our results provide a framework for the design and analysis of sequential measurement in ancilla-assisted protocols.

title: Probing the Memory of a Superconducting Qubit Environment
authors: Nicolas Gosling, Denis Bénâtre, Paul Kugler, Simon Geisert, Nicolas Zapata, Mitchell Field, Sumeru Hazra, Simon Günzler
abstract: Achieving fault tolerance with superconducting quantum processors requires qubits to operate within the regime of threshold theorems based on the Born-Markov approximation. This approximation, which models dissipation as constant energy decay into a memoryless environment, breaks down when qubits couple to long-lived two-level systems (TLSs) that become polarized during operation and retain memory of past qubit states. Here, we show that non-Poissonian quantum jump traces carry the information required to distinguish long-lived TLSs from the standard Markovian bath. By fitting the Solomon equations to measured quantum jump dynamics arising naturally from thermal fluctuations, we can disentangle the qubit’s coupling to the two environments. Sweeping the qubit frequency reveals distinct peaks, each associated with a TLS that outlives the qubit, providing a handle to understand their microscopic origin.

title: A 3D stacked surface-code architecture for routing-efficient measurement-free quantum error correction
authors: Gunsik Min, IlKwon Sohn, Jun Heo
abstract: Mid-circuit measurement latency and noise can limit surface-code quantum error correction. Measurement-free quantum error correction (MFEC) replaces measurement and classical feed-forward with coherent feedback, but planar layouts then face a different bottleneck: inter-block transversal CNOT layers require SWAP routing with depth that grows as O(d). We propose a 3D stacked surface-code architecture in which vertically aligned couplers implement these CNOTs directly while stabilizer checks remain local within each layer. For the distance-3 rotated surface code, we provide an explicit embedding of transversal coupling, syndrome extraction, reset/copy, and single-target coherent feedback. For larger distances, effective-location extrapolations are used only to isolate the routing benefit, assuming a scalable coherent decoder. Under a superconducting-inspired decoherence model, the 3D layout becomes favorable when measurement-induced idling dominates coherent-operation errors. A sensitivity sweep with pvCNOT/p2q ∈ {1, 3, 5, 10} shows that a tenfold vertical-gate penalty weakens but does not remove the 3D advantage and increases the estimated break-even ratio by approximately 12–29%. A branch-level Pauli-frame check validates the distance-3 feedback grammar. The results identify vertical connectivity as a targeted architectural resource, while dense vertical-gate arrays and correlated inter-layer crosstalk remain open hardware challenges

title: Quantum algorithms for photoreactivity in cancer-targeted photosensitizers
authors: Yanbing Zhou, Pablo A. M. Casares, Diksha Dhawan, Ignacio Loaiza, Soran Jahangiri, Robert A. Lang, Juan Miguel Arrazola, Stepan Fomichev
abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a targeted cancer treatment that uses light-activated photosensitizers to generate reactive oxygen species that selectively destroy tumor cells, generally causing less collateral damage than conventional treatments. However, its clinical success hinges on the availability of photosensitizers with strong optical sensitivity and high efficiency in generating reactive oxygen species. While classical computational methods have provided useful insights into photosensitizer design, they struggle to scale and often lack the accuracy needed for these simulations. In this work, we show how fault-tolerant quantum algorithms can help identify promising photosensitizer candidates for PDT. First, we introduce a threshold projection algorithm that estimates the dipole strength within the therapeutic window as a measure of optical sensitivity. Second, we use the intersystem crossing (ISC) evolution-proxy approach to estimate electronic singlet–triplet mixing, with a separate vibronic dynamics treatment when nuclear motion must be included. We apply these algorithms to a clinically relevant and actively pursued class of photosensitizers, BODIPY derivatives, including heavy-atom and transition-metal-substituted systems that are challenging for classical methods. For active spaces of 11–45 spatial orbitals, we estimate 278–497 logical qubits for the qubitized implementations. Two readouts per execution reduce the absorption sampling cost at the same combined filtering and statistical accuracy. These algorithms directly evaluate photophysical quantities that can guide photosensitizer design.

title: Quantum Science and Technologies: From Strangeness to Opportunities
authors: Ravo Tokiniaina Ranaivoson
abstract: Quantum physics has already shaped our daily lives through a first technological revolution: semiconductors, transistors, lasers, atomic clocks, medical imaging, and modern electronics. This first revolution primarily exploits the collective and statistical behavior of large ensembles of particles. A second revolution is now underway: it consists in controlling individual quantum systems by exploiting superposition, entanglement, interference, and measurement, while mastering decoherence. This transition opens perspectives in four major technological pillars: quantum sensing and metrology, quantum communication, quantum simulation, and quantum computing. The presentation assesses the maturity of these four pillars: quantum sensing and metrology, quantum communication, quantum simulation, and quantum computing. Particular attention is given to full-stack hardware architecture, to the distinction between physical and logical qubits, and to that between quantum advantage and fault tolerance. The presentation also addresses AI–quantum interactions, distinguishing operational AI-for-quantum methods from quantum-for-AI research and its structural limitations. It concludes with practical resources, cloud access, career pathways, and a perspective on skills, access, and post-quantum cryptography priorities. Keywords: quantum computing; quantum sensing; quantum communication; quantum simulation; post-quantum cryptography; quantum error correction; quantum machine learning, quantum software tools.

title: Quantum flow algorithm: Quantum simulations of chemical systems using reduced quantum resources and constant depth quantum circuits
authors: Bhumika Jayee, Nathan M. Myers, Duo Song, Eric J. Bylaska, Karol Kowalski, Nicholas P. Bauman
abstract: We assess the performance of the Quantum Flow (QFlow) algorithm employing cost-effective solvers based on the unitary coupled-cluster Ansatz with single and double excitations (QFlow-SD). The resulting energies are benchmarked against those obtained with an analogous QFlow formulation defined in the same active spaces but augmented by higher-rank excitations, including triples and quadruples (QFlow-SDTQ) within a matrix-based implementation, to isolate the effect of excitation rank. Across all molecular systems considered, QFlow-SD closely reproduces the QFlow-SDTQ energies thereby requiring substantially fewer variational parameters while preserving the reduced-qubit footprint of the QFlow algorithm. For this implementation, we perform a series of calculations, including a composite two-step downfolding workflow for H2O. To enable simulations beyond the matrix implementation, we introduce and demonstrate a second-quantized many-body formulation of QFlow. Using this formulation, we perform QFlow calculations of larger problems, including H8 in 6-31G, H2O in 6-31G, and a 4 × 4 two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model, reducing the parent qubit requirements (26-32 qubits) to eight-qubit active-space subproblems. We compare our results against benchmark DMRG energies and show rapid convergence over QFlow cycles and recovery of a large fraction of correlation energy.

title: Ideal optical flux lattices
authors: Ophelia Evelyn Sommer, Nigel R. Cooper
abstract: The realization of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states in cold atomic gases is a long-standing goal in quantum simulation. Established approaches, including rapidly rotating gases and tight-binding lattices, are often hampered by low interaction energies and small many-body energy gaps. While optical flux lattices (OFLs) can achieve higher effective magnetic flux densities, standard two-state configurations generate highly nonuniform fields, and extensions to multistate systems introduce significant experimental complexity. Here, we present a paradigm for engineering robust FQH phases in OFLs using only two internal atomic states. We show that the introduction of an additional scalar potential provides a generic mechanism for creating Chern bands that are simultaneously essentially flat and “ideal.” These desirable properties arise by tuning lattice parameters to certain N -flat manifolds (N = 1, 2, ⋯), where the 1-flat manifold shares its origin with certain “magic-angle” conditions familiar from moiré materials. A central result is the design of a dark-state OFL whose adiabatic Hamiltonian is of Aharonov-Casher (AC) form. This exact AC equivalence guarantees perfectly flat, exactly ideal Chern bands in the adiabatic limit. This method allows for precise tuning of band flatness and stabilizes both Abelian and non-Abelian FQH phases. Our scheme is compatible with existing experimental capabilities using vector polarizability, opening practical routes to exploring strongly correlated topological physics with cold atoms.

title: Clifford+T Templates for Circuit Optimization and Hardware-Aware Implementation
authors: MD MAZDER RAHMAN, Gerhard W. Dueck
abstract: This paper presents a set of templates for the Clifford+T gate library. Each template provides an alternative realization of an equivalent circuit, allowing gate count to be traded against hardware-dependent considerations such as connectivity, calibrated gate errors, and noise cancellation. Although shorter realizations are often preferable, longer sequences may sometimes improve measured fidelity through error cancellation or noise tailoring. This tradeoff must be evaluated on the target hardware rather than inferred from gate count alone. The presented templates provide a basis for systematic template-based synthesis and minimization of quantum circuits.

title: Adaptive Quantum Error Detection and Correction Architecture for Scalable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Systems
authors: Murali Krishna Pasupuleti
journal: International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)
abstract: Error correction in a quantum processor creates a timing problem. A decoder can extract more information from a syndrome history yet deliver its answer after a logical operation has consumed the result. This study proposes Deadline-Aware Syndrome Routing, a classical control architecture that preserves the physical check schedule and allocates additional decoding to windows in which a timely change of decision is likely to prevent a logical error. The mathematical framework couples a binary syndrome model to a queue-capacity constraint and a decision rule based on the expected reduction in terminal logical error. The numerical analysis uses published measurements from a distance-five surface-code experiment in which two decoders processed the same hardware records. The real-time and offline neural decoders yielded logical error rates of 0.350% and 0.269% per cycle, respectively. At the published processing time of 24 microseconds per cycle and acquisition interval of 1.1 microseconds, one continuously loaded patch could refer at most about 4.58% of equal-length windows to one dedicated reference worker under ideal scheduling. In a ten-cycle parity model, matching the offline error rate would require at least 16.7 net prevented errors per 100 referred windows. This requirement can be tested by measuring whether syndrome features available before a deadline predict which decoder will be correct when their decisions disagree. The paper specifies a paired hardware test that records timing, logical outcomes and every attempted decision. The architecture’s end-to-end performance remains an empirical question. Keywords Quantum error correction • fault tolerance • surface codes • syndrome extraction • erasure-aware decoding • Pauli-frame tracking • logical memory • decoder latency • selective decoding • queue stability • logical feedforward • calibration drift

title: Syndrome Resampling Enhances Quantum Error Correction Thresholds
authors: Luis Colmenárez, Áron Márton, Markus Franziskus Müller
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) enables fault-tolerant quantum computation but requires operating quantum hardware at physical error rates below code-dependent thresholds, which remains challenging for current devices. We introduce , a general method that increases QEC thresholds of any decoder and suppresses logical errors without additional hardware, decoding modifications, or code-specific assumptions beyond syndrome statistics. The method exploits the fact that syndromes with low probability are likely to lead to logical failure; therefore, biasing syndrome averages toward most likely syndromes effectively increases logical fidelities. We establish a direct connection between the Rényi coherent information (RCI) and powers of the syndrome probability distribution, showing that resampling syndromes according to these powers combined with maximum likelihood decoding (MLD) realizes a family of optimal thresholds associated with phase transitions in the RCI. Numerical simulations of surface codes demonstrate that syndrome resampling substantially increases thresholds for both optimal and suboptimal decoders and reduces logical error rates by up to four orders of magnitude in experimentally relevant regimes. We further show that syndrome resampling can be effectively implemented from finite data and combined with decoding-based postselection to achieve additional gains. Finally, applying the method to existing experimental QEC data yields up to 2 orders of magnitude reduction in logical error rates without requiring additional measurements. Our results provide a practical and decoder-agnostic route to improved logical fidelities in near-term QEC experiments.

title: Decoding quantum noise to achieve fault-tolerant computing and advanced error correction
authors: Radhakrishnan Delhibabu
abstract: This paper evaluates the scaling requirements for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) through the lens of advanced quantum error correction (QEC) protocols. While current physical two-qubit gate error rates operate near $$10^{-3}$$ , practical quantum utility demands logical error rates suppressed below $$10^{-12}$$ . This discrepancy necessitates a massive resource overhead, historically requiring 1,000 physical qubits per logical qubit in standard surface code architectures. The fundamental novelty of this work lies in establishing a unified vertical co-design framework that bridges theoretical topological bounds directly with empirical microarchitectural constraints, including cryogenic cooling budgets at 15 mK, through-silicon via (TSV) parasitics, and real-time classical decoding latency. In this review and roadmap, we analyze novel decoding algorithms capable of reducing physical qubit overhead by up to 40% under standard circuit-level depolarizing noise models ( $$p = 10^{-3}$$ ), and evaluate dynamic error mitigation strategies that demonstrate an empirical 3 $$\times$$ improvement in circuit fidelity for shallow-to-intermediate depth benchmarks ( $$d \le 60$$ ) prior to reaching the fault-tolerant break-even frontier. By projecting a hardware trajectory toward the sub- $$10^{-4}$$ physical error rate threshold, we systematically outline the microarchitectural, thermodynamic, and software co-design constraints required to synthesize a fully operational, 100-logical-qubit fault-tolerant processor.

title: Quantum Computing for Materials Discovery: Algorithms, Obstacles, and Outlook
authors: Miroslava Nedyalkova, Marco Lattuada
abstract: Materials discovery is increasingly limited by problems that classical electronic-structure methods handle poorly: strongly correlated d- and f-electron systems, multireference transition-metal complexes, and reaction intermediates whose wavefunctions resist mean-field and perturbative approximations. Because quantum computers represent quantum states natively rather than through approximation, materials simulation is widely regarded as the most credible near-term application of quantum hardware. This perspective surveys the algorithmic toolkit being applied to catalyst, battery, and correlated-electron materials, including variational quantum eigensolvers, quantum phase estimation, sample-based quantum diagonalization, and hybrid quantum-classical machine learning. It weighs recent hardware milestones in error correction against the qubit overhead, measurement bottlenecks, and benchmarking gaps that still separate demonstrations from decision-grade materials predictions. We argue that progress will come not from a single demonstration of quantum advantage but from integrating algorithms, error mitigation, and classical machine-learning workflows, focused on the narrow class of materials problems where classical methods are demonstrably weakest.

title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Iqra Bashir, Yuanfeng Wang, Mingda Huang, Keren Li, Qi Qin
abstract: A central question in quantum machine learning is which functions of an input state a model can represent when its measurement is fixed by hardware or by experimental design. We address this question for quantum neural networks with a fixed readout observable, where the trainable pre-measurement dynamics determine the effective observable in the Heisenberg picture and the scalar output is the measured expectation value itself, without trainable affine post-processing. We characterize the reachable effective observables under three physical resource classes: unitary evolution, which preserves the spectrum of the readout; mixed-unitary evolution, which relaxes this to a majorization constraint while preserving the trace; and completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) evolution, whose Heisenberg adjoint is unital rather than trace-preserving and therefore lifts the trace constraint inherited at the mixed-unitary level. The three reachable sets are a fixed-spectrum orbit, its convex hull, and an operator interval, and the inclusions are strict for any readout that is not proportional to the identity. The separation is witnessed locally: for a fixed Pauli readout $Z_j$ on an arbitrary number of qubits, the amplitude-damping observable $γ\id+(1-γ)Z_j$ lies outside the mixed-unitary level for every $γ>0$. We realize the CPTP level with a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive closed-form loss floors, $4γ^2/3$ and $γ^2$ for the unitary and mixed-unitary levels and zero at the CPTP level, which the numerics reproduce within precision. Structured-observable, Rényi-moment and classification experiments illustrate how the hierarchy manifests in finite-depth ansätze. The results identify which spectral constraint each physical resource relaxes, framing reachable-observable classes as a resource for expressivity rather than an architectural advantage.

title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing
authors: Tianyan Quantum Group
abstract: This paper presents Cqlib, a high-performance software stack for quantum computing built around a unified quantum circuit model. Its native Rust core provides efficient implementations of circuit processing, quantum-state and operator computation, compilation, and optimization, while Python and C interfaces support algorithm development and system integration. Cqlib covers quantum program construction, simulation, analysis, compilation, device adaptation, and result processing under consistent program semantics. Through OpenQASM and the Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS), Cqlib supports program representation and hardware-oriented execution. Cqlib further provides backend interfaces for device execution, with Cqlib-Tianyan serving as one implementation for QCIS-compatible quantum hardware. Evaluations using parameterized compilation tasks from Benchpress and related tests show that Cqlib achieves good functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated task scope. We develop Cqlib-Algorithm as a modular library of reusable operators and composable components for widely used quantum algorithms, including quantum search, phase estimation, and variational algorithms, with additional support for error mitigation. To complement these building blocks with domain-specific workflows, we further develop Cqlib-VQE, Cqlib-QAOA, and Cqlib-QML for application-level studies in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning, respectively. Cqlib also integrates source-grounded Skills and MCP-based tools to support agent-assisted program generation, backend execution, and result-guided workflow refinement. Overall, Cqlib provides a unified and extensible software foundation that connects quantum algorithm development, simulation, compilation, and execution on QCIS-compatible quantum hardware.

title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
authors: Jiaqing Jiang, Nathan Ju
abstract: Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $β$ to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/δ))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $β$ and linear in $1/δ$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(β)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

title: A novel quantum lattice Boltzmann methodology for cosmological radiation transport
authors: Rasmit Devkota, John Wise
abstract: Radiation transport is an essential process in many physical simulations, including cosmological codes which track stellar and diffuse radiation. Many present codes utilize ray tracing or moment methods, but these grow increasingly difficult and expensive for large simulations. Quantum lattice Boltzmann methods exponentially reduce complexity by propagating radiation over a lattice, allowing for better spatial resolution without needing to introduce adaptive ray tracing or other optimizations. However, existing formulations result in poor angular resolution for radiation point sources. In this work, we propose an angular redistribution methodology which significantly improves the resolution with minimal increase in complexity. We verify the correctness of the method on both classical processors and quantum simulators and outline how the quantum algorithm can be integrated into existing codes. This method is an important step towards fully-quantum radiation hydrodynamics simulation which could exponentially accelerate existing cosmological codes, enabling simulations at scales currently infeasible.

title: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction
authors: Guoyu Shu, Ling Hu, Hongbo Wu, Zhongchu Ni, Yanyan Cai, Xiaowei Deng, Pan Zheng, Pengbo Li
abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction relies on an accurate description of single-photon loss dissipation using an ideal annihilation operator, under which correctable loss errors act equivalently on different logical code states. In realistic weakly nonlinear bosonic modes, however, coupling to a structured environment can render photon loss Fock-state dependent, thereby modifying the effective dissipation operator and deforming the associated error space. Here, we experimentally investigate this effect in a three-dimensional circuit quantum electrodynamics system. By injecting spectrally engineered environmental noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator, we observe pronounced frequency selectivity in the measured Fock-state dynamics. While the long-time transition rates converge to the Markovian limit, the transient dynamics display distinctly non-Markovian behavior, in quantitative agreement with a second-order time-convolutionless theory. By applying narrowband noise to a binomially encoded logical qubit, we further demonstrate Fock-state-dependent dissipation channels that drive logical states beyond the nominally correctable error space. These results establish structured environmental noise as a mechanism for deforming photon-loss errors in weakly nonlinear bosonic systems and highlight the need to incorporate realistic, state-dependent dissipation into the design and characterization of bosonic quantum error correction.

title: Optimal fidelity over zero-capacity erasure channels
authors: Camilo Castro-Landolt, Rabsan Galib Ahmed, Graeme Smith
abstract: Antidegradable quantum channels have zero capacity for reliable quantum communication. However, they can nevertheless transmit quantum information with nontrivial fidelity. This raises the question: how well can quantum information be preserved through such channels? In this work, we exactly characterize the optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity of quantum erasure channels throughout the antidegradable regime. Specifically, we show that it equals $γ+\frac{1-γ}{d}$ for transmission probabilities $0<γ\le \frac{1}{2}$ and logical dimension $d$. We use fractional extendibility to establish an upper bound on the entanglement fidelity achievable by arbitrary error-correcting protocols. Furthermore, we construct a family of permutation-invariant codes that asymptotically saturates this bound.

title: Small-world networks yield tunable quantum codes at short circuit depth
authors: Samuel Bevins, Gregory Bentsen
abstract: Monitored random quantum circuits naturally generate quantum error-correcting codes. We generate quantum codes with tunable properties by implementing random Clifford circuits on Watts--Strogatz `small-world' networks and tailor code properties via three knobs: nonlocal graph rewiring, measurement rate, and circuit depth. On fully rewired networks, circuits of logarithmic depth produce codes with a finite rate and an extensive mean contiguous distance with failure probability substantially lower than codes produced from local circuits. These small-world codes form at a circuit depth growing as $\ln n$ compared to polynomial depths required for codes produced from local networks. Rewiring also moves the purification transition to higher measurement rates and changes its critical exponents. Connectivity is thus a knob for designing codes.

title: Confidence-Aware Discriminative Readout of Neutral-Atom Arrays
authors: Jaeick Bae, Kangheun Kim, Yunheung Song, Junseo Ha, Jeong Ho Han, Jaewook Ahn, Hyunsoo Ha, Soonwon Choi
abstract: Fast and reliable detection is a central requirement for neutral atom quantum computers, yet fluorescence imaging remains a limiting step for rapid experimental cycling, large-scale array operation, and quantum-error-correction protocols. In this work, we demonstrate confidence-aware readout of $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ atoms in optical tweezers using a discriminative classifier. Rather than forcing each atom-site image directly into a hard binary outcome, the proposed readout produces a measurement reliability score. This score is produced by a logistic-regression classifier trained on features derived from both the total photon count and the spatial pattern of fluorescence at each site. The resulting classifier achieves the same readout fidelity with approximately half the imaging time. At an exposure of 10 ms, it achieves $99.83\%$ readout fidelity, comparable to the $99.82\%$ achieved by conventional photon-count thresholding at 20 ms. Importantly, the classifier score enables low-confidence outcomes to be converted into measurement-level erasures, leaving fewer residual unflagged errors at a fixed erasure budget. This improvement is further accompanied by strong false-positive suppression, which is important for downstream operations such as atom rearrangement where false positives can create target defects. Monte Carlo rearrangement simulations show that the reduced false-positive rate and confidence-based erasure conversion improve predicted defect-free assembly performance. This work establishes confidence-aware readout using a discriminative classifier as a practical paradigm for fast and scalable neutral-atom quantum computing.

title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems
authors: Eitaro Ishikawa, Noah Hirai, Koichiro Miyanishi, Hana Ebi, Kazufumi Tanji, Isamu Kudo, Kenji Toyoda, Masahiro Takeoka
abstract: The quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture is a promising approach to scalable trapped-ion quantum computing, enabling flexible qubit interactions by transporting ions between dedicated trap zones. Programs for such systems require operations beyond conventional circuit primitives: ion shuttling, physical SWAPs, trap splitting and merging, and cooling. Motional excitation accumulated during transport increases the mean phonon number of ions and degrades the fidelity of the two-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates. However, existing quantum error correction (QEC) simulation frameworks do not jointly track per-ion motional excitation and explicitly schedule cooling operations with their transport time and heating costs. We develop a full-stack software framework for QEC experiments and simulations on linear QCCD systems with a single ion species, comprising an intermediate representation (IR) supporting QCCD-native operations, a compiler that translates syndrome-extraction circuits into the IR, and a heating-aware noise-injection pipeline that generates noisy Stim circuits. The compiler updates the mean phonon number of each ion throughout the schedule, and the pipeline derives gate-dependent error rates from the tracked phonon states and per-ion timing, enabling the evaluation of finite-size logical-error scaling of the rotated surface code under transport- and heating-aware noise. We show that transport-induced heating prevents logical error rates from decreasing with increasing code distance under the evaluated conditions, and that indirectly cooling the ion pairs involved in two-qubit gates, by merging them with precooled coolant ions immediately before each gate, restores this decrease. By sweeping the duration and post-cooling mean phonon number of an abstract cooling instruction, we characterize their trade-off and identify the region in which logical-error scaling is maintained.

title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search
authors: Sora Harada, Ryo Kuroiwa, Shin Nishio, Takeaki Uno
abstract: In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.

title: Geometric properties of concatenated geometric and holonomic quantum gates
authors: Rasmus Wallentin, Erik Sjöqvist
abstract: We investigate the geometric properties of concatenated quantum gates, focusing on the distinction between geometric and holonomic quantum computation. We show that, although individual gates may be purely geometric, their concatenation does not generally preserve this property, since the cyclic states of the composite operation can accumulate nontrivial dynamical phases over the course of the concatenated evolution. In contrast, we demonstrate that concatenations of arbitrary single-qubit holonomic gates remain holonomic, provided that the parallel-transport condition holds throughout the evolution and the computational subspace undergoes cyclic evolution. The preservation of geometric or holonomic character under concatenation is an important prerequisite for extending arguments underlying geometric protection from individual gates to complete quantum circuits.

title: Solving the Traveling Salesman Problem Using Quantum Devices: QUBO and HOBO Formulations
authors: G. V. Shuvalov, E. N. Krivtsova, A. V. Kapranov, M. A. Remnev
abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) forms the foundation for many logistics and optimization tasks. At the same time, this problem is NP-hard and requires significant computational resources. Quantum computing promises to substantially accelerate computations or increase solution accuracy. The TSP can be conveniently mapped onto the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulation, which in turn can be solved using variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) methods, but this mapping requires a quadratic number of qubits. The higher-order binary optimization (HOBO) formulation requires significantly fewer qubits, but it contains higher-order terms. In our work, we thoroughly investigate both formulations and provide a practical recipe for solving the TSP. We give a comprehensive study and compare in detail QUBO and HOBO formulations.

title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
authors: Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz, Mallikarjun Shankar, Nicholas Wright
abstract: Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.

title: A Hybrid Quantum Key Distribution and Post-Quantum Cryptography Orchestration for Real-Time Tactical Communication, Navigation, and Surveillance
authors: Bakhe Nleya, Beverly Pule
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Reproducibility package for the manuscript "Hybrid Quantum Key Distribution and Post-Quantum Cryptography Orchestration for Real-Time Tactical Communication, Navigation, and Surveillance". Regenerates Figures 3-6 and Table 4 from the plot data in data/, using the Python scripts in code/. See README.md for setup and expected values. The files fig3_plotdata.csv and fig5_main.csv are synthetic reconstructions satisfying the manuscript's stated anchors and are flagged in data/README.md as pending replacement with simulator output. Testbed measurements are not reproduced. Requires Python 3.10+ with numpy, matplotlib, and pandas.

title: Controlled Continuous-Time Quantum Walks for Power Grid Analysis under N-x Contingencies
authors: Mahesh N. Jayakody, Ruben Kara, Carsten Hartmann, Andrea Benigni
abstract: The combinatorial growth of network configurations under N-x contingencies presents significant computational challenges for power system analysis. In this work, we introduce a quantum algorithm based on Controlled Continuous-Time Quantum Walks (CCTQWs) that evolves a quantum walker conditioned on a contingency register held in a uniform superposition of all x-line outage configurations representing the contingency scenarios. The proposed framework encodes transmission line availability in a quantum register and employs controlled Hamiltonian evolution to account for topology changes induced by contingencies. We develop a gate-based implementation using Trotter-Suzuki product formulas and investigate the associated approximation errors and computational requirements. As a demonstration of the proposed methodology, we introduce a contingency-averaged occupation centrality measure derived from quantum-walk measurement statistics. Numerical experiments on an 8-bus power network under N-2 contingencies demonstrate the implementation of the algorithm and characterize the convergence of the resulting centrality estimates with respect to the observation window, sampling and Trotter steps. Comparison with established classical centrality measures shows a qualitatively consistent characterization of network structure, particularly in identifying the most central nodes. The proposed framework establishes a methodological foundation for quantum-walk-based analysis of power networks under contingencies, providing a starting point for future investigations of quantum algorithms for power system security assessment.

title: Stopping-Time Leakage in Blind Quantum Delegation
authors: Noureldin Mohamed, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: Blind quantum computation lets a client delegate a computation while hiding it from the server, up to a declared leakage. Its security definitions cover a single round. A variational quantum algorithm, however, delegates many rounds, and its classical optimizer decides from private data when to stop. We study what the resulting round count tells an honest-but-curious server. For protocols with one-time-padded transcripts and fresh randomness in every round, we prove that the server's best distinguishing advantage over the whole sequence equals the total-variation distance between the stopping-time distributions, so the round count is the only residual channel in this model. We also show that soundness composes as $δ\,\mathbb{E}[T]$ under adaptive stopping, given a conditional per-round soundness property that composably secure verifiable protocols provide. In simulated delegated eigensolvers for the transverse-field Ising chain, the local Polyak-Lojasiewicz ratio measured in iterations 5 to 15 predicts the noiseless stopping round with a leave-one-out error of 1.7 iterations, compared with 10.3 for a constant predictor. Across 14 configurations that differ in optimizer, stopping rule, initialization, system size, shot budget and problem family, the leakage is significant in 12 and ranges from 0.14 to 1.68 bits, and a maximum-entropy bound estimated on held-out sessions lies above it in all of them. For defense, we show that any mechanism acting after the stopping decision can only add rounds, and that differentially private padding costs the full adjacency radius. A fixed public iteration budget removes the channel completely; set at the median run length, it costs 10% of the remaining energy gap. A differentially private stopping rule based on AboveThreshold protects every pair of instances, but it must often stop too early, which makes it costly.

title: Undecidable quantum storage: no algorithm can tell from the noise rate whether a fixed circuit remembers
authors: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi
abstract: Below a threshold noise rate, error correction lets larger quantum memories store a qubit for longer, without limit. Can the noise rate alone tell us whether a given noisy circuit does this? We construct fixed local circuits for which no algorithm can, already in one dimension under single-qubit noise. Each circuit is translation-invariant and time-periodic, with depolarizing noise on every wire after every layer, including all classical control. A computable list of disjoint rate intervals is indexed by the inputs $n$ of a universal Turing machine; local noise statistics select the input that the circuit simulates, and halting triggers erasure. If the machine runs forever on $n$, a qubit is stored throughout the $n$-th interval at entanglement fidelity at least $15/16$ for a time that grows without bound with size: linearly on rings, exponentially in six dimensions. The encoding and decoding maps are noiseless and global; they depend on $n$, the system size and, for decoding, the time, but not on the rate. If it halts, the fidelity of every encoding falls below $1/2+η$, for any fixed $η>0$, after a time independent of size and rate. The labels of the intervals with unbounded storage form a $Π^0_1$-complete set, and intervals of both kinds accumulate at zero, so these circuits have no noise threshold. Without rate selection, the ring construction is a translation-invariant, time-periodic memory: from an initialized classical hierarchy it stores a qubit for a time linear in the ring length at every sufficiently small rate, addressing the memory part of a one-dimensional question raised by Dünnweber, Styliaris and Trivedi. These are existence results: registers and interaction ranges are very large and the rates astronomically small.

title: Long-time dynamics of open quantum systems: mathematical and physical aspects
authors: Daniele Amato, Paolo Facchi, Giovanni Gramegna, Arturo Konderak
abstract: Quantum channels provide the mathematical framework for describing the evolution of open quantum systems, i.e., quantum systems interacting with an environment. This review focuses on the long-time or asymptotic dynamics of open quantum systems, a topic of growing interest due to its relevance for quantum information theory and noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. We present a comprehensive analysis of homogeneous evolutions in both discrete and continuous time, treating the dynamics in full generality within the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures. By systematically studying the spectral properties of quantum channels, we present general structure theorems that characterize asymptotic behaviour, illustrated through several paradigmatic examples. We further discuss how the asymptotic dynamics can be exploited for dissipative state engineering, the identification of decoherence-free subspaces, the design of quantum error-correction schemes, and the evaluation of the asymptotic capacities of quantum channels.

title: Non-Abelian Twist Defects in Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: Rui Zeng, Li-Wei Yu
abstract: Bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity-check codes combine efficient quantum storage with a rich Abelian anyon structure, providing a compelling platform for exploring the interplay between quantum error correction and topological order. A central challenge is how to realize domain walls that host non-Abelian twist defects at their endpoints. Here we explicitly construct electric-magnetic duality walls for arbitrary bivariate bicycle codes with finite anyon content using composite, interblock, and patch checks. These checks remove the unwanted local modes while preserving charge conversion, ensuring that topologically contractible closed ribbons act trivially on encoded states. For each fixed code, check weights and interaction ranges remain bounded independently of wall length. The wall endpoints have quantum dimension $2^{Q/2}$, where $Q$ counts the independent generators in each electric or magnetic charge space. As an application, we illustrate measurement-only braiding for $Q=3$ under the correspondence between measurements and defect transport. Our construction provides a valuable basis for exploring non-Abelian defect physics and developing logical operations in quantum low-density parity-check codes with Abelian topological order in future.

title: A Qiskit-Based Simulation of Shor’s Algorithm
authors: Aarati Adhikari, Ram Krishna Tiwari, Harihar Paudyal
abstract: This study aims to explore the theoretical foundations and practical simulation of Shor’s algorithm, a quantum factoring algorithm technique that poses a considerable threat to classical cryptosystems, such as Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA). It has simulated the period finding process and the factorization of the integer N = 15 with base a = 7 by using Qiskit, a quantum computing framework. The quantum circuit correctly identified the period r = 4 from the modular exponentiation function 7x mod 15, leading to factors of 15 as 3 and 5. The simulation shows how quantum superposition, interference, and the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) were useful for speeding up the period-finding process, which is important for integer factorization. The histogram of measurement results revealed prominent peaks at 4, 8, and 12, which are multiples of the resultant period, unveiling the constructive interference produced by the QFT. However, a dominant peak at 0000 indicates hardware noise and error, pointing to the current limitations in quantum hardware. Fault-tolerant computers and error-correcting codes can overcome this limitation. As we move towards the age of quantum computers, the applicability of this algorithm poses a great threat to digital security. Applied code and visualizations provide a reproducible foundation for further study on cybersecurity and quantum computing.

title: Resilient Blockchain Architecture with Mobile Multi-Factor Authentication and PQC-Based Hybrid Cryptography (B-MMPH) in IoT Networks
authors: Suhair Alshehri
abstract: The day-by-day expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) network welcomes a massive number of smart devices to stay connected and communicate without disruption. The deployment of these resource-constrained heterogeneous devices creates a large-scale network that exchanges large amounts of data, making them vulnerable to attackers and quantum computing threats. Attackers in a network perform fraudulent tasks to enter the network and gather information. To safeguard large-scale IoT networks, we propose a Blockchain Architecture with Mobile Multi-Factor Authentication and PQC-Based Hybrid Cryptography (B-MMPH). The IoT network incorporates hybrid post-quantum cryptography within blockchain technology for authenticating and securely transferring data. The B-MMPH employs three main processes: network area partitioning, multi-factor authentication, and hybrid cryptography. Initially, Triangle–Square network partitioning is used to divide the network areas for efficient authentication by the mobile authenticator (MA). The MA moves from one partition to another and collects the device’s authentication request to perform multi-factor authentication. We consider the identity, biometric, Physically Unclonable Function (PUF), and certificate as factors for authentication; it uses a Transformer network to process the requests in parallel. The MA is trusted, and it has the ability to process multiple requests at the same time. Then, hybrid PQC is presented for secure data transmission which combines Kyber and Dilithium methods. Kyber is a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) which is used for exchanging a secret key between blockchain nodes and performs a digital signature on data with Dilithium. The proposed B-MMPH system is implemented, and its process is compared with previous research work. The parameters taken for comparison are as follows: authentication time, encryption time, decryption time, and communication overhead.

title: A Simulation-Based Framework for Interpretable Cancer Diagnosis Using Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Remote Internet of Medical Things
authors: Muhammad Ayub Sabir, Fatima Ashraf, Faisal Alhwikem, Naif Waheb Rajkhan, Tahani Alsubait, Muhammad Shahid Anwar
abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), integrated with advanced wireless communication networks, has transformed healthcare delivery, particularly through remote diagnosis and cancer monitoring. Nevertheless, the existing systems face several major challenges related to the creation of ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC), data reliability, and transparent decision-making processes. The proposed framework in this paper, named RS-MedIoT-XAI, is a novel model that synergistically combines Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS), Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), and post-quantum cryptography to address the following problems. The proposed system employs IRS-assisted beamforming to achieve a simulated reliability of 99.999% at an end-to-end latency of less than 1 ms, federated learning for privacy-preserving collaborative training for cancer detection, and transformer-based XAI models to enhance the interpretability of diagnostic decisions. The proposed three-tier edge computing architecture processes medical data locally at the network edge while maintaining quantum-resistant security through lattice-based cryptographic protocols. Simulation-based evaluation across four publicly available cancer imaging datasets demonstrates 97.0% mean diagnostic accuracy, 99.999% system reliability, and 0.83 ms end-to-end latency under idealized conditions (perfect channel state information and a controlled network environment). XAI-generated clinically meaningful explanations achieve 94.2% spatial concordance with expert radiologist annotations. The framework demonstrates resistance to classical and quantum attacks. Simulation results indicate scalability to support up to 500 concurrent patients under controlled network conditions. These simulation-based results establish RS-MedIoT-XAI as a computationally feasible framework that warrants further validation through prospective clinical studies before deployment in real-world telemedicine settings. Dataset-specific accuracies are 97.8% (MIAS mammography), 96.4% (NIH chest X-ray), 98.2% (BraTS brain tumor MRI), and 95.7% (BreakHis histopathology), with 97.0% representing the arithmetic mean across all four datasets under five-fold cross-validation.

title: QREC-MRT: A NOVEL MULTI-MATERIAL DIFFERENTIAL RESONANCE FRAMEWORK FOR ULTRALIGHT FIELD INTERACTIONS AND PRECISION QUANTUM METROLOGY
authors: Reji Kurien Thomas
journal: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences
abstract: Aims: To establish a multi-material differential resonance framework extending Quantum-Resonant Energy Coupling–Molecular Resonance Technology (QREC-MRT) into the investigation of ultralight scalar-field interactions and advanced precision metrology. Study Design: An original theoretical and methodological investigation integrating established physical models, analytical formulations, multi-sensor response architectures, quantitative evaluation of published precision-metrology benchmarks and comparative assessment of existing sensing methodologies. Methodology: The QREC-MRT Multi-Material Differential Resonance Framework integrates material-specific sensitivity coefficients, calibrated resonator transfer functions, Fourier-domain response matrices, noise-weighted singular-value analysis and linearly constrained minimum-variance estimation. State-dependent resonance interrogation, active-versus-sham comparisons, double-differential material-response analysis and Fisher-information criteria establish quantitative methods for evaluating coupling identifiability, calibration uncertainty and measurement sensitivity. Published optomechanical and optical-frequency measurements provide experimentally established reference benchmarks. Results: The principal contribution is a unified, model-constrained QREC-MRT interrogation architecture combining multi-material differential resonance analysis, nuisance-orthogonal signal reconstruction and calibration-preserving sensitivity assessment. The framework establishes matrix-rank and noise-weighted conditioning criteria for coupling identifiability, quantitative procedures for evaluating state-dependent measurement-information gains and a three-tier validation architecture distinguishing instrumental performance, material-dependent coupling signatures and independent spatial-coherence verification. Published experimental benchmarks establish reference parameters for assessing the physical measurement requirements of the framework. Conclusion: This research extends the methodological foundations of QREC-MRT into ultralight-field investigation and precision quantum metrology through a mathematically defined, reproducible and experimentally testable architecture. Its principal contribution lies in integrating coupling discrimination, calibration integrity, state-dependent resonance interrogation and independent verification into a unified framework supporting future high-sensitivity measurement applications.
