title: Multiparameter two-photon polarimetry approaching the quantum limit
authors: Joseph Niblo, Luca Maggio, Russell Brooks, Joseph Ho, Vincenzo Tamma, Alessandro Fedrizzi
abstract: Photonic quantum metrology has demonstrated advantages in precision and resource efficiency for a wide range of applications, with several schemes approaching the fundamental quantum Cramér-Rao precision bound (QCRB). However, the intrinsic incompatibility of quantum measurements represents a hurdle in extending these advantages to the simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters. In this paper, we present an experimental protocol approaching the QCRB simultaneously in two polarisation parameters, across a wide range of the parameter space, with as few as ~200 photon pairs, offering advantages for polarimetric sensing for dim sources such as in X-ray astronomy or photosensitive samples.

title: Magic without entanglement: Exact revivals and their Fisher information origin
authors: Rishabh Jha, Karun Gadge
abstract: Magic and entanglement are independent quantum resources, yet their exact relation in many-body dynamics has remained elusive. We uncover two structural principles. First, at any stabilizer state, the curvature of the second stabilizer R'enyi entropy under an arbitrary Hermitian generator equals the quantum Fisher information up to a fixed normalization, creating a bidirectional bridge between computational and metrological resources. Second, for commuting Ising evolution on any forest graph, a Clifford pruning circuit yields the full stabilizer-R'enyi family at arbitrary size and in any spatial embedding, thereby furnishing a graph-theoretic construction of families with finite magic density and vanishing entanglement density in the thermodynamic limit. We solve two paradigmatic one-dimensional realizations central to quantum simulation—an Ising quench and a kicked Floquet chain—exactly for arbitrary system size and directly in the thermodynamic limit, revealing finite magic density with vanishing entanglement density, distinct magic and entanglement revival periods, and Clifford points with zero magic but finite bipartite entanglement. The same tangent geometry fixes initial growth and perturbative revival lifting, and a replica cluster expansion establishes the stability of thermodynamic magic minima uniformly in system size. Large scale Pauli-basis matrix-product-state calculations verify all predictions, and the tangent bridge yields a concrete protocol for detecting magic near stabilizer reference states through established quantum-Fisher-information measurements.

title: Topological invariant of periodic many-body wave function from charge-pumping simulation
authors: Haoxiang Chen, Yubing Qian, Weiluo Ren, Xiang LiuXing Li, Ji Chen
abstract: Many-body topological quantum states host exotic quantum phenomena and lie at the forefront of developing next-generation quantum technologies. Recently emerged neural network wavefunction methods have established themselves as a powerful computational framework for accessing these states, enabling the variational machine learning calculation of the system’s ground state wavefunction. However, reliable computation of topological invariants remains an open challenge when the whole deterministic energy spectrum is not available. In this work, we introduce a robust approach to determining topological invariant based on simulating the charge pumping process, by monitoring the response of polarization upon flux insertion. By applying this method, we accurately extract the Chern numbers for Abelian fractional Chern insulators. Our approach also enables the first neural-network-wavefunction-based identification of anomalous composite Fermi liquid states. Our work resolves a key bottleneck in applying neural network wavefunctions to correlated topological matter, and the method proposed is also generally applicable to other many-body approaches, thereby opening up new avenues for future research in this field.

title: Symmetries, correlation functions, and entanglement of general quantum Motzkin spin-chains
authors: Varun Menon, Andi Gu, Ramis Movassagh
abstract: Motzkin spin-chains, which include `colorless' (integer spin s = 1) and `colorful' (s ≥ 2) variants, are one-dimensional (1D) local integer spin models notable for their lack of a conformal field theory (CFT) description of their low-energy physics, despite being gapless. The colorful variants are particularly unusual, as they exhibit power-law violation of the area-law of entanglement entropy (as n in system size n), rather than a logarithmic violation as seen in a CFT. In this work, we analytically discover several unique properties of these models, potentially suggesting a new universality class for their low-energy physics. We identify a complex structure of symmetries and unexpected scaling behavior in spin-spin correlations, which deviate from known 1D universality classes. Specifically, the s = 1 chain exhibits U (1) spontaneous symmetry breaking and ferromagnetic order. Meanwhile, the s ≥ 2 chains do not appear to spontaneously break any symmetries, but display quasi-long-range algebraic order with power-law decaying correlations, inconsistent with standard Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) critical exponents. We also derive asymptotic scaling expressions, with explicit additive constants, for entanglement measures in both colorless and colorful chains, generalizing previous results of Movassagh \cite{movassagh2017entanglement}, while providing benchmarks for potential quantum simulation experiments. The n entanglement scaling implies that any matrix-product-state description of these ground states requires bond dimension e Ω (n); this superpolynomial cost of the standard 1D tensor-network toolkit, along with the analytical tractability of their ground state properties, positions Motzkin spin chains as intriguing testbeds for quantum simulation of many-body physics.

title: Visualization for Quantum Computing: Current State and Future Directions
authors: Feng Liang, Xiaolin Wen, Shixian Zhou, Shaolun Ruan, Yuxuan Du, Qiang Guan, Jun Ye, Yong Wang
journal: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
abstract: Visualization has played an essential role in understanding quantum computing (QC), from the Bloch Sphere to interactive visual analytics systems. Yet existing surveys either treat visualization as part of broader interface, education, or computer-graphics discussions, or focus on quantum rendering and data-processing pipelines; none provides a comprehensive visualization-centered taxonomy for this emerging area of visualization for quantum computing (VIS4QC). We address this gap by combining a venue search from 2015 to 2025 with agentic search and snowballing, curating 69 core publications and tools, and developing a three-dimensional taxonomy informed by QC expert co-authors. The taxonomy characterizes VIS4QC by why visualizations are created (Learning & Interpretation vs. Productivity & Utility), what QC subjects they address (Qubits &States, Gates & Circuits, Machines & Systems, and Algorithm Development), and how they visualize QC data through visual representation types and data-specific strategies. The corpus remains small but has grown rapidly since 2023, suggesting that VIS4QC is still emerging. Our support-coverage analysis shows a disconnect between academia and industry: academic work mainly supports learning about quantum states, while industry tools mainly support productivity around circuit diagrams. Visualization research provides limited tooling for practitioners, while industry tools incorporate few of the richer visual representations developed in academia. Algorithm Development and Machines & Systems receive the least coverage, and productivity tools for Algorithm Development are especially sparse despite the importance of algorithm development for practical QC applications. These gaps surface in quantum education and quantum software engineering, where users need connected support across concepts, artifacts, workflows, and outcomes. Building on this analysis, we identify future directions across quantum computing (QC) subject categories: scalable visualization of quantum states, visual support for dynamic and transpiled circuits, visual analytics for quantum hardware statistics, and mechanism-based visualization of quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum-enhanced Markov Chain Monte Carlo for Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Kate V. Marshall, Daniel J. Egger, Michael Garn, Francesca Schiavello, Sebastian Brandhofer, Christa Zoufal, Stefan Woerner
abstract: Quantum computing offers an alternative paradigm for addressing combinatorial optimization problems compared to classical methods. However, despite recent hardware improvements, the execution of empirical quantum optimization experiments at scales known to be hard for state-of-the-art classical solvers is not yet in reach. In this work, we offer a different way to approach combinatorial optimization with near-term quantum computing. Motivated by the promising results observed in using quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) for approximating complicated probability distributions, we combine ideas of sampling from the device with QeMCMC together with warm-starting and parallel tempering, in the context of combinatorial optimization. We demonstrate empirically that our algorithm recovers the global optima for instances of the Maximum Independent Set problem (MIS) up to 117 decision variables using 117 qubits on IBM quantum hardware. We observe an indication of more favorable scaling relative to the tested classical MCMC methods on the chosen MIS instances. MIS is practically relevant across domains such as financial services and molecular biology. Although some MIS instances with a few hundred variables can be difficult for classical solvers, the instances studied here are solved efficiently by CPLEX.

title: Practical insights into controlling exponential concentration in quantum machine learning
authors: Fernando Mondragon-Sampedro, Diego Alvarez-Estevez
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models are often limited by exponential concentration, where quantum observables become insensitive to input variations as system size increases. In this work, we provide a comparative empirical study of this phenomenon across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), within a unified observable-based framework based on expectation-value variance. We investigate how measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity shape concentration across different architectures. Global fidelity-based kernels exhibit strong concentration driven by Hilbert space dimensionality, whereas local-observable approaches reduce but do not eliminate this effect. In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.

title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
authors: Kasidit Srimahajariyapong, Thiparat Chotibut, Suwannachad Suwannajitt, Tithivich Paka, Ricard Puig, Yudai Suzuki, Marek Gluza, Zoë Holmes
abstract: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

title: Incompressible quantum information
authors: Lasse H. Wolff, Matthias Christandl, Bergfinnur Durhuus, Christoph Hirche, Andreas Winter
abstract: For a small classical system correlated with a large one, it is always possible to compress the large system down to a size only dependent on the size of the smaller one, while preserving all correlations up to a given controllable error. Here, we show that such a statement does not hold at all when the large system is quantum mechanical. More precisely, we show that there are bipartite states such that any compression of the large system, by a non-trivial relative factor, will necessarily lead to the destruction of a significant amount of correlation, measured in mutual information. Our results therefore identify a limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning, showing that a small system specifying the relevant features contained in a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact encoding of the latter that preserves the relevant correlations.

title: Foliated surface codes for optimal skip-gate leakage correction
authors: Runjiang Bi, Nikita Astrakhantsev, Thomas B. Smith, Margaret Pavlovich, Ming Li, Shruti Puri
abstract: Skip-gate leakage --- such as atom loss in neutral-atom arrays or trapped ions, or photon loss in superconducting dual-rail qubits --- takes a qubit out of its computational subspace and removes subsequent gates acting on it. If leakage is only detectable end-of-the-line at qubit measurement, error correction circuits must be designed to periodically measure all qubits, as in SWAP-based circuits and foliation. We show that the best SWAP-based surface code, although optimal against space-like skip-gate leakage errors, is suboptimal against time-like leakage errors. By optimal, we mean that the code corrects as many leakage errors as it can detect. Remarkably, we find that the foliated surface code is optimal against both space- and time-like error configurations. We support our findings with numerical simulations. Under two-qubit gate leakage with probability 0.5%, foliation suppresses time-like errors in a distance-4 rotated stability experiment by 1380(50) per two added rounds, compared to 63(1) for the best SWAP-based circuit. In memory, the two are comparable. Under an experimentally motivated neutral-atom noise model, we find that foliation outperforms SWAP-based circuits in stability for both rotated and unrotated code geometries. This holds true for a parameter sweep that takes the neutral-atom noise model from being dominated by computational errors to atom loss. Interestingly, a SWAP-based circuit for unrotated code memory performs best when computational noise dominates over loss. Our work motivates co-designing error correction circuits with logical operations: preferring foliation when time-like errors dominate and SWAP-based circuits when space-like errors dominate.

title: Froq: Safe Speculative Execution on Live Quantum States for FTQC
authors: Yicheng Guang, Yueqi Chen
abstract: Reducing execution time is critical to fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) as longer executions expose logical qubits to more opportunities for failure. However, quantum processors could frequently stall due to slow classical error-correction decoders. Recent speculative decoding accelerates this process, but its speculation remains on the classical side, leaving quantum operations waiting for confirmed decoding results. Extending speculative execution to the quantum side is fundamentally challenging. Unlike classical processor states, quantum states cannot be arbitrarily copied or checkpointed for rollback, making recovery from mispredictions difficult. In this work, we propose Froq to enable safe speculative execution on live quantum states. Froq uses compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track how mispredictions propagate through quantum operations. It further employs a resource-aware runtime mechanism to reserve recovery workspace and dynamically balance the benefits of speculative execution against the expected costs of recovery. We evaluate Froq on eight FTQC programs across 88 configurations, building on an existing speculative window decoder. Froq reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% across all 88 configurations. The reduction reaches 18.34% across the 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and peaks at 31.1% at code distance d=21, under limited resources.

title: Engineering Discrete Local Dynamics in Globally Driven Dual-Species Atom Arrays
Site-specific electric-field tuning of two-level system defects in superconducting qubit arrays
authors: Larry Chen, Kan-Heng Lee, C. H. Liu, Brian Marinelli, Ravi Naik, Ziqi Kang, Noah Goss, Sanchayeta R. Mudi
abstract: State-of-the-art superconducting quantum processors containing tens to hundreds of qubits have demonstrated the building blocks for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation. Nonetheless, a fundamental barrier to scaling further is the prevalence of fluctuating quantum two-level system (TLS) defects that can couple resonantly to qubits, causing excess decoherence and enhanced gate errors. Here we introduce a scalable architecture for local and in-situ electric-field tuning of TLS frequencies out of the spectral vicinity of our qubits. Our method combines TLS frequency tuning and universal single qubit control into a single on-chip control line per qubit. We demonstrate that we can independently control each qubit’s dissipative environment to map its individual TLS landscape and accordingly dynamically improve both qubit coherence times and single qubit gate fidelities with a constant time overhead that does not scale with the device size. Over a period of 40 hours across 6 qubits, we demonstrate a 36% improvement in average single qubit error rates and a 17% improvement in average energy relaxation times. Critically, we realize an 8-fold suppression in the occurrence of TLS-induced performance outliers, and a complete reduction of simultaneous outlier events. These results demonstrate a resource-efficient method to control TLS-qubit interactions, which can lead to an important route toward overcoming the challenges that TLS defects pose to scaling superconducting quantum processors.

title: Blockchain–Quantum Computing Integration for Smart City Pollution Management: A Comprehensive Framework for Multi-Pollutant Mitigation, Traceability, and Environmental Sustainability
authors: Dina A.M. Darwish
abstract: Rapid urbanization and industrial expansion have exacerbated multi-domain environmental degradation, encompassing greenhouse gas emissions, air particulate pollution, aquatic contamination, solid waste accumulation, and soil toxicity. Traditional environmental management systems suffer from centralized data vulnerabilities, severe computational bottlenecks in processing high-dimensional telemetry, and lack of immutable regulatory traceability. This manuscript presents a conceptual architecture and comprehensive narrative literature review exploring the theoretical integration of blockchain technology and quantum computing for smart city pollution management. Specifically, this study examines how decentralized cryptographic ledgers, quantum machine learning (QML), and quantum optimization algorithms can be coupled with 6G wireless communication infrastructures to automate real-time multi-pollutant mitigation. Furthermore, this work explicitly broadens the analysis of blockchain's established environmental applications—including pollution-data traceability, emissions monitoring, electronic waste tracking, supply-chain transparency, and regulatory compliance—while critically assessing how blockchain capabilities directly complement quantum computing in overcoming urban pollution challenges. The investigation is structured as a systematic narrative synthesis examining literature across databases including IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink. The primary findings indicate that while quantum algorithms offer theoretical quadratic-to-exponential speedups for specific combinatorial optimization and molecular simulation problems under ideal fault-tolerant assumptions, current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware constraints necessitate hybrid classical-quantum workflows. Moreover, blockchain smart contracts combined with quantum-resistant lattice-based cryptography can secure environmental telemetry against emerging quantum decryption threats while providing immutable audit trails.

title: Reducibility of native weighted graphs on Rydberg arrays
authors: Johannes Kombe, J. D. Pritchard
abstract: We investigate the classical reducibility of random unit-disk graph (UDG) instances of the maximum independent set and maximum weighted independent set problems, which can be natively realized in Rydberg atom quantum processors. Using state-of-the-art kernelization techniques, we systematically probe how far classical preprocessing can simplify such native optimization problems of varying size and connectivity. While many small or sparse instances can be fully reduced, dense graphs often retain finite irreducible kernels even after extensive reductions. Introducing vertex weights tends to increase reducibility, whereas extending the interaction range in the underlying UDG connectivity suppresses the reduction efficiency. By exploring where classical reductions cease to be effective, we aim to delineate the regime of problem instances that remain computationally demanding—those most relevant for testing and benchmarking near-term quantum optimization hardware. We find that for the remaining finite kernels, quantum execution would require non-native embeddings with substantial resource overheads, suggesting that directly running native instances may be more practical than embedding a reduced kernel.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration for Agentic Identity Systems: A Practitioner Architecture for Regulated Multi-Cloud Enterprises
authors: Parijat Sharma
journal: International Journal of Cyber Threat Intelligence and Secure Networking
abstract: AI agents and other non-human identities depend on public-key cryptography for authentication, token signing, certificates, key exchange, software provenance, and secure service-to-service communication. Future quantum computers could undermine the RSA and elliptic-curve mechanisms these depend on, while data with a long confidentiality life is already exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later collection. This paper proposes a crypto-agile migration architecture that takes the agent identity lifecycle, rather than the application or the network protocol, as the unit of migration. It inventories cryptographic dependencies and links each to agent ownership, privilege, data sensitivity, autonomy, recovery requirement, and revocation path; classifies and prioritizes them by confidentiality lifetime and exposure; establishes crypto-agile control points that externalize algorithm choice from application code; validates post-quantum capability against certificate, token, and message size limits before any cohort moves; runs hybrid or dual-trust operation through a bounded compatibility window; migrates by risk-ordered cohort with defined stop conditions; and retires classical-only trust only once rollback, audit, and recovery criteria are satisfied. The architecture is designed and has not been validated as a completed enterprise migration. Algorithm parameter sizes used in the analysis are taken from the published standards; migration percentages, downtime, and performance impact are not claimed and are identified as pilot outputs.

title: Intent-Driven and Post-Quantum-Oriented Blockchain Authentication for the Internet of Underwater Things
authors: Ch. Rupa, G Varshitha, D Divya, Mustufa Haider Abidi, Fahad Alasim, Thippa Reddy Gadekallu
abstract: Internet of Underwater Things (IoUT) deployments need secure communication over acoustic channels characterized by limited bandwidth, high propagation delay, packet loss and intermittent connectivity. This study presents a post-quantum-oriented blockchain authentication framework for hierarchical underwater networks, using a study-specific NTRU-743 configuration for confidentiality, SHA-256 for integrity, HMAC-SHA-256 for authentication tags and HKDF-SHA-256 for key derivation, so one hash primitive underlies every construction, and an Ethereum-compatible permissioned ledger with Proof-of-Authority validators at the buoy, satellite and base-station layers. Underwater nodes hold no ledger; they submit authenticated records through opportunistic synchronization with their parent gateways. BAN logic and Scyther verify authentication, freshness, nonce secrecy and session-key secrecy under stated assumptions, with the SPDL model and settings released so the results can be reproduced. All performance figures come from an executable simulator released with the paper, in which cryptographic costs are measured and the channel, mobility, availability and validator planes are simulated; energy is a stated model output. Per authentication the protocol carries 1.41 KB of control-field payload, expanding to 8.56 KB on the acoustic link through NTRU ciphertext expansion, plus 1.38 KB validator and 1.18 KB synchronization traffic, totaling 11.13 KB. Processing takes 7.33 ms (95% CI 7.30–7.37) and 4.03 mJ, while acoustic transmission of the same exchange costs 8.42 J: the dominant cost is airtime, not computation. Over 100–1,000 nodes the design scales linearly, cluster utilization holding at 9.13% and validator utilization rising only from 0.08% to 0.80%. Replay detection attains 98.7% recall at a 0.00% false-positive rate against 86.6% and 7.95% for a certificate baseline re-implemented under identical conditions. Comparisons with figures published by prior schemes are descriptive, since those systems were not re-executed.

title: Quantum secure gradient aggregation based on ADQC
authors: Wei‐Min Shi, Jia-Wei Yuan, Zi-Xuan Xu, Yu-Guang Yang, Yi‐Hua Zhou
journal: International Journal of Modern Physics C
abstract: Current approaches to secure gradient aggregation in quantum federated learning typically employ classical or quantum cryptographic techniques to encrypt local gradients prior to transmission to the server via classical or quantum channels. In this process, local gradient information must be transmitted as communication content to take part in aggregation, which increases the potential attack surface for privacy. To address this problem, this paper proposes a quantum secure gradient aggregation scheme based on Ancilla-Driven Quantum Computation (ADQC). The scheme eliminates the direct transmission of local gradient information via either classical or quantum channels. Clients remotely construct single-qubit rotation gates through ADQC, thereby encoding their local gradients into the quantum state held by the server and achieving secure aggregation of local gradients. The proposed scheme includes two protocols for secure gradient aggregation: A serial single-qubit protocol and a parallel multi-qubit protocol. Security analysis demonstrates that both protocols are resilient to external attacks and to attacks originating from servers and clients, thereby achieving privacy protection for local gradients.

title: Reducing quantum error mitigation bias using verifiable benchmark circuits
authors: Joseph Harris, Kevin Lively, Peter Schuhmacher
abstract: We present a simple, malleable and low-overhead approach for improving generic biased quantum error mitigation (QEM) methods, achieving up to 15% fidelity improvements over standard QEM on 100-qubit circuits with up to 2000 entangling gates. We do so by constructing verifiable benchmark circuits which mirror the application circuit’s native-gate structure and thus noise profile. These circuits can be used to benchmark and mitigate the bias of the underlying error mitigation method, requiring only the application circuit and hardware native gate set. We present several methods for generating benchmark circuits; one is application-agnostic and tailored to the IBM superconducting hardware whilst others are hardware-agnostic but application-tailored. As a corollary, we introduce benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation (bnZNE) as a simple adaptation of zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), one of the most popular error mitigation methods. We consider as an example the bias-mitigated ZNE and bnZNE of Trotterized Hamiltonian simulations, observing that our approaches outperform standard ZNE using both small-scale classical simulations and 100-qubit utility-scale experiments on the IBM superconducting hardware. We consider the measurement of both single-site observables as well as two-site correlations along a one-dimensional qubit chain. We also provide a software package for implementing the error mitigation techniques used in this research.

title: Fault-Tolerant Execution of Error-Corrected Quantum Algorithms
authors: Michael A. Perlin, Zichang He, Anthony Alexiades Armenakas, Pablo Andrés-Martínez, Tianyi Hao, Dylan Herman, Yuwei Jin, Karl Mayer
abstract: Scaling up quantum algorithms to tackle high-impact problems in science and industry requires quantum error correction and fault tolerance. While progress has been made in experimentally realizing error-corrected primitives, the end-to-end execution of logical quantum algorithms using only fault-tolerant (FT) components has remained out of reach. We demonstrate the FT and error-corrected execution of two quantum algorithms, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) and the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm applied to the Poisson equation, on Quantinuum H2 and Helios trapped-ion quantum processors using the ⟦ 7, 1, 3 ⟧ Steane code. For QAOA circuits on five and six logical qubits, we show performance improvements from increasing the number of QAOA layers and the number of T gates used to approximate logical rotations, despite increased physical circuit complexity. We further show that QAOA circuits with up to eight logical qubits and nine logical T gates perform similarly to unencoded circuits. For the largest QAOA circuits we run, with 12 logical (97 physical) qubits and 2132 physical two-qubit gates, we still observe better-than-random performance. Finally, we show that adding active quantum error correction cycles and increasing the repeat-until-success limit of state-preparation subroutines can improve the performance of a quantum algorithm, thereby demonstrating critical capabilities of scalable FT quantum computation. Our results are enabled by a FT logical T -gate implementation with an infidelity of 2.7 (4) × 10 − 3 and dynamic circuits with measurement-dependent feedback. Our work demonstrates near-breakeven performance of complex, error-corrected algorithmic quantum circuits using only FT components.

title: Compilation-informed probabilistic logical-error cancellation
authors: Giancarlo Camilo, Thiago O. Maciel, Allan Tosta, Abdulla Alhajri, Thais de Lima Silva, Daniel Stilck França, Leandro Aolita
abstract: The potential of quantum computers to outperform classical ones in practically useful tasks remains challenging in the near term due to scaling limitations and high error rates of current quantum hardware. While quantum error correction (QEC) offers a clear path towards fault tolerance, overcoming the scalability issues will take time. Early applications will likely rely on QEC combined with quantum error mitigation (QEM). We introduce a QEM scheme against both compilation errors and logical-gate noise that is circuit-, QEC code-, and compiler-agnostic. The scheme builds on quasi-probability methods and uses information about the circuit’s gates’ compilations to attain an unbiased estimation of noiseless expectation values incurring a constant sample-complexity overhead. Moreover, it features maximal circuit size and code distance both independent of the target precision, in contrast to strategies based on QEC alone. We formulate the mitigation procedure as a linear program, demonstrate its efficacy through numerical simulations, and illustrate it for estimating the Jones polynomials of knots. Our method significantly reduces quantum resource requirements for high-precision estimations, offering a practical route towards fault-tolerant quantum computation with precision-independent overheads for fixed circuit size and code distance.

title: Q-Slim: Entanglement-Guided Quantum Compression for Edge Small Language Models
authors: Karthiga I., Lakshmi Narayanan P, Mohamed Hamdhan S.
journal: International Journal of Latest Technology in Engineering Management & Applied Science
abstract: Deploying Small Language Models (SLMs) with 0.5 billion to 1.5 billion parameters directly on consumer edge hardware preserves data privacy and removes cloud network latency, yet practical execution remains constrained by static Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM) capacity and memory-bandwidth bottlenecks. The objective of this study is to compress pretrained SLMs below 4-bit average precision without suffering the severe multi-step reasoning degradation observed in uniform Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) or isolated block-diagonal Hessian approximations. To achieve this objective, we propose Q-Slim, a hybrid quantum-classical post-training compression framework combining tensor-network structural profiling with variational quantum combinatorial optimization. First, Q-Slim folds transformer Self-Attention and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) weight matrices into higher-order tensors and decomposes them into canonical Matrix Product State (MPS) tensor trains to compute bond-wise von Neumann entanglement entropy as a calibration-free indicator of layer information capacity. Second, we derive an unconstrained two-qubit binary-radix variable encoding per layer group that maps discrete bit-width ({2, 3, 4, 8}-bit) and bond-truncation choices onto an 8-to-10 qubit Ising spin Hamiltonian using an exact single-layer distortion polynomial and a two-body quadratic coupling and memory surrogate, followed by deterministic greedy feasibility repair. Solving overlapping block windows with the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and unitary-folding Richardson Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) on the Qiskit Aer noisy density-matrix simulator yields a 97.6% min-max normalized approximation ratio against exact exhaustive enumeration. Evaluated on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B under strictly matched 72.0% and 78.4% memory reductions, Q-Slim achieves 9.21 and 10.92 WikiText-2 perplexity on Qwen2.5-1.5B, outperforming uniform 4-bit and 3-bit GPTQ and AWQ while delivering 13.4 to 14.5 tokens per second on a Raspberry Pi 5. In conclusion, entanglement-guided quantum combinatorial allocation provides a practical, reproducible pathway for extreme edge SLM deployment via an interactive FastAPI and React studio.

title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Anastasiia Lukianenko, Yash J. Patel, Nurbolat Kenbayev, Vedran Dunjko
abstract: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing
authors: Ishaan Kannan, Aditi Venkatesh, Jordan Cotler
abstract: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms. First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks. These protocols attain the optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit platforms, improving existing devices by changing only their pulse sequences. We then introduce quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which couples quantum sensors to a quantum processor. QCS combines two new primitives: a quantum computational frequency comb that coherently converts any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and a family of quantum algorithms that use the oracle to extract signal information in superposition. Variations can be implemented on current platforms with only one memory ancilla. We show that the ultimate limit imposed by quantum mechanics lies polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit, and that QCS achieves it. Attaining this new limit requires quantum computation, establishing a fundamental separation between conventional and quantum computational sensing. Moreover, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals under constant-strength sensor depolarization, while we prove that the same noise limits any protocol lacking quantum computation to standard-quantum-limit scaling. Our result provides the first asymptotic, beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology when noise is aligned with the signal, proving that Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing. Our work builds an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and establishes quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with quantum advantages that surpass the Heisenberg limit and that persist under noise.

title: A New Quantum Algorithm Framework for Integer Order Entropy Estimation
authors: Zongxing Xiong
abstract: Entropy estimation for unknown distributions is a basic problem in statistical property estimation. In this paper, we propose a quantum algorithm framework for estimating Rényi entropy with fixed integer order $k\geq 2$. Given purified quantum query-access to a distribution on $n$ symbols, our algorithm estimates its order-$k$ Rényi entropy to within additive error $ε$ using $$\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{n^{u_k}}{ε^{1-u_k}} + \frac{n^{(k-1)/(2k)}}ε\right)$$ queries, where $u_k=\max_{2\leq j\leq k} \frac{(3k-j)2^{j-2}-k}{k(2^j-1)}$. The main ingredient is a recursive construction of collision states in which intermediate states are retained and reused. We bound both the preparation and reflection costs, and choose the number of retained states at each order so that all recursive steps fit within a common query budget. We combine this construction with a sequence of decreasing probability thresholds, estimating the contribution of the labels found along the way separately from the remaining power sum. A batch estimator gives the required bound in the high-precision regime, and an initial search removes the need for prior knowledge of the power sum.

title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction
authors: Zhilong Liu, Xiangzhen Zhou, Yunqi Huang, Xin Hong, Pengcheng Zhu, Fanxu Meng, Zhenlong Du
abstract: Variational quantum circuit synthesis jointly searches circuit structure and continuous parameters to reduce costly two-qubit gates, but block-based workflows typically instantiate blocks independently, limiting simplification across block boundaries. Moreover, fully unitary synthesis does not exploit opportunities created by permitted output measurements and classical feedforward. We present CAVQS, a context-aware variational synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution and dynamic reconstruction. First, CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks, preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local synthesis targets to enable cross-block reductions. Second, for blocks that precede permitted terminal measurements, CAVQS constructs ancilla-free dynamic implementations with a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search and analytic branch-unitary construction, thereby minimizing expected CNOT cost. Across random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% relative to QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN, respectively, on common successful instances. On 4--6-qubit quantum algorithm benchmarks, the corresponding reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.

title: Efficient Classical Algorithms for Ground Energy Estimation of Fermions with Conjugate-Pair Orbital Interactions
authors: Ziyi Yang, Yexin Zhang, Yuexin Su, Xinzhao Wang, Xiaoyang Wang, Tongyang Li
abstract: Estimating the ground energy of interacting fermions is central to quantum many-body physics, and recent quantum algorithms provide polynomial-time guarantees for some structured families. Classical approaches commonly rely on quantum Monte Carlo, where the sign problem is a major obstacle. However, even when a nonnegative expansion without sign problem is available, rigorous guarantees for rapid mixing are still far from well understood. In this paper, we give an efficient classical randomized algorithm for approximating the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions, which includes the attractive Hubbard models. This guarantee not only holds without a physical spectral gap or a weak-coupling assumption, but also covers interactions beyond onsite density attractions. Technically, we first reduce ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation and then use a discretization with controlled energy error to obtain a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli and then apply the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem. In addition, we obtain a sharper arithmetic bound by controlling how many independent sampling runs and matrix updates are needed, and using sparse matrices to reduce the cost of each update.

title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
authors: Mohsen Bagherimehrab, Daniyaal Farooqi, Gavin K. Brennen, Barry C. Sanders, Alán Aspuru-Guzik
abstract: Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.

title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
authors: David Halpenny, Adithya Sireesh, Petros Wallden
abstract: Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates for any $ε>0$, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using $O(n^{1+ε})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $ε>0$. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.

title: Counterfactual attribution of surface-code failures under non-Pauli noise: dependence on trajectory pairing
authors: Kisung Jin, Gyuil Cha
abstract: Under Pauli noise in a stabilizer memory, attributing a quantum error-correction failure to the noise that caused it has a canonical answer; under non-Pauli noise the attribution depends on how trajectories are paired with their counterfactuals. We define a failing shot's cause set, the sites whose removal alone removes the failure, and separate it from pairing-independent net effects. The pairing enters wherever a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making it maximal at every random step selects shared random numbers, while continuity does not. In a distance-three surface code, exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures need three or more sites, against 2.3% under the twirl. Other admissible pairings move the mean coherent cause count from 1.61 to 80 times the minimum the marginals allow, yet pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models. Shot-level attributions should therefore state their pairing and report pairing-independent effects alongside.

title: Syndrome-based Calibration Using Gate-Error Amplification
authors: Andrew T. Kamen, Arielle Sanford, Frederic T. Chong, Andy J. Goldschmidt, Siddharth Dangwal
abstract: We present Gate-Error Amplification for Recalibration with Syndromes (GEARS), a runtime calibration framework that uses gate-error amplification to efficiently tune control parameters during quantum error correction. Maintaining reliable control of large qubit arrays throughout hours-long computations requires repeated calibration to compensate for hardware drift. In conventional calibration, targeted qubits are temporarily removed from the code, introducing non-negligible space-time overhead. An elegant alternative uses syndrome information already collected during error correction as feedback for in situ recalibration, but acquiring signal requires sufficient (1) measurement budget or (2) probe strength, i.e., the size of deliberate control perturbations. More measurements improve statistical precision but result in slower control updates, while stronger perturbations produce larger calibration signals at the cost of additional errors. GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with an established gate characterization technique called gate-error amplification. Our approach repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while limiting the logical cost of probing. Surface code simulations show that GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by approximately a factor of eight at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration, GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces excess expected logical failures by approximately 31-40% relative to calibration without amplification across the evaluated execution windows. Under time-dependent drift, GEARS increases the estimated critical drift frequency by approximately 1.9x. These results indicate that deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation can improve the long-time performance of quantum computations.

title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing
authors: Katrin Bolsmann, Alan Kahan, Alejandro Bermúdez, Markus Müller
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity entangling gates that can be implemented efficiently across multiple qubit pairs. We present a scheme for simultaneous pairwise entangling operations, i.e., a transversal controlled-$Z$ gate, across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture. A tailored dynamical decoupling scheme suppresses unwanted couplings with a pulse count that scales quadratically with the number of ions. We show that incorporating a genuine geometric cancellation reduces the pulse count and, for selected register sizes, allows the parallel operation to be completed faster than an equivalent sequence of two-qubit gates while requiring a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. We assess the experimental feasibility of the protocol by analyzing the impact of decoherence and crosstalk arising from laser wave-vector misalignment. To gain insight into the robustness of fault-tolerant protocols against realistic imperfections of the proposed transversal gate scheme, we investigate how crosstalk-induced gate errors affect the fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two $[[4,1,2]]$ quantum-error-detection code blocks. These results highlight the potential of transversal entangling gates as a building block for trapped-ion-based scalable fault-tolerant quantum error correction.

title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
authors: Eduardo Dueñez, Edgar Said Hernandez Sanchez, Edgar A. Duéñez-Guzmán, Suzanne Sadedin
abstract: Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.

title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
authors: Stefano Tinelli, Francisco Lázaro, Francisco García Herrero
abstract: A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
authors: Zhiyao Hu, Haidong Yuan, Liang Jiang, Zain H. Saleem
abstract: Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.

title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding
authors: Cory T. Aitchison, Lucas H. English, Benjamin Béri, Dominic J. Williamson, Campbell K. McLauchlan
abstract: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.

title: Adaptive memory-augmented Artificial Protozoa Optimization with competitive operator control for complex numerical and constrained problems
Adaptive GPU execution planning for memory-limited Hamiltonian applications
authors: Uriel Shafir, Ronnie Kosloff
abstract: Many quantum-simulation workflows, including propagation, filtering, Krylov, stochastic sampling, and observable measurement, are dominated by applications of Hamiltonians or other large operators, either to one state vector, ϕ=Ĥψ, or to several right-hand sides, Y=ĤX. These applications may be repeated many times, as in propagation and filtering, or may occur as one-shot observable, measurement, projection, or post-processing operations. The numerical algorithms used for these tasks are well established. The contribution of this work is an execution layer for these existing algorithms and operator evaluations when dense or effectively dense operator data exceed the memory of a single accelerator. The implementation first inspects the allocated hardware, including the number of GPUs (graphics processing units), available accelerator memory, and supported execution modes. It then enumerates candidate ways to apply the same mathematical operator: direct analytic action, seed-based generation, fused implicit kernels, on-demand block generation, parallel block execution, partial caching, full GPU caching, row-distributed caching across several GPUs, task parallelism, and hybrid row/task parallel execution. These candidates are ranked analytically using memory estimates, arithmetic-work estimates, cache requirements, and GPU-grouping constraints. The best analytically ranked candidates are then tested by a measured autotuner on the allocated hardware. Candidate comparisons use the same operator and input vectors and distinguish steady application time from calibration, compilation, cache construction, and tuning overhead. Plan selection minimizes expected total time for the declared number of operator uses. Validation against a fixed full-cache policy, direct GPU dense linear algebra, and a broader measured candidate search is used to quantify the benefit and overhead of adaptive planning. Logged trials may support learned ranking in future work, but no neural surrogate is used in the reported results.

title: Quantum-classical separation in bounded-resource tasks arising from measurement contextuality
authors: Shashwat Kumar, E. Rosenberg, A. Grajales Dau, Rodrigo G. Cortiñas, D. Maslov, R. Oliver, Adam Zalcman, M. Neeley
abstract: Quantum phenomena can be exploited to tackle certain problems beyond the reach of classical approaches. In this study, we focus on coordinated decision-making among many players without communication, the study of which, on current quantum processors, has remained elusive. Using a superconducting qubit processor, we show that quantum contextuality enables certain tasks to be performed with success probabilities beyond classical limits. With a few qubits, we illustrate quantum contextuality with the magic square game and quantify it through a Bell-Kochen-Specker inequality violation. To examine many-body contextuality, we implement the N-player Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger game and separately solve a two-dimensional hidden linear function problem, advancing the state of the art on fidelity and system size in both tasks. Our work introduces benchmarking of quantum processors using contextuality-based algorithms.

title: Performance comparison of QAOA mixers for ternary portfolio optimization
authors: Shintaro Yamamura, Satoshi Watanabe, Masaya Kunimi, Kazuhiro Saito, Tetsuro Nikuni
abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a quantum algorithm proposed for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices and is regarded as a promising approach to combinatorial optimization problems, with potential applications in the financial sector. In this study, we apply QAOA to the portfolio optimization problem, which is one of the central challenges in financial engineering. A portfolio consists of a combination of multiple assets, and the portfolio optimization problem aims to determine the optimal asset allocation by balancing expected return and risk. In the context of quantum optimization, portfolio optimization is often formulated using discrete variables. Unlike conventional binary formulations, we consider a ternary portfolio optimization problem that accounts for three states—holding, not holding, and short selling—and compare the performance of QAOA with different mixer operators and QWOA. For the XY-based mixers, we construct a uniform superposition over all constraint-satisfying ternary encodings to avoid the bias caused by simplified feasible initial states. Specifically, we implement QAOA with Standard Mixer, several XY Mixers (XY Ring, XY Parity Ring, XY Full, and QAMPA), and QWOA, and conduct simulations using real data based on the German stock index (DAX 30) for portfolios consisting of 5 and 8 assets. Furthermore, we introduce noise based on a depolarizing channel to investigate the behavior of QAOA with the Standard and XY-based mixers in realistic environments. The results show that, in the noiseless simulations considered here, highly connected XY-based mixers such as the XY Full Mixer and QAMPA generally achieve better performance than the Standard Mixer. However, their advantage is reduced in noisy environments, and the preferable mixer depends on both the QAOA depth and the noise strength.

title: A Secure Quantum-Resistant Mutual Authentication Protocol for RFID Systems
authors: Pierre E. Abi-Char, Youssef Sellami, Mohammed Al‐Husseini
abstract: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) systems play a key role in the Internet of Things (IoT), but their limited computational and storage capabilities make the design of secure authentication protocols particularly challenging. Moreover, most existing RFID authentication schemes rely on classical cryptographic assumptions that are vulnerable to quantum computing attacks or introduce excessive overhead for resource-constrained tags. In this paper, we propose a lightweight post-quantum RFID mutual authentication protocol based on the hardness of the Inhomogeneous Short Integer Solution (ISIS) problem. The proposed protocol replaces permutation operations with a random masking vector mechanism, reducing computational complexity while preserving security. Furthermore, a seed-based matrix generation technique is adopted to minimize storage and communication overhead by reconstructing the public matrix on demand. The protocol provides mutual authentication between the tag, reader, and server, while resisting common attacks, including replay, impersonation, man-in-the-middle, traceability, and desynchronization attacks. Security analysis demonstrates the robustness of the proposed scheme, and performance evaluation shows that it achieves lower computational, communication, and storage overhead than existing post-quantum RFID authentication protocols, making it suitable for practical RFID deployments.

title: Efficient time-dependent dynamics of matrix product states using average Hamiltonians
authors: Belal Abouraya, Jirawat Saiphet, Fedor Jelezko, Ressa S. Said
abstract: Simulating quantum many-body systems (QMBS) is one of the long-standing, highly nontrivial challenges in condensed matter physics and quantum information due to the exponentially growing size of the system's Hilbert space. To date, tensor networks have been an essential tool for studying such quantum systems, owing to their ability to efficiently capture the entanglement properties of the systems they represent. One of the well-known tensor network architectures, namely, matrix product states (MPS), is the standard method for simulating one-dimensional QMBS. Here, we propose a simple, yet efficient, method to augment the already available MPS algorithms to simulate the dynamics of time-dependent Hamiltonians with better accuracy and a faster convergence rate, giving a second-order convergence compared to the first-order convergence of the Riemann method available in standard software packages. We apply our proposed method to simulate the dynamics of a chain of single spins associated with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color centers in diamond, which has potential applications for practical and scalable quantum technologies, and find that our method improves the average error for a system of a few NV centers by a factor of about 1000 for moderate step sizes. Additionally, we compare our method to the midpoint rule, which has second-order convergence as well, and show some of the trade-offs between the two methods. Our work paves the way for efficient simulation of QMBS under the influence of time-dependent Hamiltonians.

title: Low-resource quantum energy gap estimation via randomization
authors: Hugo Pages, Chusei Kiumi, Yuto Morohoshi, Bálint Koczor, Kosuke Mitarai
abstract: Estimating the energy spectra of quantum many-body systems is a fundamental task in quantum physics, with applications ranging from chemistry to condensed matter. Algorithmic shadow spectroscopy is a recent method that leverages randomized measurements on time-evolved quantum states to extract spectral information. However, implementing accurate time evolution with low-depth circuits remains a key challenge for near-term quantum hardware. In this work, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical protocol that integrates time evolution via probabilistic angle interpolation (TE-PAI) into the shadow spectroscopy framework. TE-PAI enables the simulation of time evolution using shallow stochastic circuits while preserving unbiased estimates through quasiprobability sampling. We construct the combined estimator and derive its theoretical properties. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that our method accurately resolves energy gaps and exhibits enhanced robustness to gate noise compared to first-order Trotter-based shadow spectroscopy. We further validate the protocol experimentally on up to 20 qubits using IBM quantum hardware. This makes TE-PAI shadow spectroscopy a promising tool for spectral analysis on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

title: Antisymmetrization of composite fermionic states for quantum simulations of nuclear reactions in first-quantization mapping
authors: Ionel Stetcu
abstract: I present a first-quantization deterministic algorithm for antisymmetrizing a spatially separated target–projectile system containing N T and N p identical fermions, respectively. The method constructs a fully antisymmetric wavefunction from the product of two independently antisymmetrized many-body states, each of which may be a superposition of Slater determinants. The algorithm uses a Dicke-state ancilla register that coherently encodes all one-particle exchange channels between the two subsystems and, crucially, requires only swaps to generate the full antisymmetric structure. After consolidating distinct control conditions using logical operations, the optimized circuit uses (N_TN_p) single-particle exchanges, up to (N_p) of which can be performed in parallel. The correct fermionic phase is incorporated through the application of Z gates on N T ancillae, after which the ancilla register is efficiently uncomputed using a compact sequence of controlled operations. This construction provides a nontrivial and scalable protocol for preparing fully antisymmetric states in reaction and scattering simulations, significantly expanding the range of systems that can be addressed with first-quantized quantum algorithms.

title: Universal quantum gate set for multimode Schrödinger cat states stabilized by nonlocal dissipation engineering
authors: Jesper Lind-Olsen, Jonas Lidal, Tron Omland, Joakim Bergli
abstract: Schr\"odinger cat states provide a hardware-efficient platform for bosonic quantum error correction by encoding logical information in protected manifolds of harmonic oscillators. While previous work has demonstrated the dissipative stabilization of multimode Schr\"odinger cat states as robust quantum memories, a framework for universal quantum computation has remained unavailable. Here we work toward this by introducing a universal gate set for dissipatively stabilized multimode cat qubits as a necessary resource for computation. Using a chain of Kerr nonlinear oscillators coupled through engineered nonlocal dissipation and an effective low-dimensional description, we show how single-qubit control can be achieved through arbitrary rotation around the $X$ axis and $\ensuremath{\pi}/2$-rotation around the $Z$ axis. We further show how coupling two such stabilized arrays through just one oscillator on each respective array enables coherent entangling operations through implementation of the $X{X}_{\ensuremath{\pi}/2}$ gate. Numerical simulations demonstrate high-fidelity gate dynamics and entanglement generation under realistic parameters. Finally, we analyze the effects of induced and intrinsic photon loss, disorder, and the validity regime of the effective low-dimensional theory. Our results establish dissipatively stabilized multimode Schr\"odinger cat states as a potential architecture for universal bosonic quantum computation.

title: Patent Application: HYBRID CLASSICAL-QUANTUM PROCESS FOR THE IN SILICO RECOMBINATION OF PLANT GENOMES WITH EVALUATION BY MEANS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
authors: Paolo Ciccolella
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Plant genomics with a hybrid classical-quantum model Artificial intelligence and quantum computing for the digital design of plant genomes Italian patent application no. 102026000034324, filed on 18 November 2026. Inventor, applicant and sole rights holder: Paolo Ciccolella. This invention proposes combining artificial intelligence and quantum computing to explore possible combinations of plant DNA and identify those worth investigating further. For businesses interested in plant genomics, the idea is to provide early guidance for computational design: turning a vast number of possibilities into selected, evaluated and documented digital candidates. The challenge is easy to picture. If DNA is a large instruction book, studying alternative versions of some passages means comparing many combinations. Three alternatives for each of twenty regions already produce more than three billion possibilities. The method tackles this complexity by dividing the work between a classical computer, two AI models and a quantum search component. HOW THE HYBRID MODEL WORKS The idea is to choose one alternative for each DNA region being studied, put the choices together and evaluate the resulting combination. Everything happens on a computer. The process follows six steps. • Prepare the data. The computer starts with a digital version of the plant’s DNA, called a reference genome. It identifies the regions to study and organises the available alternative sequences for each one, recording where they come from. • Give each alternative an initial score. The first AI model examines each alternative separately. Having learned from other cases, it can provide guidance before any complete combination in the new case has been evaluated. The computer also measures similarity between the ends of sequences that will be placed next to one another. These scores and measurements define the selection problem. [B12] • Search for combinations. The quantum component receives this problem expressed in numbers. It uses QAOA, an algorithm whose role is to propose combinations while seeking to favour those with better scores. Qubits represent the possible choices; the DNA sequences remain on the classical computer, which sets and updates the algorithm’s parameters. [B11] • Evaluate the whole combination. The computer checks that each combination selects exactly one alternative per region and assembles valid choices into a digital candidate. The second AI model evaluates the complete candidate, including relationships between its parts that the first AI model could not observe when examining them separately. • Guide the next search. The system compares the overall evaluation with the score predicted at the start and uses the difference to update the search. When only a few results are available, it limits the correction’s influence to avoid relying too heavily on sparse information. • Return verifiable proposals. For each selected candidate, the system retains the chosen sequences, their provenance and the evaluations performed. It also records a digital fingerprint, a code used to check the content. Researchers can reconstruct the proposal and understand how it was selected. If necessary data are missing, the system flags this. A concrete example: the patent uses the digital reference for Micro-Tom tomato and considers three regions, each with three alternatives created for the test. There are 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 possible combinations. The search uses a nine-qubit quantum circuit simulated on a classical computer. This tests the computational method without producing plants. [B14] INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS The patent describes the production of verifiable digital representations of candidate genomes. Its industrial role lies in designing and selecting hypotheses, ahead of experimental work. Applications across sectors require data and models suited to the objectives under study. • NGT and assisted evolution techniques. NGTs, or new genomic techniques, include approaches known in Italy as TEA, meaning assisted evolution techniques, which enable targeted changes to genetic material. The proposed method could support research by comparing genomic hypotheses before experimental work. For seed and biotechnology companies, the prospect is to build a reasoned set of digital candidates for further investigation within NGT/TEA programmes. • Seed industry and variety development. For seed companies and research teams, the method could support the preliminary selection of combinations for further study. Research objectives could include drought or salinity tolerance, disease resistance and yield stability. Its contribution would be to establish research priorities while preserving the reasoning behind them. • Fresh produce and food processing. Computational design could focus on commercial characteristics such as product quality, shelf life and processing suitability. Tomato, pepper and aubergine are examples of supply chains that future projects could address, connecting growers’ and processors’ needs with the criteria used to evaluate candidates. • Nutraceuticals and plant ingredients. One possible development concerns plants of interest for functional ingredients, extracts and bioactive compounds. The method could explore genomic combinations in programmes focused, for example, on pigments or plant metabolites, providing documented candidates to guide subsequent analysis. • Plant biotechnology and industrial raw materials. For crops intended for oils, fibres or biomass, the method could help compare genomic hypotheses against supply chain objectives. Reconstructible digital records would support information exchange between teams developing the models and those planning subsequent experimental work. • Bioinformatics and computing centres. The most direct application is within the information systems of laboratories, computing centres and plant genomics businesses. The process could underpin software modules or analytical services that explore combinations and return candidates with scores and execution logs, integrating quantum search into the workflow.
