Full-stack analog Gaussian optical quantum computing platform with one hundred inputs
authors: Shota Yokoyama, Atsushi Sakaguchi, Warit Asavanant, Kan Takase, Yi-Ru Chen, Hironari Nagayoshi, Jun-ichi Yoshikawa, Takahiro Kashiwazaki
abstract: Optical technology is a highly promising platform for quantum computing due to its enormous potential for large-scale, ultrafast computation. However, realizing a programmable and scalable system remains a significant challenge. Here, we present a high-speed programmable Gaussian quantum computing platform with one hundred inputs based on a continuous-variable full-stack architecture. Our system features a 100 MHz clock frequency and integrates a cloud-based interface with an open-source Python software development kit, mqc3, significantly enhancing accessibility and operational flexibility. We provide a comprehensive characterization of our system and its capabilities through multi-input and multi-step teleportation, as well as the programmable routing of quantum states across 101 input modes. This platform represents a critical milestone in scalable analog quantum information processing, offering a robust testbed for the future integration of non-Gaussian resources.

title: Tunable spectral correlations of highly multimode visible light via broadband quantum frequency conversion
authors: Federico Presutti, Logan G. Wright, Shi-Yuan Ma, Tianyu Wang, Benjamin K. Malia, Tatsuhiro Onodera, Peter L. McMahon
abstract: Multimode squeezed states of light are a resource for achieving quantum advantage in computing and sensing, where spatial or temporal modes have been the experimental norm. In our experiments, we generated highly frequency-multimode infrared quantum light and showed how adiabatic frequency conversion can be used to convert the quantum state to visible wavelengths while concurrently manipulating the joint spectrum by realizing a configurable many-port frequency-domain beamsplitter unitary transformation. We report near-unity efficiency quantum frequency conversion over a bandwidth >45 terahertz, which allowed us to measure the state with an electron-multiplying CCD (EMCCD) camera-based spectrometer, at noncryogenic temperatures. The parametric amplification and conversion of >400 frequency modes yielded an overall mean of ∼700 visible photons per shot and photon statistics consistent with squeezing. Our work shows how many-mode quantum states of light can be generated, manipulated, and measured with efficient use of hardware resources, motivating the use of frequency encoding in quantum optics.

title: C2 |Q⟩: A Robust Framework for Bridging Classical and Quantum Software Development
authors: Boshuai Ye, Arif Ali Khan, Teemu Pihkakoski, Peng Liang, Muhammad Azeem Akbar, Matti Silveri, Lauri Malmi
journal: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
abstract: Quantum Software Engineering (QSE) is emerging as a critical discipline to make quantum computing accessible to a broader developer community; however, most quantum development environments still require developers to engage with low-level details across the software stack—including problem encoding, circuit construction, algorithm configuration, hardware selection and result interpretation—making them difficult for classical software engineers to use. To bridge this gap, we present C2 \(|{\rm{Q}}\rangle\), a hardware-agnostic quantum software development framework that translates specific types of classical specifications into quantum-executable programs while preserving methodological rigour. The framework applies modular software engineering principles by classifying the workflow into three core modules: an encoder that classifies problems, produces Quantum-Compatible Formats (QCFs) and constructs quantum circuits, a deployment module that generates circuits and recommends hardware based on fidelity, runtime and cost and a decoder that interprets quantum outputs into classical solutions. This architecture supports systematic evaluation across simulators and Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) quantum devices, remaining scalable to new problem classes and algorithms. In evaluation, the encoder module achieved a 93.8% completion rate, the hardware recommendation module consistently selected the appropriate quantum devices for workloads scaling up to 56 qubits. End-to-end experiments on 434 Python programs and 100 JSON problem instances demonstrate that the full C2 \(|{\rm{Q}}\rangle\) workflow executes reliably on simulators and can be deployed successfully on representative real quantum hardware, with empirical runs limited to small- and medium-sized instances consistent with current NISQ capabilities. A proxy-based usability analysis further indicates substantial reductions in handwritten lines of code and explicit configuration steps compared to conventional quantum SDK workflows. These results indicate that C2 \(|{\rm{Q}}\rangle\) lowers the entry barrier to quantum software development by providing a reproducible, extensible toolchain that connects classical specifications to quantum execution. The open source implementation of C2 \(|{\rm{Q}}\rangle\) is available at https://github.com/C2-Q/C2Q and as a ready-to-use Python package at https://pypi.org/project/c2q-framework/.

title: Parametric-amplification-enhanced Gaussian quantum metrology in non-Markovian environments
authors: Jia-Xin Peng, Wei Li, Zhucheng Zhang, Chengsong Zhao, Zhong-Wei Yu, Chunfeng Wu, Zhe Sun
abstract: We study the quantum estimation of the optomechanical coupling strength in a cavity optomechanical system that includes a parametric amplifier and is coupled to a structured mechanical reservoir. We show that parametric amplification, together with non-Markovian effects, yields a significant enhancement of the estimation precision, which is directly linked to the spectral properties of the bath. We find that parametric amplification increases the difference between the estimation precision in non-Markovian and Markovian environments by amplifying the steady-state shift induced by the initial information backflow, a previously unidentified effect. The ultimate precision bound can be nearly saturated by a joint Homodyne measurement of the cavity’s amplitude quadrature and the mechanical oscillator’s position. We also treat the total sensing time as a resource and analyze the information acquisition rate. This analysis shows that the metrological advantage of non-Markovian effects over the corresponding Markovian case remains when time is taken into account as a resource and is further enhanced by increasing the parametric gain. Our results establish a direct connection between non-Markovian reservoir engineering and quantum metrology in optomechanical systems.

title: AI-assisted hyperspectral interferometry and single-cell dispersion imaging
authors: Kamyar Behrouzi, Tanveer Ahmed Siddique, Megan Teng, Walid Redjem, Li-Wei Lin, Boubacar Kanté
abstract: Interferometry techniques are essential for extracting phase information from optical systems, enabling precise measurements of dispersion and highly sensitive detection of perturbations. While phase sensing offers enhanced sensitivity compared to conventional spectroscopy methods, this sensitivity often makes systems more vulnerable to external factors such as vibrations, introducing instability and noise. In this work, we demonstrate a broadband and AI-enhanced interferometry method, denoted general polarization common-path interferometry (GPCPI), that relaxes the polarization constraints of traditional common-path interferometry. The polarization decoupling feature enables simultaneous amplitude and phase measurements supplemented with deep neural autoencoders to detect phase anomalies in the spectrum through the analysis of second-order derivative mapping of the phase profile, enhancing the accuracy of broadband phase measurements. The approach enables an order of magnitude improvement in phase stability compared to state-of-the-art interferometry techniques, leading to higher accuracy in phase sensing. Plasmonic metasurface phase sensing and hyperspectral single-cell dispersion imaging demonstrate the capability and sensitivity of the method over conventional spectroscopy. Our own adapted version of deep learning model, ConvNeXt V2, enables single-shot and real-time tracking of phase variation with minimized noise. Interference fringes affected by the cell-cultured samples reveal the fingerprints of the normal (CCD-32Sk) versus cancerous (COLO-829) skin cells, demonstrating application in cell classification and disease diagnosis at single-cell level through hyperspectral dispersion imaging as a proof of principle. The proposed interferometry technique offers a reliable, compact, and stable solution for broadband phase measurements and single-cell dispersion imaging for applications in metrology, molecular diagnostics, drug discovery, and quantum sensing.

title: Classical analog emulation of quantum circuits via time-averaged dynamic states
authors: Matias Miguel Castillo Valle, Tim Tuuva, Benjamin Apffel, Hervé Lissek, Romain Fleury, Mathieu Padlewski
abstract: Between the digital and quantum paradigms lies the emerging field of quantum-inspired analog computing, in which classical waves emulate quantum circuits. We introduce wavebits---classical wave analogs of qubits whose amplitudes are carried by physical oscillatory signals---and show that any nonseparable $N$-qubit state can be encoded in $2N$ narrowband signals that remain locally separable at every instant; the nonseparable correlations are recovered at readout by time-averaged demodulation over auxiliary carrier frequencies, the nonseparability channels. We prove that any two-qubit gate unravels into the time-averaged tensor product of two local time-varying operators, and that arbitrary circuits are emulated with a base-frequency count scaling linearly in the number of entangling two-qubit gates, independent of qubit number for a fixed gate count. The exponential cost of the ${2}^{N}$-dimensional state reappears at readout and in the averaging time of circuits with many two-qubit gates, not in circuit execution, as quantified by an analytic error bound that doubles as a hardware design rule. A mixed-signal prototype emulates Bell state generation, controlled-not gates, phase kickback, and Bloch-sphere rotations at fidelities above 0.99, and numerical benchmarks against exact state vectors validate the scheme for up to six qubits. The architecture is directly implementable in acoustic, photonic, and mixed-signal platforms.

title: Efficient logical operations in quantum low-density parity-check codes using simple resource states
authors: Mark Webster, Nicolas Delfosse
abstract: Quantum LDPC codes provide a substantial reduction in qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computation compared to surface code, thanks to their high encoding rate. However, operating simultaneously on multiple logical qubits encoded in the same block is more challenging and may slow down logical operations. Prior work addresses this problem by designing complex resource states to perform logical measurements in LDPC codes. Here, we propose an approach that only consumes cat states. Whereas previous work on cat-based measurements focuses on a single logical measurement, we design a protocol for the joint measurement of ℓ commuting logical operators. The key ingredient is the design of a scheduler code determining the measurement sequence and allowing for the decoding of all logical measurement outcomes. Numerical simulations with the LDPC codes Q70 and Q102 of the walking cat architecture show a reduction of nearly 3 × in the number of cat-based measurements required versus the Viterbi method for measuring ℓ = 20 commuting logical operators. Combining our logical measurement protocols with a new variant of the CliNR partial error correction scheme, we achieve a reduction of up to 73 × versus the Viterbi method for random Clifford circuits. Our approach also applies to non-Clifford gates, producing a reduction of up to 5 × versus the Viterbi method for Toffoli gates.

title: Quantum noise suppression at scale with crosstalk-robust gate sets
authors: Andy J. Goldschmidt, Emilio Peláez, Ryan Sitler, Kevin Olsson, Kaitlin N. Smith, Gregory Quiroz
abstract: We introduce crosstalk-robust gate sets, which are obtained using a novel, scalable optimal control problem exploiting quantum crosstalk’s pairwise operator structure. Crosstalk-robust gate sets suppress quantum crosstalk throughout arbitrary computations, whereas conventional dynamical decoupling primarily targets idle periods. We use the IBM Quantum Platform as a testbed for our gate sets, where we study their efficacy via error suppression protocols and randomized parallel single-qubit circuits of up to eight qubits. Using a Hamiltonian simulation of a four-qubit transverse field Ising model, we show that crosstalk-robust gate sets enhance median algorithmic performance by a factor of four over baseline Gaussian gates using the same calibration procedures. Lastly, we provide numerical evidence that crosstalk-robust gate sets can enable larger qubit-qubit coupling strengths that can cut two-qubit gate times in half, demonstrating how hardware-software co-design using quantum optimal control can create new opportunities for quantum computing architectures.

title: Near-Heisenberg-limited parallel amplitude estimation with logarithmic-depth circuits
authors: Kohei Oshio, Kaito Wada, Naoki Yamamoto
abstract: Quantum amplitude estimation is one of the core subroutines in quantum algorithms. This paper gives a parallelized amplitude estimation (PAE) algorithm that simultaneously achieves near-Heisenberg scaling in the total number of queries and sub-linear scaling in the circuit depth, with respect to the estimation precision. The algorithm is composed of a global GHZ state followed by separated low-depth Grover circuits optimized by quantum signal processing techniques; the number of qubits in the GHZ state and the depth of each circuit is tunable as a trade-off way, which particularly enables even near-Heisenberg-limited and logarithmic-depth algorithm for amplitude estimation. We prove that this trade-off scaling is nearly optimal with use of the parallel quantum adversary method, against folklore on the impossibility of efficient parallelization in amplitude estimation. The proposed algorithm has a form of distributed quantum computing, which may be suitable for device implementation.

title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
authors: Yueen Chen, Mohammad Sharifian, Abolfazl Bayat
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

title: Assessing Trade off between efficiency and Security Concern in AI adaption in Defense sector with India & Global Perspective
Quantum AI for Cancer Detection: Emerging Approaches in Intelligent Precision Oncology
authors: Syed Arshad Ali, Somya Priya Mishra, Swayam Bhatia
abstract: Cancer is the second biggest cause of death worldwide, killing nearly 10 million people annually with pancreatic, lung and colorectal cancer being the most prevalent cases, where patients are still diagnosed late in the disease process. In the past decade (2015-2024), the landscape of this picture has changed significantly: Deep learning architectures, notably convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have surpassed previous classifiers like support vector machines (SVMs) and artificial neural networks (ANNs) and are now nearing, and in some studies achieving, human diagnostic capabilities. More recently, the development of quantum machine learning (QML) and quantum neural networks (QNNs) has opened up yet another avenue for more detailed molecular simulation, quantum-enhanced liquid biopsies and AI-guided nano therapy. It summarizes over a dozen peer-reviewed research papers spanning that decade, from the classical machine learning era (2015-2018), to the deep learning surge (2019-2021), to the advent of hybrid quantum-AI systems (2022-2025), which is an area of quantum-AI-specific research that has increased by a factor of 10+ since 2015. The paper suggests a novel Quantum-AI Nano-Swimmer framework: a system comprising quantum biosensors, which can detect cancer biomarkers at the molecular level, and AI-guided nano robots, that have the potential to reach an accuracy of up to 99 percent when navigating the bloodstream to deliver targeted treatment. The paper concludes with key research gaps of the field and future research directions for the field in the near future, such as quantum drug discovery and the application of privacy-preserving federated learning for 2025–2030.

title: Resource-efficient digitized adiabatic quantum factorization
authors: Felip Pellicer, Juan José García‐Ripoll, Alan C. Santos
abstract: Digitized adiabatic quantum factorization is a hybrid algorithm that exploits the advantage of digitized quantum computers to implement efficient adiabatic algorithms for factorization through gate decompositions of analog evolutions. In this paper, we harness the flexibility of digitized computers to derive a digitized adiabatic algorithm able to reduce the gate-demanding costs of implementing factorization. To this end, we propose a new approach for adiabatic factorization by encoding the solution of the problem in the kernel subspace of the problem Hamiltonian, instead of using ground-state encoding considered in the standard adiabatic factorization proposed by Peng et al (2008 Phys. Rev. Lett. 101 220405). Our encoding enables the design of adiabatic factorization algorithms belonging to the class of quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) methods, instead the polynomial unconstrained binary optimization (PUBO) used by standard adiabatic factorization. We illustrate the performance of our QUBO algorithm by implementing the factorization of integers N up to 8 bits. The results demonstrate a substantial improvement over the PUBO formulation, both in terms of reduced circuit complexity and increased fidelity in identifying the correct solution.

title: Digital quantum simulation of the Holstein-Primakoff transformation on noisy qubits
authors: Kelvin Yip, Alessandro Monteros, Sahel Ashhab, Lin Tian
abstract: Quantum simulation of many-body systems offers a powerful approach to exploring collective quantum dynamics beyond classical computational reach. Although spin and fermionic models have been extensively simulated on digital quantum computers, the simulation of bosonic systems on programmable quantum processors is often hindered by the intrinsically large Hilbert space of bosonic modes. In this work, we study the digital quantum simulation of bosonic modes using the Holstein-Primakoff (HP) transformation and implement this protocol on a cloud-based superconducting quantum processor. Representative bosonic dynamics, including the driven harmonic oscillator, bosonic squeezing, and the Jaynes-Cummings (JC) model, are simulated on quantum hardware. Using data obtained from the quantum simulations, we systematically examine the interplay between algorithmic and hardware-induced errors to identify optimal simulation parameters. The dominant algorithmic errors arise from the finite number of qubits used in the HP mapping and the finite number of Trotter steps in the time evolution, while hardware errors mainly originate from entangling-gate infidelity, decoherence, and readout errors. We demonstrate two-excitation JC dynamics and squeezed-state generation involving qubit-qubit interactions under the HP transformation, extending the simulations beyond the simple single-excitation regime. Furthermore, we show that quantum error mitigation substantially improves the fidelity of the quantum simulations on current hardware. Our results demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of HP-based digital simulation of bosonic degrees of freedom on current quantum processors and provide a framework that can be extended to more complex spin-boson and multimode cavity models.

title: AI-Driven Analysis of Quadruple-Node-Upset Self-Recovery Latches (LQNTL)
authors: Fazal Shah, Maryam Tariq, Sahar Ali, Abdulaziz Aldali
journal: International Journal of Computers and Informatics
abstract: In particular, Single Event Upsets and Multiple Bit Upsets created by radiation lead to severe problems for mission critical computing systems such as aerospace, nuclear, as well as safety critical embedded processors. Although QNU remains the most severe error, TMR Latches [3], ECC Latches [4], and DICE [1] are no longer viable because while remaining low power consuming, they incur significant delay overhead to inject QNU. In this paper, the Quadruple Node Upset Self Recovery Latch (LQNTL) is proposed, a fault tolerant latch that employs multi feedback redundancy with machine learning based optimization aimed at soft error resilience improvement. The methodology is evaluated in terms of the fault recovery efficiency through simulation using HSPICE and transistor level, and fault injection using MC; and using AI models based on LSTM, SVM and Random Forests networks. In the second category, Maskov Models are used to probabilistically model transitions between fault state and Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms are employed to choose the best self-recovery mechanism through RL in order to make transitions between fault states adaptively in real time. Simulation shows that LQNTL is superior at PVT variations to conventional latches and has 95% recovery success, a much reduced Mean time to Recovery (MTTR) (~10–15ns vs. 20–30ns in conventional latches), and a much safer and more robust latch using state-of-the art processes. LQNTL consumes a factor of 10–20 % more power than LQNTL but has superior fault tolerance and capability to determine errors a la deterministic. This thesis contributes to a thorough literature review of previous fault tolerant latch implementation, the gaps in the current design and the future direction for fault tolerant latch design using AI driven optimizations for next generation of radiation hardened computing architecture. The results indicate that LQNTL could constitute a foundation for future fault tolerant microprocessors, FPGAs and memory architectures in such environments of extreme demand, low power and self-recovery. Adaptive power management, neuromorphic inspired fault prediction, as well as extensions for quantum error correction of latch reliability are all considered for future work.

title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
authors: José Daniel Viqueira, Andrés Gómez, David Mera
abstract: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.

title: Restoring quantum neural network trainability through reusable calibration
authors: Ruizhe Shen, Xianquan Yan, Kenji Kawaguchi, Ching Hua Lee
abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs) rely on measured quantum observables to guide optimization, but hardware noise can suppress the parameter-dependent signals essential for learning. Here, we develop a structure-preserving error-mitigation framework that improves QNN trainability through reusable calibration of the quantum circuit's effective noise response. By calibrating a reference circuit with the same gate architecture as the trainable circuit, we construct regularized estimators of local quantum features that remain fixed throughout training. We quantify how calibration errors and response mismatches affect the recovery of both observables and their derivatives. Numerical simulations demonstrate enhanced loss-landscape contrast, faster convergence, and improved classification performance, and an IBM Quantum experiment confirms improved closed-loop variational optimization under hardware noise. We further demonstrate calibration reuse in a modular QNN comprising 25 independent four-qubit channels, corresponding to 100 qubits in aggregate. Our results establish reusable feature calibration as a practical approach to improving noise-limited quantum machine learning without repeated calibration at every training step.

title: Efficient color image encoding using chroma-subsampled hybrid quantum representation
authors: Vrushali Nikam, Manish Motghare, Reena Gupta, Vikas Panchal, Basudeb Dey, Smita M Nirkhi, Raiyaan Patel
abstract: Quantum image representation (QIR) is a fundamental component of quantum image processing, but existing color-image encoding approaches often require substantial qubit resources, gate counts, and circuit depths. This work presents CS-HQR (Chroma-Subsampled Hybrid Quantum Representation), a hybrid quantum classical framework that integrates YCbCr color space transformation and 4:2:0 chroma subsampling with quantum state preparation. The proposed framework preserves the luminance component at full spatial resolution while encoding chrominance components at reduced resolution, thereby reducing the amount of color information requiring quantum encoding. CS-HQR employs a dual circuit architecture in which the luminance component is encoded using 16 qubits and the subsampled chrominance components use 15 qubits including a channel selection qubit. The framework was evaluated using 6097 medical brain MRI images, with circuit level analysis performed across the complete dataset and reconstruction-quality analysis conducted on a representative subset. Compared with MCQI, CS-HQR requires 16 rather than 18 qubits and achieves approximately 54.0% reduction in transpiled gate count and 72.2% reduction in transpiled circuit depth, while maintaining high reconstruction quality. To assess generality beyond grayscale derived medical images, additional experiments were conducted on the Kodak, BSD500, and USC-SIPI natural colour benchmarks, obtaining mean SSIM values of 0.987, 0.981, and 0.984, respectively, with approximately 50% gate reduction. These results indicate that classical perceptual redundancy reduction can be incorporated into quantum image encoding to reduce state preparation resources while maintaining high reconstructed-image quality. The study provides a simulation-based evaluation of CS-HQR and establishes a basis for further investigation on hardware-aware and noise-resilient quantum image processing systems.

title: Geopolitical icebergs of the High North: the Arctic frontier of Nordic diplomacy
Quantum annealing for customer segmentation: a proof-of-concept QUBO framework for supply chain clustering
authors: Raphaël Bouchet, Alena Puchkova
abstract: This article investigates the potential of quantum clustering, specifically through quantum annealing, to enhance supply chain segmentation compared with classical K-Means. Using a proof-of-concept framework, clustering is translated into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimisation formulation, tested on customer datasets via both classical Simulated Annealing and D-Wave’s Leap hybrid solver, with penalty parameter optimisation introduced to address solver sensitivity. Performance is benchmarked against K-Means on runtime, accuracy metrics, and scalability, across dataset sizes from 200 to 5,000 points. Results show that while K-Means maintains superior inertia and stability, the hybrid quantum approach achieves faster solver-reported runtimes and, on a simplified 200-point, two-feature benchmark, delivers improved silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, and Dunn scores once penalties are optimised — metrics which, it is noted, reward the balanced partitions structurally favoured by the pairwise QUBO objective. However, scalability remains constrained by current qubit capacity and solver access, limiting practical deployment beyond mid-sized datasets. The study concludes that classical methods remain dominant for industrial-scale segmentation; the demonstrated framework, penalty-optimisation pipeline, and objective-level analysis nonetheless provide a documented foundation, grounded in a customer segmentation case study, upon which future quantum-assisted supply chain clustering can build as hardware matures.

title: Born-rule statistical dynamical quantum phase transitions under measurement
authors: Guan-Hua Chen, Guo-Yi Zhu
abstract: Dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) occur at times when a quantum state exhibits a nonanalytic change in its return probability. This can be viewed as the probability of collapsing the evolved state to the initial state by quantum measurement. However, the initial wave function usually has exponentially small amplitude in the late time evolved state. Here, we perform statistical characterization of all the possible postmeasurement states distributed according to the Born rule, by sampling a one-dimensional quantum Ising chain after quantum quench dynamics. The statistical ensemble can also be viewed as a mixed state when the time evolved state is subjected to maximal dephasing noise in a certain basis. We map the distribution to a statistical model, and introduce its effective ``energy'' spectrum and the average dynamical free energy, establishing a framework for the statistical DQPTs. We show the recovery of the DQPT under high-moment averaging and a delocalized level distribution following critical times. Through analytic continuation into the complex time plane, we investigate the extension of Yang--Lee--Fisher zeros and the emergent level crossing near critical times. Finally, we propose a measurement-based quantum computation protocol to simulate the unitary evolution via single-qubit measurements on a two-dimensional cluster state. Our results provide a way to experimentally investigate statistical DQPTs in quantum devices, shedding light on the structured circuit sampling with insights from DQPT and generalizing the understanding of mixed states owing to decoherence beyond equilibrium.

title: Cybersecurity and legal aspects of critical infrastructure protection under global threats: the Ukrainian perspective
authors: Oleh Semenenkо, Ihor Mylashenko, Maryna Sliusarenko, Микола Ліневич, Oleksandr Leonenko
abstract: The research gap addressed in this article concerns the limited integration of technical, organisational, and legal dimensions of cybersecurity protection for Ukraine’s critical infrastructure in the face of growing global cyber threats and military aggression. The purpose of the research was to assess the current state of cybersecurity in Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and to develop an integrated protection model. The study hypothesises that a combination of advanced technological solutions and a robust legal framework can significantly enhance the resilience of critical infrastructure. The methodology involved systematic analysis of national-level cyber risks, the effectiveness of multilayer protection, and international standards in comparison with national regulations. Key findings revealed critical vulnerabilities in Ukraine’s energy, transport, financial, and governmental sectors, including inadequate protection of automated control systems, outdated software, limited access control, and a lack of backup communication channels. The findings indicate that multilayer protection, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and the Zero Trust Model may reduce risks and improve system adaptability. Legal analysis highlighted Ukraine’s evolving regulatory framework, which integrates international cybersecurity standards and promotes coordination between the public and private sectors. The article contributes to logistics systems research by linking cyber-resilience with continuity of operations, crisis response, and military readiness. The conclusion emphasises the need for continuous updates to cyber-risk assessment methods and the adoption of advanced technologies like quantum cryptography, AI, and Zero Trust Models to mitigate risks and ensure the resilience of Ukraine’s critical infrastructure.

title: CRZRing: Scalable Fidelity Quantum Kernels Beyond Exponential Concentration
authors: Danilo Cavaliere, Giuseppe Fenza, Lukasz Gajewski, Vincenzo Loia
abstract: Quantum kernel methods are among the most promising paradigms for hybrid quantum–classical machine learning, combining quantum feature maps with classical learning algorithms. Their scalability, however, is fundamentally limited by kernel concentration, making concentration-resistant feature maps a central challenge for quantum AI. This paper addresses this challenge through a novel fidelity-kernel quantum support vector machine (QSVM) feature map. Fidelity-kernel QSVMs embed classical data into the Hilbert space of n qubits and use the resulting state fidelity as a kernel for a classical support vector machine (SVM). For highly expressive feature maps, off-diagonal kernel entries concentrate around 2−n with variance that decays exponentially in n, rendering the Gram matrix nearly rank-deficient and collapsing the classifier toward majority-class predictions. This paper introduces CRZRing, a fidelity feature map encoding 2n singular value decomposition (SVD) components via single-qubit RY rotations followed by a nearest-neighbor ring of data-dependent controlled-RZ (CRZ) gates. CRZRing is benchmarked against the instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP), hardware-efficient embedding (HEE) and ZZ-Ising quantum feature maps and a classical Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) kernel on two natural language processing tasks, SST-2 and AG News. In the tested regime (up to 16 qubits for the variance and 20 for classification), CRZRing is the only map whose off-diagonal kernel variance does not decay with n, including when it receives the same n components as the baselines. Its accuracy is on par with that of the RBF kernel, while the three quantum baselines degrade toward chance. In noisy simulations at eight qubits with kernels estimated from 1000 shots, CRZRing remains the most accurate quantum map up to a depolarizing probability of 10−2 per gate, beyond which all maps degrade: HEE is ahead on AG News at p=0.05, and, for p≥0.1, every map falls to the majority-class level. Under a noise model calibrated on an IBM Heron processor, CRZRing loses at most 1.2 points.

title: Scalable and Interpretable Quantum Mixture of Experts for High-Dimensional Spatio-Temporal Data
authors: Junghoon Justin Park, Anna Jung, Kyumin Lee, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, Huan-Hsin Tseng, Shinjae Yoo, Jiook Cha
abstract: Quantum Mixture of Experts (QMoE) architectures offer a promising path toward scalable quantum machine learning, yet existing approaches remain largely confined to low-dimensional benchmarks and often rely on naive input partitioning that disrupts feature dependencies. We address these gaps by introducing Feature-Partitioned QMoE, which partitions high-dimensional spatio-temporal inputs into functionally coherent feature groups and assigns each group to a dedicated quantum expert. We further propose a hierarchical interpretability framework that leverages the modular structure of QMoE to produce circuit-level gating analysis, per-expert gradient saliency, and heterogeneity-based subtype discovery. Applied to ADHD classification from resting-state fMRI (N=4,458, ABCD Study, 180 brain ROIs, 363 timepoints), the proposed Theory-Driven QMoE achieves performance comparable to matched-capacity classical and quantum baselines while enabling circuit-attributable interpretation. The framework identifies FDR-corrected ADHD-associated biomarkers in executive-control and anterior default-mode networks and reveals three neurobiologically meaningful ADHD subtypes. These results position Feature-Partitioned QMoE as a scalable and interpretable methodology for applying quantum machine learning to high-dimensional biomedical data.

title: Quantum-Resistant Intrusion Detection Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Dileep Kumar Padidem, B. Abdul Raheem, G. Nithya, Putta Brundavani, G. Sujatha, M. Kondaiah
journal: The International Journal of Maritime Engineering
abstract: The rising cyber threat complexity heightens the need for advanced Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) capable of swiftly identifying familiar and new attack methods, highlighting an urgent concern. Feature selection, by diminishing input features, boosting detection accuracy, and cutting computational time, significantly enhances machine learning-based IDS performance. To tackle these issues a model has developed QIDSMR caters to 6G-enabled Internet of Things (IoT), tackling quantum-attackers and network variations. A multi-slice 6G architecture with NEUROSAFE-6G, encompassing layers for security adaptability. The Threat Model addresses cryptographic vulnerabilities, integrity breaches, and diverse attacks from classical and quantum adversaries. IoT-Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) customizes key generation based on device capabilities and security needs. Quantum entropy and anomaly scores enhance detection in Q-IDS. Quantum Evolutionary Algorithms (QEA) utilizes probabilistic qubit encoding and gate adaptation for diversity. Integration of quantum entropy variations and anomaly scores improve detection efficiency. Energy-efficient interferometry aids intrusion detection. Hyperparameter optimization involves Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classifiers and Quantum Particle Swarm Optimization (QPSO). A QCNN hybrid with variational quantum circuits detects complex attacks. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning strengthens detection methods. DSAC focuses on scalable deployment with energy-aware optimization and collaborative learning. The simulation parameters are detection accuracy, response time, attack detection delay, overhead, false positive rate, and communication overhead.

title: Fabrication and Utilization of NV Flakes for High-Pressure Quantum Sensing above 1.5 Megabar
authors: Wuhao Chen, Qinyue Luo, Xiaoran Zhang, Jin Cheng, Ying Liu, Yating Jia, Shanmin Wang, Xiaobing Liu
abstract: High-resolution quantum sensing under extreme conditions is essential for condensed matter physics. Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers enable in situ magnetic imaging inside a diamond anvil cell, yet current approaches rely on either randomly oriented particles or custom-fabricated diamond anvils─offering ease of integration or field imaging, respectively, but not both. Here we present NV flakes as a unified platform: micrometer- to submicrometer-thicksingle-crystal flakes characterized by optically detected magnetic resonance and photoluminescence. We clarify the origins of anomalous spectral features and demonstrate robust NV sensing above 1.5 megabar. Detecting the Meissner effect in a 100 nm YBCO film confirms the flakes’ promise for high-pressure quantum metrology.

title: Task-Sufficient Memory under Stochastic Clocks: Coarse-graining operators, fixed points, and finite-policy certification
authors: Marcos Eduardo — Elias
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: What information about environmental memory must a quantum controller retain to guarantee a specified computational output? This preprint formulates that question in terms of task-sufficient process representations, intervention-valid predictions, stochastic clock laws, and explicit resource accounting. The central requirement is to preserve the outcomes and costs of the permitted decisions, with a stated accuracy contract and a finite-sample certificate. The paper connects two complementary lines of analysis. An operational construction studies Gaussian dephasing and controlled qubit tasks. A separate stochastic-clock analysis studies direct and inverse time changes, fractional relaxation, and the information that temporal coarse graining must transport. These constructions address related modelling questions but are not identified as a single microscopic noise model. The main elements are: Identical uncontrolled channels, different controlled responses. A continuum of Gaussian phase processes has the same uncontrolled coherence at every time and zero Breuer-Laine-Piilo backflow, yet different spin-echo responses. The construction shows why an uncontrolled channel family alone can fail to determine an intervention-dependent control decision. Task-sufficient equivalence and resource contracts. The manuscript defines a contract functional collecting accepted-output moments, acceptance probabilities, and physical costs over a declared policy family. Its finite linear task quotient identifies distinctions relevant to those predictions. Approximate sufficiency is accompanied by stability bounds that expose the sensitivity of conditional guarantees to low acceptance probabilities and small feasibility margins. Simultaneous finite-policy certification. Conservative confidence bounds certify conditional task bias and expected cost per accepted outcome after selection among a fixed, finite set of candidate policies. The assumptions include independent reset attempts, bounded observations and costs, and a trusted ideal reference. Failure to certify a candidate is explicitly distinguished from proof that no feasible physical policy exists. An explicit coarse-graining framework for stochastic clocks. The proposed decorated phase space records the process, permitted policy family, observable set, and clock law. The clock component transports stable laws under their natural scaling and relates domains of attraction to regular variation of waiting-time tails. Within the stated two-parameter clock-and-coupling family, the relaxation-rate direction scales with eigenvalue c^alpha. These clock results are placed in the established probabilistic renormalization literature; they do not establish hyperbolicity or convergence for the full decorated operator. A reset-sensitive fractional-relaxation calculation. Direct subordination of a quantum dynamical semigroup is distinguished from inverse-stable time change. For the latter, the paper compares uninterrupted evolution with independent renewal of the hidden clock and relevant environment. At half order and dimensionless rate one, the exact erfcx representation gives the short-time defect Delta(h) ~ 0.660989212585294 sqrt(h). The difference concerns the declared reset protocols, rather than a general assertion that every physical gate resets its environment. The reported classical benchmark uses ten candidate policies with explicit pulse depolarisation and separate X- and Z-expectation contracts. At the quasistatic endpoint, midpoint echo increases average identity-gate fidelity from 0.789293 to 0.990050. The fidelity crossover near r = 0.0467883 is distinct from the stricter X-task feasibility threshold r >= 0.9688074. For the selected Z-task input, dephasing is harmless and unnecessary echo pulses reduce the expectation. Conventional calibrated echo matches the best tested control performance; calibration, sampling, rejected attempts, and amortisation remain part of the resource account. Two questions are isolated as conjectures: boundedness of the task-quotient dimension along the coarse-graining orbit, and rigidity of the task quotient as a complete contract invariant. The manuscript specifies falsifiable numerical and experimental tests, including rescaled relaxation-profile collapse and finite tests of quotient-rank growth. It establishes no hardware advantage, scalable task-compression theorem, logical error-rate improvement, or error-correction overhead reduction. This illustrated version 2.0 contains 30 pages, four scientific figures, derivation and reproduction appendices, a methodological comparison with renormalization in one-dimensional dynamics, a glossary, and 58 references. The manuscript is dated 12 November 2026 and supersedes version 1.0 of 10 November 2026. The four figures show the uncontrolled/control-response contrast, task-dependent protection, finite-policy certification alongside dimensionless fractional relaxation, and the exact scalar clock-reset defect.

title: Synthesis of fault-tolerant state preparation circuits using Steane-type error detection
authors: Erik Weilandt, Tom Peham, Robert Wille
abstract: Fault-tolerant state preparation is essential for reliable quantum error correction, particularly in Steane-type error correction, which relies on robust ancilla states for syndrome readout. One method of fault-tolerant state preparation is to initialize multiple ancilla states and check them against each other to detect problematic errors. In the worst case, the number of states required for successful initialization grows polynomially with the code distance, but it has been shown that this can be reduced to constant ancilla overhead; in the best case, only four states are required. However, existing techniques for finding low-overhead initialization schemes are limited to codes with large symmetry groups, such as the code. In this work we propose a general, automated synthesis methodology for Steane-type fault-tolerant state preparation circuits that applies to arbitrary Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes and does not rely on code symmetries. We apply the proposed methods to various codes up to a distance of 7 and simulate the successful fault-tolerant initialization of logical basis states under circuit-level depolarizing noise. The circuits synthesized using the proposed methodology provide an important step towards experimental realizations of high-fidelity ancilla states for near-term demonstration of fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Hybrid Krotov gradient descent Optimization for Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Maximilian Fröhlich, Martin Eigel, Michael Hintermüller
abstract: We introduce and study a Krotov-inspired discrete adjoint optimization scheme for quantum machine learning and focus on a hybrid online-to-batch schedule. The method transfers the forward/costate/local-update logic of continuous-time optimal control to parameterized quantum circuits by replacing time locality with gate-index locality. For a broad class of fixed-generator variational gates and terminal-state losses, we show that the batch Krotov direction coincides with the exact gradient of the empirical loss. Under standard smoothness assumptions, this yields monotonic descent and convergence of the batch method, and convergence of the tail of the hybrid method after a finite switch to the batch phase. Empirically, we benchmark hybrid Krotov against the tuned PennyLane optimizer suite and L-BFGS-B on a four-bit parity classifier and on the Pérez-Salinas data re-uploading classifier for the crown problem. Across matched hyperparameter sweeps with three seeds per configuration, hybrid Krotov dominates every tuned first-order baseline and matches the strongest structured PennyLane methods on parity, while approaching the accuracy of L-BFGS-B on Pérez-Salinas at first-order per-iteration cost.

title: Parameter-shift rules for gradients in boson sampling experiments
PQC-Guard: A Unified Cryptographic Framework Integrating Hybrid Encryption and Key Exchange for Comprehensive Post-Quantum Data Security
authors: Dasari Veera Reddy,  Padmaja Madugula
journal: International Journal of Electronics and Communication Engineering
abstract: The advent of quantum computing threatens conventional public-key cryptographic systems, and there is an urgent need for comprehensive frameworks to aid the shift towards post-quantum cryptography. Current approaches that establish a key and encrypt data separately suffer from disjointed protection, limited protection capabilities, integration complexity, and inadequate consideration of the performance-security relationship. In this study, we propose a hybrid cryptographic framework, PQC-Guard, for post-quantum-oriented information security that combines hybrid key establishment and multilayer encryption. The proposed GuardFusionAlgo is a hybrid key establishment (as DSKE), hybrid session-key derivation, encryption-specific sub-key generation, multilayer protection (as MDES), QBM transformations, secure transmission and reverse-order data recovery. Experimental evaluation shows that PQC-Guard has a ciphertext entropy of 7.997 bits/byte, an avalanche effect of 50.21%, a key sensitivity of 50.18%, a plaintext-ciphertext correlation of 0.0012, a 100% tampering detection rate, a 99.6% replay detection rate, and a 98.9% partial key-compromise resistance rate. The framework yields an end-to-end throughput of 15.72 MB/s for a 500 MB workload, negligible ciphertext expansion, manageable computational resource consumption, and 100% successful recovery in all experiments conducted concurrently. Ablation and comparative analyses of the individual components, along with statistical analyses, further highlight each component's contribution and confirm a strong overall performance-security trade-off. PQC-Guard offers a viable solution for post-quantum-ready cloud storage, enterprise communication, secure file transfer, and distributed data protection environments.

title: Hardware-tailored logical Clifford circuits for stabilizer codes
authors: Eric J. Kuehnke, Kyano Levi, Joschka Roffe, Jens Eisert, Daniel Miller
abstract: Quantum error correction is the art of protecting fragile quantum information through suitable encoding and active interventions. However, it is notoriously difficult to manipulate encoded quantum data without causing uncorrectable errors. Here, we introduce a mathematical framework for constructing hardware-tailored circuits that implement any desired Clifford unitary on the logical level of any given stabilizer code. We formulate this task as a discrete optimization problem that minimizes the number of CZ gates while naturally incorporating a parameterization of all Clifford stabilizers. Despite the intrinsic difficulty of the circuit compilation problem, our methods scale to at least 16 physical qubits. Because our circuits require very few CZ gates, they provide excellent starting points for constructing fault-tolerant implementations using flag gadgets. Using a brute-force search, we develop several such flag gadgets, including weakly fault-tolerant logical Hadamard circuits for the [[8, 3, 2]] code that require an unprecedentedly small number of physical two-qubit gates. Our work introduces both the mathematics and software for compiling hardware-tailored logical Clifford circuits. From a broader perspective, we turn away from the standard generator decomposition and instead focus on the holistic compilation of entire logical circuits, leading to significant savings in practice.

title: Python-Based Quantum Chemistry Software in the Era of Quantum Computing: Educational Tools, Platforms, and Research Integration for 2025
authors: Cyprian Moyo
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This presentation was given at the 45th SACI National Convention of the South African Chemical Institute, themed “Chemistry: A Window for Change.” It surveys Python-based quantum chemistry software in 2025 and asks how GPU acceleration, cloud access to quantum hardware, and interactive teaching platforms can be brought into chemistry education and research, especially in African institutions. Contents: Foundations. The quantum mechanical basis of computational chemistry and its main approximations: Born–Oppenheimer, Hartree–Fock, DFT, perturbation theory and coupled cluster. How method and basis set together define a “level of theory.” Where computational and data-driven chemistry sit among the paradigms of science, from empirical through computational to data-driven and AI. The software landscape. Quantum chemistry codes available through South Africa’s Centre for High Performance Computing (CHPC), and the Python ecosystem around MolSSI QCArchive (QCEngine, QCFractal, QCPortal). These give students one interface that works across many electronic-structure programs. Why quantum computing. The caffeine example shows how exact molecular simulation quickly outgrows classical resources, which motivates qubit-based approaches. The talk compares major quantum hardware and cloud providers on educational access and African partnerships, and gives an overview of Africa’s software-first quantum strategy. GPU-accelerated quantum chemistry. GPU4PySCF (v1.4.0, April 2025): reported speedups of up to about 1000× for density-fitting algorithms over single-core PySCF, and 20–50× for general DFT over a 32-core CPU node. CPU–GPU switching through to_gpu() / to_cpu(), and example applications. Educational platforms and pedagogy. Cloud quantum education programmes (IBM Quantum, Microsoft Azure Quantum, Google Quantum AI, QubitxQubit), interactive Jupyter-based teaching (eChem), and the main barriers to teaching quantum chemistry with matching technological fixes. A staged learning pathway runs from traditional theory through Python, interactive notebooks, GPU computing and real quantum hardware (e.g., VQE) to research integration. Applications and outlook. Industry case studies in drug discovery, energy and materials. Strategic recommendations for bringing GPU acceleration, quantum hardware access and proven educational platforms into quantum chemistry training. Author: Cyprian B. Moyo, Nelson Mandela University and National Institute for Theoretical and Computational Sciences (NITheCS), South Africa. Acknowledgements: CHPC/NICIS, NITheCS, the Wits Quantum Initiative (WitsQ), and IBM Quantum.

title: Analytical Investigation of Two-Spin Entanglement Generated by Different Types of Bosonic Environments
authors: A. I. Smetana, A. R. Kuzmak

title: Beauty and charm jet identification with end-to-end training on a superconducting quantum processor
authors: Lucio Anderlini, Pietro Asinari, Gianluca Bertaina, Davide Calonico, Marco Coïsson, Alessio Gianelle, Donatella Lucchesi, Giovanni Passaleva
abstract: The identification of heavy-flavor jets, i.e. collimated streams of particles originating from the fragmentation of beauty and charm quarks produced in proton-proton collisions, represents one of the most challenging classification tasks in measurements at Large Hadron Collider experiments. In recent years, advanced machine learning techniques have been successfully employed to address this problem, while quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising alternative approach. However, the high dimensionality of the problem, typically involving hundreds of observables, raises an open question: whether the current generation of quantum computers, characterized by limited qubit count, can effectively tackle such complex tasks. In this work, a variational quantum circuit for the classification of b- and c-jets at the LHCb experiment is implemented on a 5-qubit superconducting quantum computer manufactured by IQM and installed at the Politecnico di Torino. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a quantum algorithm for jet identification using simulated data from an LHC experiment in which all stages of the machine-learning workflow, including training and testing, are performed on real quantum hardware. The results demonstrate that the impact of hardware-induced quantum noise does not significantly degrade the performance. A framework for the evaluation of the training time on the quantum hardware and for the circuit optimization is also proposed. These findings pave the way for future applications on larger quantum devices based on superconducting qubits, featuring a larger number of qubits enabling the encoding of information beyond the reach of classical simulation and providing a step toward investigating whether quantum advantage may eventually be achievable in high-energy physics classification tasks.

title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory
authors: Marie Kempkes, Jakob Spiegelberg, Evert van Nieuwenburg, Vedran Dunjko
abstract: A large body of work in quantum machine learning has centered on characterizing the expressivity and performance of quantum models. In contrast, little attention has been paid to the reliability of predictions beyond average performance measures such as accuracy. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware quantum classification framework based on Dempster-Shafer theory. This theory allows to express uncertainty through weights assigned not only to individual classification labels but to sets of labels. We introduce a training strategy that enables parameterized quantum circuits to learn such assignments directly from data. This provides an efficient way to prepare the corresponding quantum states and enables the application of different post-processing strategies. In particular, it offers a practical setting for quantum Dempster-Shafer fusion procedures with polynomial resource requirements, even when the corresponding mass functions are defined over exponentially many subsets. Overall, our work represents a step toward enabling quantum models to express uncertainty about their predictions, thereby extending the evaluation of quantum models beyond predictive performance alone.

title: Quantum metrology of spin sensing with free space electrons
authors: Santiago Beltrán-Romero, Michael Gaida, Philipp Haslinger, Dennis Rätzel, Stefan Nimmrichter
abstract: Recent advances in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) have opened the path toward spin resonance spectroscopy with single-spin sensitivity. To assess this potential, we investigate the quantum precision limits for sensing magnetic moments with free-electron probes. Using a scattering model where an electron wavepacket interacts with a localized spin, we study two metrological tasks: estimating the magnitude of the magnetic moment and discriminating the presence of a spin. The sensitivity for a given measurement setting is generally determined by the classical Fisher information, which we benchmark against the quantum bound optimized over all measurements. We find that conventional TEM imaging can saturate the quantum bound when backaction (BA) of the probe electron onto the spin state is negligible. We also find that, when BA is relevant, one could do better by realizing a measurement of the electron’s orbital angular momentum state. These results establish the quantum limits of spin sensing in TEM and guide the development of future experiments probing individual electron spins or nanoscale ensembles of nuclear spins.

title: Bipartitioning of graph states for distributed Measurement-Based Quantum Computing
authors: Kjell Fredrik Pettersen, Matthias Heller, Giorgio Sartor, Raoul Heese
abstract: Measurement-Based Quantum Computing is inherently well-suited for Distributed Quantum Computing: once a resource state is prepared and distributed across a network of quantum nodes, computation proceeds through local measurements coordinated by classical communication. However, since non-local gates acting on different Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) are a bottleneck, it is crucial to optimize the qubit assignment to minimize inter-node entanglement of the shared resource. For graph state resources shared across two QPUs, this task reduces to finding balanced bipartitions with minimal cut rank. We introduce a simulated annealing-based algorithm that efficiently updates the cut rank when two vertices swap sides across a bipartition, such that computing the new cut rank from scratch, which would be much more expensive, is not necessary. Testing our approach on grid graphs, random graphs and measurement-based Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm instances, we find that it matches the quality of established hypergraph partitioning with the potential advantage of remaining invariant under local Clifford operations and thus independent of the chosen representative of the graph state.

title: The Subordinator Renormalization Problem: When Markovian Error Models Misidentify Quantum Memory
authors: Marcos Eduardo Elias Eliashberg Elias
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A quantum processor is controlled through a sequence of operations distributed across time. Its reliability therefore depends on more than the decay observed when the device is left undisturbed. Environmental correlations, stochastic timing, intervention history, acceptance rules, and the observable being computed can all change which errors matter and which protection strategy is justified. The Subordinator Renormalization Problem examines this dependence through an integrated treatment of stochastic clocks, fractional dynamics, multi-time quantum processes, task-specific protection, and finite-sample certification. Its central question is precise: how can temporal resolution be changed and environmental memory compressed while preserving the predictions required by a specified quantum task, including the effects of permitted interventions and their full physical cost? Scientific motivation Coherence time, average gate fidelity, qubit count, and scalar measures of non-Markovianity characterize different aspects of a quantum device. They do not individually determine whether a particular computation can deliver a reliable answer within a given resource budget. A reduced model may reproduce uncontrolled relaxation while omitting correlations that become consequential under pulses, measurements, resets, or subsequent gates. This manuscript investigates the information that must survive a reduction of the noise description. It develops task-sufficient memory as an operational requirement: two process descriptions may be treated as equivalent only when they preserve the declared output expectations, acceptance probabilities, and costs for every allowed future continuation. Stochastic clocks and fractional quantum dynamics The mathematical framework connects Lévy subordinators, Bernstein functions, inverse stable clocks, renewal processes, Caputo fractional derivatives, and Mittag–Leffler relaxation with completely positive quantum dynamics. A central distinction concerns direct and inverse time changes. Direct Bochner subordination of a quantum dynamical semigroup can preserve the semigroup composition law while modifying its generator. An inverse stable clock generally produces a fractional evolution family without that composition law. Fractional powers of generators and fractional derivatives in physical time consequently represent different constructions and cannot be interpreted interchangeably. The manuscript also separates a change of time units from a physical change of the clock law. It derives an exact scaling identity within a fixed stable family and specifies the dimensions of the corresponding relaxation parameter. This identifies what scale covariance establishes and what would require additional evidence of physical control over the environment. The clock-reset problem For inverse stable relaxation, uninterrupted evolution and evolution with an independently renewed hidden clock generally yield different predictions. The paper derives a short-time expansion quantifying the difference between the coherence multiplier after uninterrupted evolution for twice a given duration and the product obtained from two independently renewed intervals. This result makes an otherwise hidden modeling assumption experimentally meaningful. A reset assumption changes the predicted observable response. Whether a real operation renews the relevant environmental variables must therefore be part of the physical model. The analysis includes closed-form calculations for the half-order Mittag–Leffler relaxation, checks of scale covariance, and verification of the deterministic-clock limit. Identical decoherence curves and different control responses An explicit Gaussian dephasing construction provides a separate identification counterexample. A continuum of noise processes produces exactly the same uncontrolled quantum channel at every time, while displaying different responses to spin echo. The entire family has zero Breuer–Laine–Piilo backflow in its uncontrolled reduced dynamics. Nevertheless, its temporal correlations determine whether an echo helps or harms once pulse imperfections are included. The construction shows why uncontrolled channel information alone can be insufficient for an intervention-dependent decision. The relevant distinction is operational: noise processes that look identical during idle evolution can require different control choices. The Gaussian construction and the inverse stable clock analysis are distinct models. Together, they expose complementary requirements on a predictive description, without identifying either construction as a universal microscopic model of a quantum device. Task-sufficient representations and mathematical guarantees The paper formulates exact equivalence of multi-time processes relative to a specified family of interventions, terminal observables, acceptance rules, and resource costs. For a finite linear family, it characterizes the corresponding task quotient and establishes its minimal dimension within linear encoders admitting exact recovery of the contract predictions. Approximate reductions are treated through explicit stability bounds. These bounds show how errors in unnormalized output moments, acceptance probabilities, and attempt costs propagate into conditional expectations and cost per accepted outcome. Low acceptance can amplify a small modeling error and erase an apparent resource advantage. A robust-selection result identifies the feasibility margins required when choosing a policy from approximate predictions. The framework thereby connects process reduction to a concrete accuracy requirement. Finite-sample certification and resource accounting The manuscript derives simultaneous finite-sample certificates for conditional task bias and expected cost per accepted outcome. The guarantees remain valid after data-dependent selection within a fixed finite candidate family, under the stated assumptions of independent reset attempts, bounded observations and costs, and an independently trusted ideal reference. The accounting includes rejected attempts and distinguishes systematic task bias from statistical sampling uncertainty. It also charges characterization, compilation, classical computation, and revalidation to the total resource objective. This distinction matters because a nominal reduction in the cost of one execution can require an unaffordable calibration campaign. A useful controller must improve the complete calculation at matched task accuracy and confidence. Reproducible numerical investigation A classical numerical study evaluates ten pulse policies across three correlation regimes and two contracted observables. The calculations include analytic population predictions, Gaussian trajectory sampling, density-matrix consistency checks, and repeated finite-shot calibration experiments. The results exhibit task-dependent protection choices: a sequence beneficial for one observable can introduce unnecessary error for another. They also distinguish the absence of a certified policy from a general claim that no feasible control exists. Conventional calibrated Hahn echo and the corresponding two-pulse sequence match the best control performance in this benchmark. The study establishes identification and certification results within its declared models; scalable compression, hardware advantage, and reductions in fault-tolerance overhead remain open research objectives. Meaning of the subordinator renormalization problem The title names an operational research problem: construct a change of temporal resolution together with a compressed memory representation and a consistent update rule that preserve all contracted predictions under the permitted controls. The challenge includes causality, complete positivity where applicable, normalization, conditional updates, approximation error, and total resource cost. A small collection of fitted moments is insufficient unless these properties can be maintained through subsequent interventions. The manuscript uses renormalization in the sense of scale change and retention of operationally relevant information. It formulates the conditions a useful reduction must satisfy rather than claiming a completed Wilsonian flow or a new universality class. Relevance and readership The work is intended for researchers in quantum computing, open quantum systems, quantum control, noise characterization, quantum error correction, stochastic processes, fractional calculus, and mathematical model reduction. Its broader engineering relevance is the connection between a model’s predictive sufficiency and the reliable computational output obtained for the resources consumed. The proposed research direction is to identify physical families in which the memory relevant to a useful task can be represented, learned, and updated more efficiently than a full process description. Manuscript contents Version 2.0 comprises 23 pages, four figures, four propositions, one corollary, a finite-sample certification theorem, mathematical appendices, a glossary of 47 terms, and 49 bibliographic references. The bibliography covers stochastic clocks and fractional analysis, quantum dynamical semigroups, environmental memory, process tensors, noise spectroscopy, control, fault tolerance, and statistical certification. About the author Dr. Marcos Eduardo Elias is a Brazilian engineer, mathematician, computer scientist, and entrepreneur based in São Paulo. He is Chairman of Instituto Ramanujan and works with Holosystems on quantum algorithms, stochastic modeling, and the connection between mathematical research and physical computation. His interests include open quantum systems, adaptive quantum–classical optimization, cryptography, and decision-making under uncertainty.
