title: Quantum approximate optimization algorithm with cat qubits
authors: Pontus Vikstål, Laura García-Álvarez, Shruti Puri, Giulia Ferrini
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)–a prominent candidate for near-term quantum computing applications–is tailored to find approximate solutions to combinatorial optimization problems using shallow quantum circuits. In this work, we investigate implementations of QAOA based on cat qubits, where the logical states $$|0\rangle$$ and $$|1\rangle$$ are represented by coherent states of opposite amplitudes, $$|\alpha \rangle$$ and $$|-\alpha \rangle$$. Within this encoding, the primary source of noise–photon loss–induces a bias toward Z -type errors. We focus specifically on an imlementation employing Kerr resonators. By numerically simulating the gate sequences required for QAOA on these nonlinear resonators, we analyze performance on Max-Cut problems and benchmark it against conventional qubits realized as ideal two-level systems subject to single-photon loss. Our findings indicate that the use of cat qubits leads to improved approximation ratios for random Max-Cut instances compared to standard qubit encodings.

title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Bisma Majid, Shabir Ahmad Sofi, Mir Mohammad Yousuf
abstract: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $χ^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.

title: Quantum AI for road safety and beyond: A scoping review of applications in intelligent transportation systems
authors: Naima Goubraim, Zouhair Elamrani Abou Elassad, Hajar Ouhmidou, Hajar Mousannif
abstract: Background Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) increasingly draw on artificial intelligence for prediction, classification, and control tasks. Quantum computing and quantum machine learning (QML) have emerged as candidate tools, though current hardware remains in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. Objective This review maps the literature applying quantum or quantum-inspired AI to ITS, with attention to road-safety applications. Methods A PRISMA-ScR-adapted scoping review searched five databases (Web of Science, ScienceDirect, arXiv, Scopus, IEEE Xplore). Screening was conducted jointly by the review author and a co-author against structured eligibility criteria; an independent, criteria-blind AI-assisted second pass assessed reliability (substantial agreement, kappa = 0.77). From 271 records identified, 50 were synthesized: 41 primary studies and 9 background reviews. A five-item quality checklist was applied to the 15 primary studies with confirmed full-text access. Results The 41 primary studies span five application themes, led by collision/accident detection and avoidance (22 studies), ahead of traffic-state forecasting, ITS operations, electric-vehicle systems, and network security. Reported methods include quantum neural networks, support vector machines, variational circuits, game theory, annealing/QAOA, and federated learning. Quantum and hybrid approaches outperformed classical baselines on structured, interaction-heavy tasks using markedly fewer parameters, though fixed quantum-kernel methods showed recurring overfitting; most studies ran on simulators rather than physical hardware. Conclusion Quantum AI for ITS is a young, rapidly growing field (mostly 2024–2026) in which road safety is the largest application cluster. Reported advantage centers on parameter efficiency, not raw accuracy. Key gaps include near-absent physical-hardware validation, standardized benchmarks, and fully independent dual screening.

title: Improved Join Order Optimization for Database Queries Using Hybrid Quantum-Classical Approaches for QUBO Problems
authors: Nitin Nayak, Sven Groppe, Tobias Winker, Umut Çalıkyılmaz, Jinghua Groppe
abstract: Efficient query optimization is crucial for relational database systems, especially for optimizing join orders in complex queries. This work introduces a hybrid approach that integrates Eliminating Cartesian Products (ECP) with splitting the QUBO search space (SQSS) to reduce the size of the QUBO problem, minimizing binary variables and constraints. This improves the performance of the quantum algorithm while lowering hardware requirements. We evaluate our method using real-world SQL queries from the ErgastF1 dataset on quantum and classical algorithms, including Quantum Annealing (QA), Simulated Annealing (SA), QAOA, and VQE, implemented on D-Wave’s Quantum Annealer and universal gate-based simulators. Additionally, we analyze the impact of selectivity and SQSS on QUBO weight distribution and algorithmic performance, highlighting optimization efficiency for QA and SA. Experimental results show consistent optimal join orders and enhanced query optimization for various selectivity conditions, and it also highlights the limitations of current quantum hardware for complex queries. This study further confirms the potential of hybrid quantum-classical methods for scalable quantum-enhanced database optimization.

title: Learning unified control of intrinsic nonlinear spin dynamics in atomic qudits for magnetometry
authors: C. Z. Cao, J. Z. Han, M. Xiong, M. Deng, L. L. Wang, Q. Liu, X. Lv, M. Xue
abstract: Generating and preserving metrologically useful quantum states is a central challenge in quantum-enhanced metrology. In low-field atomic magnetometry with multilevel atoms, the nonlinear Zeeman (NLZ) effect is both a resource and a limitation. It can generate internal spin squeezing within a single atomic qudit, but under fixed readout, it also rotates and distorts the measurement-relevant quadrature, limiting the usable metrological gain. The problem is further complicated by the time dependence of both the squeezing axis and the nonlinear evolution itself. Here we show that reinforcement learning can transform NLZ dynamics from a source of readout degradation into a sustained metrological resource. Using only experimentally accessible low-order spin moments, a trained agent identifies a unified control policy for this class of intrinsically nonlinear sensing dynamics. We illustrate the approach in the $f=21/2$ manifold of $^{161}\mathrm{Dy}$, where the learned policy rapidly prepares strongly squeezed internal states and stabilizes more than $4\text{ }\mathrm{dB}$ of fixed-axis spin squeezing under continuous NLZ evolution. Including state-preparation overhead, the learned protocol yields a single-atom magnetic-field sensitivity of $13.9\text{ }\mathrm{pT}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$, approximately $3\text{ }\mathrm{dB}$ beyond the standard quantum limit. Our results establish learning-based control as an experimentally feasible route for converting unavoidable intrinsic nonlinear dynamics in multilevel atomic sensors into operational metrological advantage.

title: Controlling Rydberg atom-polariton interactions: from exceptional points to fast readout
authors: Tamara Šumarac, Emily H. Qiu, Shai Tsesses, Peiran Niu, Adrian J. Menssen, Wenchao Xu, Valentin Walther, Uroš Delić
abstract: Rydberg atoms represent a platform underpinning many recent developments in quantum computation, simulation, sensing, and metrology. They further facilitate optical nonlinearity at the single-photon level when coupled to photons propagating in atomic clouds, which form collective atomic excitations called Rydberg polaritons, strongly interacting with each other. Here, we experimentally explore interactions between a Rydberg polariton in an atomic ensemble and a single, adjacent, Rydberg atom. We discover three different regimes of quantum dynamics corresponding to polariton blockade, coherent exchange, and probabilistic hopping, which are defined by their distinct transmission characteristics, with theoretical calculations suggesting that a transition through an exceptional point occurs between blockade and coherent exchange. We investigate the applications of such interactions for fast, non-destructive detection of Rydberg atoms and present proof-of-principle demonstrations for their potential application in nonlinear photonic networks.

title: Enhanced quantum sensing mediated by a cavity in open systems
authors: Quinn Langfitt, Zain H. Saleem, Michael A. Perlin, Tian Zhong, Anil Shaji, Stephen K. Gray
abstract: We simulate the dynamics of systems with multiple qubits coupled to a cavity in order to assess their potential for quantum metrology of a parameter in the open systems limit. The qubits and the cavity are both allowed to have losses and the system is studied under various coupling strength regimes. The focus is primarily on the coupling between the qubits using the quantum Fisher information as the measured parameter. Some results on estimating the qubit-cavity detuning parameter are also presented. We investigate the scaling of the uncertainty in the estimate of the qubit–cavity coupling with the number of qubits and for different initial states of the qubits that act as the quantum probe. As initial probe states, we consider Dicke states with varying excitation numbers, the GHZ state, and separable X -polarized states. It is shown that in the strong coupling regime, i.e. when the coupling between the qubits and the cavity is greater than the decay parameters of both the qubits and the cavity, Dicke states with a large excitation number can achieve the Heisenberg limit, with the precision scaling improving as the excitation number increases. A particularly intriguing finding of our study is that in the weak coupling regime, as well as in situations where either the qubit or cavity decay parameters exceed the coupling, the separable X -polarized state is the best in terms of scaling and exhibits strongly superlinear, and in some regimes near-quadratic, finite-size QFI scaling over the system sizes considered.

title: Gate-based readout and cooling of neutral atoms
authors: Richard Bing-Shiun Tsai, Lewis R. B. Picard, Xiangkai Sun, Yuan Le, Kon H. Leung, Manuel Endres
abstract: Neutral atom arrays have seen tremendous progress in quantum simulation, quantum metrology, and fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, hardware constraints such as atom loss and heating remain significant challenges. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive ancilla-based toolbox for optical tweezer experiments that utilizes high-fidelity Rydberg entangling gates and ancilla atoms to mitigate these physical limitations. First, we demonstrate repeated ancilla-based atom readout, achieving improved detection fidelity over multiple rounds with minimal perturbation to data atoms. Second, leveraging the quantized motional states in tweezer-trapped strontium atoms, we transduce quantum information from the electronic to the motional manifold. This enables us to perform mid-circuit ancilla-based atom loss detection in a coherence-preserving fashion. Finally, we demonstrate algorithmic cooling, a circuit-based sequence that deterministically cools data atoms by transferring their motional entropy to the electronic states of ancilla atoms. We observe a marked reduction in the atomic temperature of data atoms. These tools offer a pathway to continuous operation in tweezer clocks and complement recent developments in continuous reloading experiments.

title: Which data samples matter when training a quantum model?
authors: M. Emre Sahin, Cenk Tüysüz, David Galvin, Oscar Wallis, Alex Gregory, Paul Edwards, Christa Zoufal
abstract: The expressivity, loss landscapes, and generalization behavior of quantum machine learning models have been studied extensively, yet mainly from a model-centric point of view. Little is known about the compatibility of particular quantum models with specific datasets. In this work, we study quantum machine learning models with a data-dependent focus by establishing a quantum-compatible form of the V-usable information. This metric quantifies the information a model can extract from a dataset, enabling a direct, data-centric comparison of different models. We employ this metric to study which data points contribute most significantly to a model's learning process. This enables us to develop an informed preselection strategy for data subsets that can significantly improve the data efficiency of the training pipeline. This work establishes the V-usable information as a powerful diagnostic tool for learning dynamics and a practical route to data-efficient quantum machine learning.

title: Quantum Computing in the NISQ Era: A Scientometric Mapping of Research Trends, Hotspots, and Emerging Frontiers (2018-2025)
authors: Mahadevaswamy Shanthamallappa, Pradeep Kumar Benakanahalli Puttappa
abstract: In recent years, quantum computing has gained more and more of a research interest, especially with the emergence of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) systems. This study is a bibliometric analysis of the publications related to NISQ quantum computing from 2018 to 2025. Publications were pulled from the OpenAlex database and narrowed down by the relevance of the records to NISQ related quantum computing. A total of 2,524 publications were selected for the final analysis. The study covers the growth of publications, citation characteristics, main research areas, research hotspots, leading contributors, geographic distribution and new research areas. The results indicate that the publishing activity has been significantly rising, peaking in 2022-2023. Based on the thematic analysis, the key directions for NISQ research are found to be quantum algorithms, variational quantum methods, quantum machine learning, quantum hardware, optimization, and error control. The analysis also indicates that there is greater thematic variety, indicating that NISQ research has diversified to a number of related fields. The United States is the primary source, followed by China, the United Kingdom and various major universities and research institutions. The citation maturity indicates that more mature citation is seen in the older publications, while newer publications are still building up their level of citations. The 2025 research snapshot also shows that there are strong linkages between the fields of quantum computing, computer science, physics, mathematics, optimization, and AI. The study gives a structured insight into the development and evolution of the research interest in NISQ quantum computing, and identifies areas that will likely continue to be the focus of research.

title: Adaptive error management for fault-tolerant quantum computing across hardware-level suppression, system-level diagnosis, and real-time decoding
authors: Marwa R. Donkol, Naima Kaabouch
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing reached a milestone in December 2024 when Google’s Willow processor demonstrated below-threshold error correction on a superconducting chip, a result since reproduced on neutral-atom and alternative superconducting platforms. Yet the classical decoders needed to sustain this performance face a scaling challenge: noise becomes increasingly structured and correlated as systems grow, while decoders must respond within microsecond coherence windows. This survey asks whether error suppression, noise diagnosis, and decoding are better treated as one adaptive control problem than as three separate research programs. Drawing on a scoping review of 146 records, it organizes the field into a three-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 (Hardware-Level Suppression) integrates protection into the physical substrate; bosonic cat qubits exponentially suppress bit-flip errors, projecting up to 90% overhead reduction versus surface codes. Layer 2 (Diagnosis) employs probabilistic models and computational intelligence to characterize error sources; neuro-fuzzy architectures and the Bias–Entropy decomposition separate hardware drift from logical faults, subject to an identifiability limit that we characterize. Layer 3 (Real-time Decoding) targets the integration of machine learning within strict latency constraints. Hardware acceleration now approaches superconducting cycle times, which shifts the case for learned decoders from speed toward accuracy under correlated noise; recent advances favor hybrid, physics-informed architectures: Neural Belief Propagation resolves degeneracy issues in quantum low-density parity-check codes by embedding topological constraints directly into the network’s loss function. These results suggest a transition toward closed-loop AI architectures that treat error management as continuous control rather than static algorithm selection.

title: Advanced semiconductor materials for future electronic systems: from conventional to quantum devices
authors: Ali Ahmed Alqudaihi, N. Dhasarathan, Amaleswari Rajulapati, Vijayakumar Sivasundar, Akanksha Mishra, Santosh Kumar Sahu, Ravi Kumar V., Mohammed Aman
abstract: Modern electronics have advanced through the continuous improvement of semiconductor technology. However, the fundamental limitations of conventional silicon, including scaling constraints, short-channel effects, and quantum phenomena, necessitate advanced semiconductor materials and next-generation device architectures. This review discusses the development of semiconductor materials from conventional elemental and compound semiconductors to wide-band-gap, two-dimensional (2D), organic, and quantum semiconductors for future electronic systems. It covers semiconductor physics, band structure engineering, material characterization, device performance metrics, and recent advances in crystal growth, epitaxial growth, film deposition, nanofabrication, and doping techniques. This review also examines emerging semiconductor devices, including FinFETs, gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, neuromorphic and memristive devices, spintronics, and quantum semiconductor devices. Atomically thin 2D semiconductors offer remarkable electrostatic control for future miniaturization, while wide-band-gap semiconductors provide higher breakdown field strength and stability than silicon. Furthermore, the review evaluates defect engineering, interface reliability, quantum–material quality, heterogeneous integration, and fabrication compatibility, particularly the BEOL thermal budget below 400 °C, which is critical for integrating new semiconductor channels with silicon logic. Consequently, low-temperature deposition processes such as atomic layer deposition (ALD), plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD), and selective CVD/MOCVD methods provide beneficial routes for heterogeneous integration.

title: Atomic thermometry in optical lattice clocks: Model discrepancies and their impact on lattice light shifts
authors: Irene Goti, Tommaso Petrucciani, Stefano Condio, Filippo Levi, Davide Calonico, Marco Pizzocaro
abstract: Accurate measurement of atomic temperature is fundamental for a wide range of applications, from quantum sensing to precision metrology. In optical lattice clocks, precise characterization of atomic temperature is required to minimize systematic uncertainties at the 10 − 18 level. In this work we investigate atomic temperature measurements in the ytterbium optical clock developed at INRIM, IT-Yb1, employing sideband and transverse Doppler spectroscopy across a wide range of trapping conditions in a one-dimensional optical lattice. By implementing clock-line-mediated Sisyphus cooling [], we reduce the atomic temperature and enable operation at shallower lattice depths to D = 50 E R, where E R is the photon recoil energy. We compare temperature estimates obtained from the perturbed harmonic oscillator model with those derived using a Born-Oppenheimer model []. Discrepancies of up to a factor of four are observed between the temperature estimates obtained with the two approximations. We assess the impact of these modeling differences on the evaluation of lattice light shifts and find relative frequency deviations of up to 8 × 10 − 17. Although sufficiently low atomic temperatures and the consistent use of theoretical models reduce these discrepancies to the low 10 − 18 level, these results motivate further investigations that will be relevant to state-of-the-art optical lattice clocks.

title: Improving microwave quantum memories with approximate error correction
authors: Thibault Desrousseaux, Eva M. González-Ruiz, Pierre Cussenot, Audrey Bienfait, Nicolas Sangouard
abstract: Quantum architectures that integrate quantum memories offer a scalable path to fault-tolerant quantum computing. By leveraging long-lived storage, they enable the execution of large-scale algorithms with processors that are several orders of magnitude smaller than those required in conventional processor-only architectures. In envisioned implementations, standard solid-state qubits – such as superconducting circuits or silicon spin qubits, which naturally couple to microwave photons – are interfaced with solid-state memories functioning as a microwave-photon qubit register, where the address of each qubit is identified by a temporal and a spatial index. Photon-echo storage techniques are particularly promising, as they intrinsically provide large photon storage capacity, high efficiency, and long storage times. A central question in this context is what an experiment representing a landmark step toward fault-tolerant, memory-assisted quantum computing could look like. Here, we propose such an experiment in which a small-scale processor is exploited to actively enhance the performance of a microwave memory. We first identify the dominant source of noise in photon-echo techniques and show that it can be modeled as an amplitude-damping channel. We propose using the [[4,1,2]] Leung’s code to perform approximate quantum error correction of amplitude-damping and improve the memory efficiency. Through a detailed feasibility study including realistic processor noise, we identify the experimental requirements for achieving a logical microwave memory surpassing the break-even point. This proposal paves the way for a near-term experimental demonstration of error-corrected quantum light storage in a proof-of-principle memory-assisted quantum computing architecture.

title: Quantum Computing in 2026: A Comprehensive Architectural, Physical, and Algorithmic Analysis of the Transition from Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) Processors to Fault-Tolerant Logical Qubits, High-Rate qLDPC Codes, and Quantum-Centric Supercomputing
authors: Sandeep, Gautam, Sankalp, Dr. Vishal Shrivastava, Dr.Akhil Pandey, Er.Ram Babu Buri
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The years 2025 and 2026 mark a historic inflection point in quantum information science: the definitive transition from the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era toward early Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) and Quantum-Centric Supercomputing. For nearly three decades, the central impediment to scalable quantum computation was that adding physical qubits increased aggregate decoherence faster than Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes could suppress it. This barrier was decisively shattered by recent experimental milestones demonstrating below-threshold exponential error suppression on superconducting surface codes (Google's 105-qubit Willow and USTC's 107-qubit Zuchongzhi 3.2), high-rate Bivariate Bicycle quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) memory modules reducing physical qubit overhead by over 90% (IBM's Heron, Nighthawk, and 2026 Kookaburra architectures), reconfigurable neutral-atom optical tweezer arrays executing transversal logical gates (QuEra and Harvard), 99.92%–99.99% fidelity trapped-ion systems (Quantinuum Helios and Oxford Ionics), bosonic cat-qubit processors (AWS Ocelot), and topological InAs-Al nanowire interferometry (Microsoft Majorana 1). This paper presents a comprehensive architectural, mathematical, and algorithmic investigation of the 2026 quantum computing landscape. We formalize a five-layer Quantum-Centric Supercomputing reference stack integrating heterogeneous physical modalities, 4K cryo-CMOS and NVQLink GPU-QPU interconnects, sub-microsecond real-time syndrome decoders, CUDA-Q/Qiskit 2.0 hybrid compilers, and domain applications. We formulate rigorous mathematical models for Lindblad open-system decoherence, surface-code below-threshold scaling (Lambda > 1), Bivariate Bicycle [[144, 12, 12]] qLDPC codes, bosonic cat-qubit bit-flip suppression, and hybrid Variational/FaultTolerant Hamiltonian simulation. Finally, we evaluate NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography (FIPS 203 ML-KEM and FIPS 204 ML-DSA) migration imperatives and chart the roadmap toward mega-quop fault-tolerant machines.

title: FTCircuitBench: A Benchmark Suite for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation and Architecture
authors: Adrian Harkness, Shuwen Kan, Chenxu Liu, Meng Wang, John M. Martyn, Shifan Xu, Diana Chamaki, Ethan Decker
abstract: Realizing large-scale quantum advantage is expected to require quantum error correction (QEC), making the compilation and optimization of logical operations a critical area of research. Logical computation imposes distinct constraints and operational paradigms that differ from those of the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) regime, motivating the continued evolution of compilation tools. Given the complexity of this emerging stack, where factors such as gate decomposition precision and computational models must be co-designed, standardized benchmarks and toolkits are valuable for evaluating progress. To support this need, we introduce FTCircuitBench, which serves as: (1) a benchmark suite of impactful quantum algorithms, featuring pre-compiled instances in both Clifford+T and Pauli Based Computation models; (2) a modular end-to-end pipeline allowing users to compile and decompose algorithms for various fault-tolerant architectures, supporting both prebuilt and custom optimization passes; and (3) a toolkit for evaluating the impact of algorithms and optimization across the full compilation stack, providing detailed numerical analysis at each stage. FTCircuitBench is fully open-sourced and maintained on GitHub.

title: Evaluation of Quantum Machine Learning Models for Network Anomaly Detection
authors: Swathi Chandrasekhar, Shiva Raj Pokhrel
abstract: The proliferation of Internet-connected devices has intensified the risk of large-scale network intrusions, necessitating more advanced detection methodologies for the post quantum era. This work presents, to the best of our knowledge, a com- prehensive investigation of quantum machine learning (QML) for anomaly detection on the BoT-IoT dataset, a widely adopted benchmark for IoT security. Leveraging feature-engineered rep- resentations, we implement and evaluate four representative quantum classifiers: Quantum Support Vector Classification (QSVC), Quantum Neural Networks (QNN), and Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC).

title: Enhancing the sensitivity and phase independence of two-mode-squeezed-vacuum–based interferometers via coherent photon subtraction
authors: Hongbin Song, 荷雨 黄, Haohai Wu, Guofeng Zhang, Hidehiro Yonezawa, Ai Zhou, Shitai Yang
abstract: Quantum interferometry is a core technology in quantum precision measurement, wherein the phase measurement sensitivity directly determining the performance of quantum sensors and related detection systems. However, traditional quantum interferometers based on two-mode squeezed vac- uum (TMSV) states still face bottlenecks such as limited phase measurement sensitivity and strong dependence on the measured phase, which restrict their practical application in high-precision de- tection scenarios. To address these issues, we propose an approach to enhance the phase sensitiv- ity of a TMSV-based Mach–Zehnder interferometer (MZI) via coherent-photon subtraction. After coherent-photon subtraction from the entangled modes of a TMSV state, a non-Gaussian entangled state, coined as CPS-TMSV, is generated, which exhibits a higher average photon number than NOON states (N=2), conventional TMSV states, and photon-subtracted two-mode squeezed vac- uum (PS-TMSV) states. Comprehensive evaluations using the parity operator, phase uncertainty, quantum Fisher information (QFI), and quantum Cram ́er-Rao bound (QCRB) demonstrate that the proposed CPS-TMSV-based MZI achieves both superresolution and supersensitivity even at low squeezing strengths. More importantly, this architecture exhibits phase-independent sensitivity over the entire measurement range, eliminating the need for a priori information on the target phase. This work not only provides a novel technical path for improving the performance of TMSV-based quan- tum interferometers but also lays a theoretical foundation for their applications in high-precision quantum sensing and quantum metrology, where stable measurement performance is required across a wide phase range.

title: Long-range spectral entanglement and quantum correlations in highly nondegenerate multi-comb and ultrafast systems
authors: Sahil Pontula, Debasmita Banerjee, Marin Soljacic, Yannick Salamin
abstract: Frequency combs are multimode photonic systems that underlie countless precision sensing and metrology applications. Since their invention over two decades ago, numerous efforts have pushed frequency combs to broader bandwidths and more stable operation. More recently, quantum squeezing and entanglement have been explored in single-comb systems for continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum-enhanced spectroscopy. However, the production of bright quantum light across multiple nondegenerate pulses or frequency combs, a key technology for multispectral applications, remains largely unexplored. In this work, we explore a mechanism that generates a series of nonlinearly coupled bright frequency combs through cascaded three-wave upconversion and downconversion processes mediated by a single idler comb. We consider both discrete combs and broadband ultrafast pulse systems, showing how these systems generate inter- and intracomb two-mode squeezing and entanglement directly in the frequency basis, spanning a large spectral range. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these systems can be engineered to produce target cluster states and concentrated two-mode squeezing through covariance matrix optimization. Our findings uncover a new multimode quantum regime enabled by hierarchical nonlinear interactions in two frequency dimensions, unlocking applications such as entanglement-assisted spectroscopy, squeezing-enhanced pump-probe measurements, quantum spectral multiplexing, and spectrally addressable cluster state generation for quantum information science.

title: Fast, high-fidelity erasure detection of dual-rail qubits with symmetrically coupled readout
authors: Jimmy Shih-Chun Hung, Arbel Haim, Mouktik Raha, Gihwan Kim, Ziwen Huang, Ming-Han Chou, Mitch D'Ewart, Erik Davis
abstract: Erasure qubits are a promising platform for implementing hardware-efficient quantum error correction. Realizing the error-correction advantages of this encoding requires frequent mid-circuit erasure checks that are fast, high-fidelity, and scalable. Here, we realize erasure detection with a hardware-efficient circuit consisting of a single readout resonator dispersively and symmetrically coupled to both transmons of a dual-rail qubit. We use this circuit to demonstrate single-shot erasure detection in 384 ns with minimal impact on the dual-rail logical manifold, achieving a residual error per check of 6.0 ( 2 ) × 10 − 4 , with only 8 ( 3 ) × 10 − 5 induced dephasing per check, and an erasure error per check of 2.54 ( 1 ) × 10 − 2 . The high degree of matched dispersive readout coupling ( χ -matching) within the dual-rail qubit code space also allows us to realize a new modality: time-continuous erasure detection performed in parallel with single-qubit gates. Here we achieve a median 7.2 × 10 − 5 error per gate with < 1 × 10 − 5 error induced by erasure detection. This demonstrates a reduction in erasure detection overhead as well as a crucial ingredient for soft information quantum error correction. Together, these results establish symmetrically coupled dispersive readout as a fast, hardware-efficient, and scalable component for erasure-based quantum error correction using transmon dual-rail qubits.

title: Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems
authors: Aldana Al-Sulaiti, Kuan-Cheng Chen, Muhammad Bilal Akram Dastagir, Ahmed Farouk, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.

title: Implicit differentiation for measurement-efficient bilevel quantum-classical optimization
authors: Tobias Rohe, Markus Baumann, Federico Harjes Ruiloba, Maximilian Zorn, Jonas Stein, Claudia Linnhoff–Popien
journal: Frontiers in Quantum Science and Technology
abstract: Quantum optimization has shown promising results for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems. Real-world applications, however, often involve polynomial coefficients that depend on tunable external factors—such as demand forecasts or risk preferences—giving rise to bilevel optimization structures. We show how variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) can efficiently handle such parametric problems, thus making three contributions. First, we propose a bilevel optimization model for diagonal cost Hamiltonians where coefficients depend on a tunable outer parameter: an outer loop adjusts this parameter—reshaping the cost landscape—while an inner VQA optimizes circuit variables. Second, since derivative-free probing methods incur multiplicative overhead when each outer evaluation requires a complete inner solve, we develop correlator-reuse implicit differentiation (CR-ID), which obtains outer gradients by reusing quantum measurements already collected during inner energy estimation, thus requiring essentially no additional circuit executions. Experiments across three coefficient families show that CR-ID consistently improves budget-normalized efficiency by 4% in 1D and over 14% in multi-dimensional settings, showing a significant performance advantage compared to finite-difference methods. Third, we show that this property is architecture-dependent: the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) admits exact reuse gradients, whereas the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) introduces a state-dependent term that creates a cost–bias trade-off.

title: Fully quantum algorithmic framework for partial differential equation-constrained optimization
authors: Yuki Sato, Jumpei Kato, Hiroshi Yano, Kosuke Ito, Naoki Yamamoto
abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE)-constrained optimization, where an optimization problem is subject to PDE constraints, arises in various applications such as design, control, and inference. Solving such problems is computationally demanding because it requires repeatedly solving a PDE and using its solution within an optimization process. In this paper, we first propose a fully quantum algorithmic framework for solving PDE-constrained optimization problems. The proposed method combines a quantum PDE solver that prepares the solution vector as a quantum state, and a quantum optimizer that assumes oracle access to a quantized objective function. The central idea is the explicit construction of the oracle in a form of block-encoding for the objective function, which coherently uses the output of a quantum PDE solver. This enables us to avoid classical access to the full solution that requires quantum state tomography canceling out the potential quantum speedups. We also derive the overall computational complexity of the proposed method with respect to parameters for optimization and PDE simulation, where quantum speedup is inherited from the underlying quantum PDE solver. We numerically demonstrate the validity of the proposed method by applications, including a parameter calibration problem in the Black-Scholes equation and a material parameter design problem in the wave equation. This work presents the concept of composing quantum subroutines so that the weakness of one (i.e., prohibitive readout overhead) is neutralized by the strength of another (i.e., coherent oracle access), toward a bottleneck-free quantum algorithm.

title: DESIGN AND DEVELOPMENT OF A QUANTUM METROLOGY-BASED NETWORK FOR ULTRA-SENSITIVE MAGNETIC AND ELECTRIC FIELD DETECTION
authors: K Maddileti, Y. S. Reddy
journal: ShodhKosh Journal of Visual and Performing Arts
abstract: In the field of quantum sensing, biomedical diagnostics, nanoscale characterization and advanced electromagnetic monitoring, the detection of weak magnetic and electric fields demands ultra-sensitive sensors with low noise levels, high spatial resolution, and high sensitivity. But, the conventional sensors are sensitive, limited in spatial resolution and have poor noise immunity. This study presents a theoretical and numerical simulation-based investigation of Quantum Metrology-Based Ultra-Sensitive Magnetic and Electric Field Detection (QMUFD) framework, which involves NV-center diamond sensing, preparation of a quantum state, adaptively interrogating the NV-center, suppressing the decoherence, optimizing the Fisher information, and estimating a joint field. The proposed method aims at optimizing the quantum interrogation parameters without sacrificing the quantum coherence effect in the process, to achieve the best possible weak-field detection. The quantitative evaluation results are that the sensitivity of magnetic field is 0.80 nT/√Hz, the sensitivity of electric field is 8.5 V/cm/√Hz, and the SNR is 49.7 dB, the estimation error is 0.62% and the gap of the QCRB is reduced to 4.2%. Ablation analysis shows that adaptive optimization and suppression of the decoherence significantly help in boosting performance. The framework suggested in this work can therefore be used as a promising basis for the high precision measurement of nanoscale magnetic and electric fields, for biomedical, semiconductor, material and quantum based measurement systems.

title: Variational Fast Forwarding for Efficient Evaluation of Many-Body Green’s Functions
authors: Xiang Zhang, Xiangzhen Zhou, Fanxu Meng, 振龙 杜, Pengcheng Zhu, Hengyue Li, Shenggang Ying
abstract: Many-body Green’s functions are essential for characterizing excitation and spectral properties in strongly correlated quantum systems; however, their long-time dynamical evaluation remains computationally intractable on classical computers. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative for simulating such dynamics, yet existing approaches based on Trotterized time evolution suffer from a critical drawback: circuit depth grows linearly with simulated time, severely limiting performance on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices due to gate errors and decoherence. In this work, we propose a fixed-depth quantum circuit framework to evaluate real-time many-body Green’s functions via Variational Fast Forwarding (VFF). By integrating a fixed-depth VFF-based evolution module into a standard ancilla-assisted interferometric measurement scheme, we enable direct extraction of Green’s function values. Numerical simulations on the two-site Hubbard model demonstrate that the approach reconstructs both the real-time Green’s function and the corresponding frequency-domain spectral function. Under a hardware-motivated noise model, a first-order Trotter circuit with step △ t = 0.1 suffers a fidelity collapse below 0.2 as its depth grows with t, whereas the compiled VFF circuit keeps a state fidelity above 0.8 over the same window. At t = 25 the evolution blocks U (t) contain 4751 and 79 CNOT gates. Training uses exact probabilities, without finite-shot sampling. The practical training cost and the performance on larger systems remain open.

title: Quantum Forensics in Cybercrime Investigation and Digital Forensics: From Digital Footprints to Strategic Decision-Making
Advances in Quantum Technology: A Comprehensive Survey of Hardware Platforms, Quantum Algorithms, Error Correction, Cryptography, and Emerging Applications Across the Quantum Computing Ecosystem
authors: Korra Srinivas, V Anil Santhosh, E.Gurumoorthi, B Giridhar, K.Aarathi
abstract: The move from lab demonstrations to designed quantum technology is underway, but the development in hardware, algorithms, error correction and safe communication is uneven. The survey is comprehensive, covering the full stack: superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, photonic, silicon-spin and topological qubits; Shor, Grover, HHL, VQE, QAOA and quantum machine learning; stabilizer and surface-code error correction; quantum key distribution and post-quantum cryptography; and applications in chemistry, finance, logistics, healthcare and security. Published benchmarks up to 2025 are normalized to common metrics and augmented by reproducible simulations. Surface-code simulations at the circuit level show that the threshold is around 0.7-1.0%, and the error-suppression factor increases from 1.6 to 11 when the physical error rate is reduced from 0.6% to 0.1%. UCCSD-VQE reproduces H₂ precisely but misses chemical accuracy for a stretched H₄ chain (5.2 mHa), and a 48-CNOT compilation fails it already at 0.01% two-qubit error. For MaxCut on 3-regular graphs, the QAOA depth required to beat Goemans-Williamson rounding increases from 4 qubits to 6 qubits. The asymptotic decoy-state BB84 reaches 1.5 Mb s−1 over 100 km, whereas the twin-field protocols beat the repeaterless bound beyond 280 km. So, physical fidelity and fault tolerance are still the limiting factors for broad quantum advantage, not qubit count. These comparisons also inform computational decision-making by relating algorithm selection to solution quality, physical error rates, and resource constraints. They provide a basis for assessing where quantum optimization may complement established classical methods in practical decision-support applications.

title: Quantum machine learning for quantitative finance
authors: Piotr Mironowicz, Akshata Shenoy H., Antonio Mandarino, A Ege Yilmaz, Thomas Ankenbrand
abstract: Machine learning (ML) and quantum ML (QML) have gained significant importance, as they offer powerful tools for tackling complex computational problems across various domains. An overview of QML’s uses in quantitative finance is presented here. The connection between quantum computing and ML in financial applications, spanning a range of use cases including portfolio optimization, market prediction and trading, pricing and risk management is examined. The different applications from the literature review are categorized based on specific use cases, ML approaches, optimization methods, and the types of quantum hardware utilized. To facilitate this examination, we employ a morphological box, which allows us to analyze different combinations of these elements across financial use cases.

title: Wave-based dispatch for circuit cutting in hybrid HPC–quantum systems
authors: Ricard Santiago Raigada García, Josep Jorba, Sergio Iserte
abstract: Hybrid High-performance Computing (HPC)—quantum workloads based on circuit cutting decompose large quantum circuits into independent fragments, but existing frameworks tightly couple cutting logic to execution orchestration, preventing HPC centers from applying mature resource management policies to Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) workloads. We present DQR (Dynamic Queue Router) , a runtime framework that bridges this gap by treating circuit fragments as first-class schedulable units. The framework introduces a backend-agnostic fragment descriptor to expose structural properties without requiring execution layers to parse quantum code, a wave-based coordinator that achieves pipeline concurrency via non-blocking polling, and a production-ready implementation on the CESGA Qmio supercomputer integrating both QPUs local on-premises (Qmio) and remote cloud (IBM Torino) backends. Experiments on a 32-qubit Hardware-Efficient Ansatz (HEA) circuit demonstrate not only makespan improvements over a monolithic CPU baseline but also transparent per-fragment failover recovery —specifically rerouting tasks from the local QPU to classical simulators upon encountering hardware–level incompatibilities—without pipeline restart. For deeper circuits, the coordination residual accounts for only 5% of the total execution time, highlighting the framework’s scalability. These results show that DQR enables HPC centers to integrate NISQ workloads into existing production infrastructure while preserving the flexibility to adopt improved cutting algorithms or heterogeneous backend technologies.

title: Enhanced weak-field sensing using detuned motional squeezing
authors: Li-Wen Zhang, Yang Liu, Han‐Jie Zhu, Wei Qin
abstract: Achieving measurement precision beyond the standard quantum limit (SQL) is a fundamental object in quantum metrology. In this manuscript, we propose a streamlined protocol for weak signal sensing in a trapped-ion spin-oscillator system that simultaneously exploits detuned motional squeezing and spin-oscillator entanglement. By combining these two quantum resources, the phase accumulation in this spin system is significantly accelerated, as a result achieving an exponential improvement in the sensitivity over unsqueezed cases. Remarkably, we show that the significant metrological gain provided by our protocol persists in noisy environments, with the sensitivity remaining below the SQL. In particular, our protocol retains a distinct advantage in the short interrogation time regime, thus demonstrating the practical potential in quantum-enhanced sensing.

title: Simulation-based hybrid quantum–classical QAOA–QWS heuristic for tourist–scenic spot–ICH ternary matching in rural cultural tourism
authors: Jing Wang, Jing Ha
abstract: Rural cultural tourism resource allocation requires coordinated matching among tourist preferences, scenic spot capacities, and intangible cultural heritage (ICH) project services, forming a constrained high-dimensional ternary matching problem. This study develops QAOA-QWS, a simulation-based hybrid quantum–classical heuristic that combines the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) with Quantum Walk Search (QWS). A sparse candidate-triplet representation is first constructed, after which the exact-assignment and resource-capacity constraints are incorporated into a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization formulation and mapped to an Ising-type cost Hamiltonian. QAOA performs blockwise low-energy sampling, and QWS subsequently refines the measured candidate subspace through energy-selective marking and graph-dependent quantum-walk evolution. Across five problem scales, QAOA-QWS achieves the highest mean normalized objective value among QAOA only, QUBO-SA, Tabu Search, and genetic algorithms. On the largest instance, it obtains a normalized objective value of 0.869 ± 0.022, a low-energy feasible sampling ratio of 60.5 ± 3.9%, and a post-procedure feasible-state ratio of 90.8 ± 2.2%. Under a separate common fixed-wall-clock protocol, QAOA-QWS retains the highest objective value on all scales and achieves 0.866 ± 0.022 on the largest instance. On the tractable S1 and S2 instances, its gaps to the exact MILP optima are 1.71% and 2.16%, respectively. Sensitivity analyses further show trade-offs between utility preservation and constraint enforcement under different weight and penalty settings. These results support QWS-based candidate-subspace refinement within the tested circuit-simulation setting.

title: Beyond Classical Optical Limits: The Macro-Design Methodology for Next-Generation Photonic Quantum Chips
authors: Bhattharawut Bhoomarat
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This research presents a macro-level architecture and design methodology for Photonic Quantum Integrated Circuits (PQICs), entitled the Photonic Quantum Chip Architectural Framework, which is developed to overcome the fundamental physical limitations of legacy optical systems, namely optical scattering, decoherence, and phase drift. The framework systematically divides the design process into four core stages: Stage 01 Topological & Quantum Field Formulation, Stage 02 Core Solver & Phase Realization, Stage 03 Circuit Topology & Quantum Gate Routing, and Stage 04 Benchmark Validation & System Mapping. Furthermore, to validate hardware robustness, this work incorporates an in-depth simulation testbench suite (eqx_photonic_quantum_core_tb.v) encompassing Fault Injection and High-Frequency Noise Injection testing. Simulation results confirm that the interlock system and automated mechanisms (Automated Assertions) can accurately detect field drops and execute safety responses within prescribed clock cycles, while exhibiting exceptional transient noise filtering capabilities (Noise Immunity). These findings demonstrate that the proposed architecture significantly enhances quantum gate fidelity, reduces decoherence rates, and enables scalable, high-efficiency room-temperature operations.

title: Lụneï ∿ Oryun: Exact Minimax Recovery for Complex Schur Channels, Semidefinite Packing, and Sharp Quantum Storage Rigidity
authors: Artificial Hyperintelligence, Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki, Maciej Nowicki
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Lụneï ∿ Oryun presents an exact characterization of optimal deterministic recovery for every finite-dimensional complex Schur channel, together with constructive decoders, matching converse bounds, and structural results for quantum erasure-correcting subspaces. The release includes an 18-page mathematical manuscript, editable LaTeX source, four numerical verification programs, recorded computational results, and reproducibility materials. The central result identifies the smallest achievable diamond-norm recovery error and the largest achievable worst-case entanglement fidelity through a single semidefinite optimization. One explicitly constructed recovery channel attains both optima. A common adversarial input proves optimality against every deterministic completely positive trace-preserving recovery, including recoveries outside the Schur and unitary classes. PureOne/LUNEI-Complex-Schur-Recovery · Datasets at Hugging Face The work also develops sharp code-repair bounds, an analytic separation between general recovery and mixed-unitary correction, and an obstruction to completing approximately maximum-dimension codes. Exact optimal recovery for arbitrary complex Schur channels Let (C) be a complex positive semidefinite matrix with unit diagonal. Its associated Schur channel acts by entrywise multiplication: [\mathcal M_C(X)=C\circ X.] Choose unit Gram vectors (c_i\in\mathbb C^r), where (r=\operatorname{rank}C), satisfying (c_i^\dagger c_j=C_{ij}). Define \min_{q\in\Delta}\lambda_{\max}!\left(\sum_iq_i c_ic_i^\dagger\right),] where (\Delta) is the probability simplex. The manuscript proves the operational identities [\inf_{\mathcal R}\left|\mathcal R\circ\mathcal M_C-\mathrm{id}\right|_\diamond=2[1-v(C)]] and [\sup_{\mathcal R}\inf_\rhoF_e!\left(\rho,\mathcal R\circ\mathcal M_C\right)=v(C).] Both optimizations range over all deterministic completely positive trace-preserving recovery channels on the fixed logical space. The diamond norm is unhalved, and entanglement fidelity uses the squared-overlap convention. These identities characterize optimal approximate recovery; perfect recovery occurs when (v(C)=1). The optimization uses an (r\times r) density matrix, or an equivalent spectral minimization over classical probabilities. This replaces an unrestricted search over recovery channels with a smaller problem on the Gram span. Constructive decoder and universal optimality witness An optimal density matrix (\sigma) determines a recovery correlation matrix explicitly. Writing [M_{ij}=c_i^\dagger\sigma c_j,\qquad f_i=M_{ii},] the construction is \frac{v(C)\overline{M_{ij}}}{f_if_j}+\delta_{ij}\left(1-\frac{v(C)}{f_i}\right).] The resulting Schur recovery (\mathcal M_A) attains both operational optima. Its recovered channel satisfies [C\circ A\succeq v(C)J,] where (J) is the all-ones matrix. This yields a convex decomposition containing an identity-channel component of weight (v(C)). The decomposition describes the deterministic channel; it does not assert an experimentally heralded successful branch. A dual-optimal probability distribution supplies a single reference-entangled input witnessing the converse bound against every competing recovery. Feasible primal and dual solutions also provide quantitative bounds on the optimal value and achievable recovery error. Connection to established semidefinite packing theory For the rank-one projectors (P_i=c_ic_i^\dagger), the reciprocal (1/v(C)) equals the established classical–quantum semidefinite packing number. The manuscript credits the packing framework studied by Duan and Winter rather than claiming the parameter as a new construction. The proposed contribution is its precise deterministic recovery interpretation: 2\left(1-\frac{1}{\mathsf A(P)}\right),\qquadF_{\mathrm{opt}}=\frac{1}{\mathsf A(P)},] together with the explicit common optimal decoder and universal adversarial witness. This interpretation concerns ordinary deterministic recovery and does not require a no-signalling assistance resource. Further operational and structural results Tensor-product recovery. The value obeys [ v(C\otimes E)=v(C)v(E). ] Product optimal decoders therefore attain the optimum against arbitrary collective recovery on the fixed tensor-product logical input space. This statement does not optimize additional redundant encodings across channel uses. Strict advantage over mixed-unitary correction. An explicitly solved tetrahedral tight-frame family exhibits a recovery channel that strictly outperforms every mixed-unitary recovery. For the four-dimensional family (C_t=(1-t)I+tG), the exact values are [ v(C_t)=\frac{1+t}{4}, \qquad D_{\mathrm{opt}}=\frac{3-t}{2}. ] The strict separation holds for (t>0). A convex quadratic subclass. For real entrywise nonnegative correlation matrices, [ v(C)=\min_{q\in\Delta}q^{T}Cq, ] and identity recovery is optimal. The general complex theorem covers phases for which this simpler conclusion fails. 1- \frac{ \sqrt{(1+a)(1+b)} + \sqrt{(1-a)(1-b)} }{2}. ] A sharp consequence is [ D_{\mathrm{opt}}\le1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2} ] when the compression has operator norm at most (\varepsilon). Complete classification at maximum dimension. For complement-invariant binary supports of size (2K\ge4) and minimum Hamming distance at least two, every dimension-(K) code correcting any one known-coordinate erasure is classified by phase-weighted complementary pairs. Sharp constructive repair. Every rank-(K) trial projector on such a support admits an explicitly constructed closest exact code. Its squared Frobenius distance is bounded by the centered local compression defect divided by the support’s minimum Hamming distance. The uniform coefficient is globally sharp. Operator-norm repair. In the full central excitation sector, a complementary stability theorem controls the distance to an exact maximum-dimension code using local operator-norm defects. Its coefficient depends on physical blocklength rather than logical dimension. Failure of uniform near-capacity completion. A family of exactly erasure-correcting codes approaches the maximum dimension ratio while remaining far from every maximum-dimension code within the specified support. This establishes a limitation on extending the rank-half rigidity theorem to smaller ranks. Computational verification and release contents The accompanying programs record 157 case-level checks: 47 rigidity cases, 50 real minimax-recovery cases, 17 structural-extension cases, and 43 complex-recovery cases. Coverage includes explicit decoders, independent semidefinite formulations, primal–dual comparisons, tensor products, tight-frame examples, sharpness witnesses, and noncompletion constructions. The release contains the manuscript and source, verification scripts, full JSON reports, a consolidated verification table, dependency specifications, citation metadata, and integrity checksums. The prepared repository also provides a runner that preserves the recorded results while writing regenerated reports separately. These computations supplement the analytic proofs. They are finite floating-point checks rather than formal verification or interval-arithmetic certificates. Solver statuses and numerical residuals are retained in the reports. Research status and scope The proposed novelty concerns the precise operational equivalence, constructive optimal recovery, mixed-unitary separation, and stated structural theorems. Established packing parameters, packing multiplicativity, complement-pair constructions, and recovery methods are credited in the manuscript. Worldwide priority remains unconfirmed. The principal recovery theorem applies to finite-dimensional Schur channels on a fixed logical space. The erasure and rigidity results require their stated support and rank assumptions. The release makes no claim of solving unrestricted quantum recovery or demonstrating a physical fault-tolerant device. Author: Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki. Version: Consolidated edition 3, 2 November 2026.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum error correction for constant-excitation stabilizer codes under coherent noise
authors: Ching–Yi Lai, Pei-Hao Liou, Yingkai Ouyang
abstract: Collective coherent (CC) noise poses challenges for fault-tolerant error correction (FTEC), as it is not captured by conventional stochastic noise models. Constant-excitation (CE) codes are inherently immune to CC errors, but a fault-tolerant framework for operating these codes under circuit-level noise has not yet been established. Here, we develop an FTEC framework for CE CSS codes based on dual-rail concatenation. We show that conventional transversal CNOT gates violate the CE constraint and develop CE-preserving logical CNOT gates together with modified Shor- and Steane-type syndrome extraction schemes using zero-controlled NOT gates and CE-compatible ancilla states. We further develop an extended stabilizer simulation algorithm that tracks both stochastic and CC noise. Using this framework, we identify small distance-3 CE CSS codes demonstrate that the [[14, 1, 3]] code maintains robust performance under coherent noise. Our results establish a fault-tolerant framework for CE codes under circuit-level noise and demonstrate their potential for quantum processors affected by CC noise.

title: Imaginary-time-enhanced feedback-based quantum algorithms for ground-state preparation
authors: Thanh Nguyen Van Long, Lan Nguyen Tran, Le Bin Ho
abstract: Preparing ground states of strongly correlated quantum systems is a central goal in quantum simulation and optimization. The feedback-based quantum algorithm (FALQON) provides an attractive alternative to variational methods with a fully quantum feedback rule, but it fails in the presence of spectral degeneracies, where the feedback signal collapses and the evolution cannot reach the ground state. Using the Fermi-Hubbard model on lattices up to 3 × 3, we show that this breakdown appears at half filling on the 2 × 2 lattice and extends to both half-filled and doped configurations on the 3 × 3 lattice. We then introduce an imaginary-time-enhanced FALQON (i FALQON) scheme, which inserts short imaginary-time evolution steps into the feedback loop. This proposed method suppresses excited-state components, escapes degenerate subspaces, restores monotonic energy descent, and improves ground-state convergence across the tested fillings. We further benchmark its performance against existing methods, showing improved results for i FALQON, demonstrating the potential of hybrid real-imaginary-time feedback dynamics for ground-state preparation in strongly correlated quantum systems.

title: Heterogeneous architectures enable a 138 × reduction in physical qubit requirements for fault-tolerant quantum computing under detailed accounting
authors: Pranav Mundada, Aleksei Khindanov, Yulun Wang, Claire Edmunds, Paul Coote, Michael J. Biercuk, Yuval Baum, Michael Hush
abstract: Quantum computer hardware performance and scale have accelerated rapidly over the past few years, enabling real workloads to be run using hundreds of physical qubits, and industry roadmaps predict systems with hundreds of thousands of qubits coming online in the next decade. Moving to this scale requires major advances in quantum error correction (QEC) and its useful integration into real hardware systems. Despite significant theoretical and experimental QEC progress, quantum computer architecture has suffered a significant gap, with bottom-up physical-device-driven challenges largely disconnected from top-down QEC-code-driven considerations. In this work, we unify these two views, presenting a complete heterogeneous quantum computing architecture incorporating task-specific hardware selection and QEC encoding, and agnostic to code selection or physical qubit parameters. The architecture is based on the observation that due to the lengthy idling periods encountered in common algorithms, it can be advantageous to separate quantum processing operations from quantum memory, enabling expanded flexibility in qubit modality and code choice between subsystems. Our approach further enables special-purpose processing modules, and includes a full microarchitecture for fault-tolerant implementation of interfaces between quantum processing units and quantum memories. Using this architecture and a new fully featured compiler functioning across subsystems at the scale of 1000 logical qubits, we schedule and orchestrate a variety of algorithms down to hardware-specific instructions; a detailed accounting of all operations reveals up to 551 × reduction in algorithmic logical error and up to 138 × reduction in physical-qubit overhead compared to a monolithic baseline architecture. We then consider the factorization of 2048-bit RSA-integers; using an experimentally demonstrated grid-coupling topology, factoring RSA-2048 requires 381k physical qubits and 9.2 d, which can be reduced to 4.9 d via addition of an algorithm-specific accelerator for the Adder subroutine (requiring 439k qubits). Finally, assuming hypothetical long-range coupling, implementing quantum memory using qLDPC codes reduces the resources required for factoring to just 190k qubits and under 10 d. These results and the tooling we have built indicate that heterogeneous quantum-computer architectures can deliver significant, verifiable benefits on realistic hardware.

title: Physics‐Informed Quantum Machine Learning with Hard Constraint Embedding for Nonlinear Differential Equations of the First Order
authors: Mengke Xu, Xi Li, Xiao Chen, Xunan Wang, Wanli Huo, Long Ma, Weiqi Yan
abstract: Quantum algorithms based on linear‐system approaches for solving differential equations demand qubit and precision resources beyond near‐term capabilities. To address these challenges, this work proposes a physics‐informed quantum machine learning (PIQML) framework with hard constraint embedding, designed for NISQ era. Within this framework, parameterized quantum circuits serve as machine learning models, where the input variable is encoded into a high‐dimensional feature space via a Fourier feature map. Subsequently, to eliminate approximation errors in critical physical conditions, the solution is constructed through a rigorously designed function mapper that analytically enforces initial conditions as hard constraints. Crucially, we compute derivatives with respect to the input variable using the parameter‐shift rule—a quantum native gradient evaluation technique that avoids classical discretization. Unlike generic loss functions that target abstract data patterns, our loss function focuses on the differential equation residual and reference data. This design ensures that the trained model not only approximates the data but also intrinsically satisfies the physical constraint expressed by the DE itself. Our method is validated on several differential equations, including highly oscillatory ones, demonstrating its capability to tackle challenging nonlinear dynamics. Results demonstrate that our quantum model learns the solution, showing close agreement with a high‐precision classical numerical benchmark.

title: Accelerating noisy variational quantum algorithms with physics-informed denoising networks
authors: Jie Liu, Xin Wang
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms are promising for near-term quantum computing, but are severely limited by hardware noise and the substantial circuit overhead required for error mitigation methods such as Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE). We propose a Physics-Informed Denoising Network (PIDN) that reduces the cost of ZNE by learning a surrogate model of its optimization dynamics. By viewing the variational update as a trajectory in the parameter space, PIDN is trained to reproduce ZNE-mitigated expectation values and gradient directions while incorporating a physics-informed loss that preserves the gradient descent dynamics. Once trained, PIDN replaces repeated multi-noise evaluations with denoised expectation and gradient estimation directly from the current noisy observation and the historical trajectory, significantly reducing circuit executions. We benchmark the approach on the quantum approximate optimization algorithm for 3-regular graphs, Sherrington-Kirkpatrick, and transverse-field Ising models, as well as the variational quantum eigensolver for LiH, BeH2 and H2O. Across all tasks, PIDN attains performance comparable to ZNE, while reducing the number of circuit executions by a factor of approximately 4 to 6. Gradient cosine similarity with ZNE remains above 0.95 throughout training. Robustness analysis shows that PIDN fails only when ZNE itself becomes unreliable, and ablation studies confirm the necessity of the physics-informed loss for maintaining directional consistency. We further find that PIDN tracks optimization dynamics most accurately when the effective loss landscape retains strong low-frequency structure. These results establish PIDN as a scalable, resource-efficient strategy for noise-resilient variational optimization in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum regime.

title: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for a Frustrated Ising Model: Simulations and Quantum‐Hardware Experiments
authors: Seunghan Lee, Hunpyo Lee
abstract: A frustrated Ising model on a two‐dimensional square lattice is investigated using exact diagonalization and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), with additional benchmarks on IonQ quantum hardware. The dependence of the ground‐state sampling probability on the number of QAOA layers and the frustration strength is analyzed. In weakly frustrated regimes, the probability increases rapidly with a modest increase in the number of QAOA layers. In contrast, in the strongly frustrated regime, the probability remains limited even at larger circuit depths, reflecting the enhanced degeneracy and low‐energy competition induced by frustration. This behavior indicates that strongly frustrated, nearly degenerate regimes present a greater challenge for finite‐depth QAOA. Hardware‐oriented tests are also performed in the non‐frustrated regime, where ideal QAOA simulations reproduce the exact result. On a noisy simulator and IonQ quantum hardware, however, the probability decreases as the number of layers increases, showing that hardware noise still limits the achievable performance of deeper QAOA circuits.

title: Beyond Classical Computing: Exploring the Power and Potential of Quantum Computing
authors: Mehvish Malik, Riya Choudhary, Tasmia Ghazi, Abhilash Saxena
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Beyond Classical Computing: Exploring the Power and Potential of Quantum Computing Mehvish Malik Riya Choudhary Department of Computer Application Department of Computer Application Moradabad Institute of Technology, Moradabad , Moradabad Institute of Technology, Moradabad , India India E-mail :mehvishmalik467@gmail.com E-mail : riyabachhal907@gmail.com Tasmia Ghazi Abhilash Saxena Department of Computer Application Asst. Prof. Moradabad Institute of Technology, Moradabad , Department of Computer Application India Moradabad Institute of Technology, Moradabad , E-mail : tasmiaghazi2@gmail.com India E-mail : abhilashsaxenamit@gmail.com ABSTRACT: Quantum computing is a completely different approach to information processing that makes use of ideas from quantum mechanics, such as superposition, entanglement, and quantum interference. Unlike classical computers, which use binary bits to process data, quantum computers use qubits to represent and manipulate quantum states. These ideas enable quantum algorithms to provide significant computational benefits for certain classes of problems, including integer factorization, unstructured search, molecular simulation, and optimization. However, practical quantum computing is still constrained by issues like quantum decoherence, noise, gate errors, limited qubit scalability, hardware complexity, and the substantial overhead of quantum error correction.An overview of the basic ideas of quantum computing is given in this paper, along with an analysis of its benefits, drawbacks, and new uses in fields like cryptography, drug development, materials science, artificial intelligence, finance, and optimization. Future directions are also covered, such as the creation of useful quantum algorithms, fault-tolerant quantum computing, hybrid quantum-classical architectures, and quantum-resistant cryptography. The study highlights that quantum computing is a complementary computational paradigm whose usefulness depends on the interaction between quantum algorithms, hardware capabilities, and problem structure rather than a universal substitute for classical computing. Reliable quantum advantage for significant real-world computational problems may be made possible by ongoing developments in quantum technologies.
