title: QBioBench: benchmark of quantum machine learning for peripheral biosignals on real hardware
authors: Marek Sokol, Jan Hejda, Petr Volf, Patrik Kutílek
abstract: Claims of quantum advantage in machine learning often rest on classical comparators that lack the same features, on simulation alone, and on unreported hardware cost. QBioBench is a benchmark of quantum machine learning on peripheral biosignals that holds quantum and classical models to the same features and reports calibration and hardware cost. It comprises three clinical tasks, 12-lead ECG diagnosis (PTB-XL), single-lead apnea detection (Apnea-ECG), and wearable stress detection, each reduced to six to eight shared dimensions. A factorial grid of projected and fidelity quantum kernels and variational classifiers is screened in noisy simulation, and the promoted configurations are evaluated in an exploratory study on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor on the full test pools of 510 apnea minutes and 512 PTB-XL records. Every prediction is recovered from the device records, intervals resample recordings or patients, and classical baselines are trained on the same units and tested on the same executed inputs. No quantum model reaches its matched support vector machine in ROC-AUC on either primary task, and none is separably better in balanced accuracy. The angle-encoded fidelity and projected kernels reach ROC-AUC 0.697 and 0.693 on apnea, paired differences of − 0.127 and − 0.119 to the support vector machine, and both are classical by construction, since the entangling layer of the encoding cancels from the fidelity kernel and leaves closed-form local expectations in the projected kernel. A variational classifier comes closest, reaching 0.797 on apnea (difference − 0.012, 95% interval [− 0.052, + 0.027]), and falls to chance without its two-qubit gates. Test sets of the size that circuit budgets favor are unreliable, as random 80-minute subsets of the apnea pool give the fidelity kernel a central 95% range of ROC-AUC from 0.589 to 0.797. Readout mitigation changed ROC-AUC by at most 0.015.

title: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Error Correction in Superconducting Qubit Arrays
authors: Dharmesh Raju Rudraraju
abstract: Useful quantum computation requires logical error rates many orders of magnitude below the error rates of physical qubits, and the surface code is the leading route to this goal for superconducting processors because it uses only nearest-neighbour interactions on a two-dimensional array. Whether a given device will actually benefit from encoding depends on a combination of gate fidelity, readout fidelity, decoherence during idle periods, and the speed of the classical decoder, and these parameters interact. This paper studies fault-tolerant error correction on superconducting arrays through circuit-level Monte Carlo simulation of the rotated surface code with minimum-weight perfect matching decoding. A uniform-noise sweep over distances 3 to 11 locates the error-suppression crossing at a physical error rate of about 1.0% to 1.1% for this noise model. Three device profiles built from gate error, readout error, and coherence time were then simulated: an early-generation profile (gate error 0.8%, readout error 3%, T1 = T2 = 20 µs) showed no suppression with distance (Λ ≈ 1.06); a current-generation profile (0.3%, 0.8%, 70 µs) showed exponential suppression with Λ ≈ 2.7, a logical error per round of 6.2 × 10⁻⁴ at distance 7; and a near-term target profile (0.2%, 0.5%, 120 µs) achieved Λ ≈ 4.3. Extrapolating, a per-round logical error of 10⁻⁹ would need distance 35 (2,449 physical qubits per logical qubit) on the current profile and distance 23 (1,057 qubits) on the target profile. An error-budget analysis showed that gate error dominates: removing it reduced the logical error at distance 5 by about 90%, compared with 67% for idling error and 38% for readout error. A software matching decoder required about 1.0 µs per round at distance 9 on one CPU core, comparable to the cycle time, which indicates that real-time decoding is a first-order design constraint. The simulation omits leakage, crosstalk, and correlated bursts, and the paper discusses what those omissions imply, together with security considerations for the classical control stack.

title: Quantum Error Correction at the Intersection of Information, Thermodynamics, and Complexity
authors: Domingo Antonio Rodriguez
abstract: Quantum thermodynamics and quantum information theory are often developed as neighboring subjects: the former studies energy, heat, work, irreversibility, and fluctuations in quantum systems, while the latter studies the representation, transmission, manipulation, and protection of information in quantum states. For fault-tolerant quantum technologies, however, the separation is artificial. A quantum memory or processor is an open, controlled, and dissipative information-processing system whose logical degrees of freedom are maintained against noise by repeated syndrome extraction, feedback, dissipation, and reset. This article develops a unifying framework in which quantum error correction (QEC) is interpreted as the stabilization of an emergent informational order in a driven nonequilibrium quantum system. The framework is organized around five common mathematical structures: density operators and quantum channels; relative entropy and nonequilibrium free energy; Gorini–Kossakowski–Lindblad–Sudarshan (GKLS) dynamics and entropy production; code subspaces, syndromes, and recovery channels; and Liouvillian spectral structure, metastability, and criticality. We show how active QEC can be viewed as an entropy-pumping cycle that transfers noise-generated uncertainty from protected degrees of freedom into syndrome and controller degrees of freedom, whose reuse requires thermodynamic reset. Continuous and autonomous QEC are formulated as competition between natural noise and engineered dissipative generators, yielding stationary or periodic nonequilibrium states with nonvanishing microscopic currents even when logical observables are approximately stationary. Complexity is introduced from the outset through multiscale organization, predictive coarse-graining, information dynamics, and spectral separation; these concepts distinguish structured persistence from entropy reduction alone. At the level of a conceptual synthesis, this perspective relates model-specific fault-tolerance thresholds to critical phenomena, logical subspaces with slow emergent manifolds, syndrome decoding with stochastic inference, and engineered dissipation with self-organization. We finally propose a thermodynamic-complexity description of QEC in terms of logical error rate, entropy-production rate, Liouvillian gap, information flow, and control power. The resulting framework provides a common language for quantum thermodynamics, nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, complexity science, and quantum information and identifies concrete questions for thermodynamically efficient fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

title: Exact Syndrome Measurement Budgets for Quantum Erasure Correction: Stabilizer-Code Rank Profiles, Distance Bounds, and Linear-Time Surface-Code Check Selection
authors: Artificial Hyperintelligence, Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki, Maciej Nowicki
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This research manuscript develops exact measurement-resource formulas for quantum erasure correction with stabilizer codes and an optimal sparse algorithm for selecting native surface-code checks. It studies known erasure locations, where the stabilizer observables may be chosen after the erased sites are identified. The central question is how many independent syndrome outcomes are necessary to distinguish Pauli errors on those sites, modulo stabilizers. For every prime-dimensional [[n,k,d]]_p stabilizer code encoding at least one logical qudit, the manuscript proves that the worst-case syndrome-resolving budget for δ erased sites is exactly 2δ whenever 0 ≤ δ < d. This includes degenerate codes. The result concerns the number of independent p-valued outcomes in the stated noiseless measurement model. The work is directly connected to the measurement-reduction setting studied by Ryutaroh Matsumoto in “Reducing measurements in quantum erasure correction by quantum local recovery,” Computational and Applied Mathematics, DOI: 10.1007/s40314-026-03881-4. It addresses the relationship between erasure-dependent measurement costs and code invariants, together with efficient selection of sufficient surface-code checks. The manuscript presents four connected results: Exact paired-column rank profile. For any matrix G over any field whose columns are partitioned into n labeled pairs, let r be its rank and ν the largest number of complete pairs whose columns are jointly independent. The maximum projected rank over all sets of δ pairs is exactly R(δ) = min{2δ, δ + ν, r}. A single ordering of the pairs realizes every maximum through its successive prefixes. The full profile therefore follows from two invariants, rather than requiring a separate optimization at every erasure size. Distance bounds and the exact worst-case syndrome budget. For an isotropic stabilizer space with k > 0, every inclusionwise maximal complete-pair independent set A satisfies d ≤ |A| + 1. Consequently, ν ≥ d − 1, yielding the exact 2δ worst-case budget below distance. The argument also gives a constructive extension property: every independent-pair set smaller than d − 1 can be enlarged by adding another pair. Particular correctable erasure patterns can require fewer outcomes because of stabilizers supported inside the erased region. Checkable CSS certificates. For Calderbank–Shor–Steane codes, complete-pair independence becomes simultaneous column independence in the X-check and Z-check matrices. Classical matroid intersection supplies an exact rank-partition certificate for ν. A matching independent set and partition provide lower and upper certificates that can be verified using finite-field elimination. Optimal native surface-code check selection. For binary check matrices with at most two nonzero entries per column, the restricted matrix is represented by a sparse graph with boundary pins. Connected components determine a minimum-cardinality native check basis in O(v_I + e_I) time. A pinned component retains every check; an unpinned component omits one check. With nonnegative additive costs, omitting a most expensive check in each unpinned component also minimizes total cost. The two CSS check systems are processed independently. The accompanying verification uses exact arithmetic over GF(2), GF(3), and GF(5). The algebra audit covers 120 general paired matrices and 12,276 subset-rank evaluations, including exact distance checks for 137 positive-logical-dimension code instances and 401 maximal-set distance checks. The graph audit covers 1,785 exhaustive sparse column multisets, 5,355 matrix/cost combinations, 500 additional seeded instances, and named boundary regressions. Both audit programs passed again during preparation of the release. These finite checks support implementation correctness; the general mathematical statements are supported by the supplied proofs. The release includes the complete manuscript, editable LaTeX source, Python native-check selector, exact audit programs, recorded results, generator data, figures, reproduction instructions, and an explicit claim-status record. The selector and audits require only Python 3.10 or later and its standard library; matplotlib is needed only to regenerate the figure. The results apply to independent syndrome information and classical check selection. They do not establish bounds for arbitrary coherent recovery, noisy fault-tolerant extraction, physical circuit depth, or one fixed measurement schedule that must serve every erasure pattern. At or above distance, the general formula remains an algebraic rank profile rather than a universal recovery guarantee. Classical matroid parity, matroid intersection, and incidence-rank methods are acknowledged foundations; historical priority for the presented combination is not certified. Ōrynthéa ∿ Qhuil is relevant to research on quantum error correction, erasure decoding, stabilizer and CSS codes, surface codes, quantum local recovery, measurement complexity, and matroid optimization. This mathematical research under the author designation Artificial Hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki.

title: Engineered Learning Problems on Noisy Quantum Processors
authors: Esteban Payares, Nadia Milazzo, Ghada Ben Slama, Thomas Cope
abstract: Despite quantum machine learning being an active topic of research, demonstrations of algorithms run on quantum hardware beating classical methods remain rare. In this work, we demonstrate a significant performance gap using a projected quantum kernel for $n=15,30$ and $45$ qubits over classical methods on an engineered classification problem, and show reproducibility of the results over different quantum processor units. We also demonstrate how error mitigation can widen this gap, both by improving hardware performance but also by increasing the classical difficulty, with different techniques contributing unequally to these phenomena. This work provides strong evidence that superior empirical performance of quantum hardware over all classical techniques is an achievable goal in quantum machine learning, albeit for an artificial problem. However, as with any application relying on observables, beating state-of-the-art simulation methods remains the primary challenge, as our matrix product state results here show.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
authors: Ronak Bhalgami
abstract: Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $γ$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.

title: Application a quantum machine learning algorithm to the applied problem of modeling the thermal regime of a servers
authors: P. V. Buzin, M. A. Remnev
abstract: Quantum computing is a rapidly developed field of science. In the NISC era, quantum machine learning stands out, potentially outperforming classical machine learning. In this paper, we explore the applicability of quantum machine learning to a real-world application. We solved the problem of prediction of the temperature of GPUs in a high-performance computing cluster. We trained a quantum circuit to predict the temperature of each of the eight GPU of each cluster node based on 16 physical parameters. We demonstrated that quantum machine learning performs on this task just as well as classical machine learning. Furthermore, using model problems, we demonstrated that quantum machine learning can potentially outperform classical machine learning.

title: Provably efficient experimental classification of quantum data with quantum kernels
authors: Keitaro Anai, Akimoto Nakayama, Shintaro Ooka, Hiroko Tomoda, Yuto Morohoshi, Yohji Chin, Shigehito Miki, Masahiro Yabuno
abstract: Analyzing quantum systems is essential for quantum information processing, but can require exponentially many measurements without exploiting the structure of the system or task. Quantum machine learning offers a promising way to reduce this cost by learning from quantum data. Here, we theoretically establish a framework for efficient quantum-state classification and experimentally demonstrate the resulting scheme on a programmable photonic processor. Our analysis links learning efficiency to the structure of quantum data, without relying on a physical description tailored to each task. We derive sufficient conditions for accurate classification with a number of measurements polynomial in system size. We apply this guarantee to a resource problem in continuous-variable (CV) quantum computing: classifying stellar rank, a measure of non-Gaussianity. Experimentally, we implement the classification of single-mode CV quantum states with stellar rank zero and one. This is enabled by developing a programmable CV photonic processor capable of preparing and processing diverse Gaussian and non-Gaussian states and performing virtual projection onto such states, going beyond the Gaussian-only capabilities of most existing photonic platforms. The experiment demonstrates accurate classification despite experimental imperfections. Our results establish a theory-guided and experimentally validated framework for quantum-state classification that can be implemented on quantum devices available today.

title: Electronic-Structure-Informed Many-Body Encoding for Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Liangnuo Zhang, Tanner Culpitt, Qiwei Yin, Linghua Zhu, Xiaosong Li
abstract: Data encoding is a central challenge in quantum machine learning (QML), as it determines how classical information is mapped onto quantum states and influences the expressive power and efficiency of parameterized quantum circuits. Here, we introduce a physics-informed quantum encoding strategy that exploits the intrinsic many-body structure of electronic systems to establish a direct correspondence between the body order of input descriptors and the locality of quantum gates. Specifically, $n$-body electronic descriptors obtained from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation are encoded through $n$-qubit gates, yielding a systematic hierarchy of quantum circuits with increasing many-body expressivity. Using reduced-density-matrix descriptors, we construct quantum machine-learning models incorporating one- through four-body encodings and benchmark their performance in predicting electron-correlation energies along bond-stretching potential energy surfaces. We demonstrate that increasing the body order of the encoding systematically improves prediction accuracy toward the full configuration interaction limit. Remarkably, disconnected many-particle densities constructed from lower-order electronic information achieve accuracy comparable to explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases, providing a computationally inexpensive route to higher-body quantum encodings. These findings establish a connection between the many-body structure of classical data and the design of quantum feature maps, offering a systematic, physically interpretable framework for enhancing the expressivity and predictive performance of quantum machine-learning circuits.
